#3690. Dungeon Crawler Carl Isn't For Kids, But I Have A Pitch For How It Could Be

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Discover the latest entertainment updates and trailers.

Read reviews, interviews and deep dives on new releases.

Get the latest movie, TV and streaming news delivered to your inbox.

My Son And Students Have No Desire To See Avengers: Doomsday. Here's Why I Think That's Very Telling

I Can't Decide If I Love Or Hate Matt Dinniman's Dungeon Crawler Carl TV Show Update

The Red Rising Movie Is Going To Be Really Hard To Get Right, For A Few Reasons

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

I think this would be as big a hit as the books.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I'm buzzing through the Dungeon Crawler Carl series this year, and my 8-year-old daughter gets so jealous every time she sees it. She loves cats, dinosaurs, and adventure, so in her mind, there's no reason she shouldn't be able to read it as well or watch the upcoming series when it premieres for those with a Peacock subscription.

Of course, anyone who has read the books knows that they're hardly appropriate for a young audience. One would have to remove all the gore, swearing, and raunchy jokes for it to even begin to pass for most parents, which gave me an idea. What if Princess Donut was able to retell the events of DCC, but in the way she'd tell it to her dinosaur "child," Mongo?

I love the way Princess Donut treats and refers to Mongo like he's a child, despite the fact that he's a raptor regularly tearing their enemies to bits. She's always worried about him being traumatized, or "appalled," which got me thinking. It would be hilarious to read Donut recalling their past adventures to Mongo, and self-censoring the raunch along the way.

I just imagine my daughter laughing as I'd tell her about Princess Donut dancing in the club, zapping goblins with her laser vision, and going on side tangents about her hatred for Cocker Spaniels. It would still be the Donut we know from the books, but she's adjusting it all for the audience it's intended for.

I think it would be important to have that, rather than standard narration. Donut is a gem of a character, and I think introducing children to that early on would only encourage them to check out the novels in full when they're of age later in life.

I've often thought about Carl being the narrator in Dungeon Crawler Carl, and how much the story might change if it were anyone else narrating. The things they'd focus on, compared to him, and the things they'd notice well before he did. I'm of the opinion that Donut might have a more entertaining telling of it all, which is part of the reason she's just the best.

Matt Dinniman Can Thank Jeopardy! For Making Dungeon Crawler Carl's Success Feel Real For His Mom's Friends

All this to say, part of this plight is because I also want to see how much I'd enjoy Donut retelling the story, even if it were geared toward children. Plus, there are already spinoffs in the works, like the upcoming comic featuring Florin.

If I could get the ball rolling on making Princess Donut's Bedtime Stories For Mongo, I definitely would. I'm not the author, however, so Matt Dinniman, if you have time between making the rest of the series, perhaps consider this pitch to sell the fun of Dungeon Crawler Carl to the children?

In the meantime, I'll keep reading the stories, waiting for the new books and announcements related to the upcoming series. I have a feeling we're about to be overwhelmed with news about the franchise over the next year, but I promise I won't let it break me.

That’s why the scene that you asked about, we don’t want to be straightforward, but we are giving some suggestions that will probably reveal the state of the world in more comic books and other stuff. So there are discussions. There are discussions, but we are not setting one kind of ending.â

If held up to some scrutiny, the supposed V cameo is questionable. As some fans point out, the characterâs hairstyle isnât exactly the same as that of the âdefaultâ female V, and her cyberware isnât identical to that seen in 2077âs promo art, so even if the show were to be âcanonizingâ a specific version of V, this person doesnât look quite like the one you see on the gameâs box art. But ultimately, the show goes out of its way to not directly address Vâs fate, which can go in several directions depending on the playerâs choices.Â

âWhen we were creating Edgerunners [season one] and multiple comic books and board games, the canon was before the game, so we knew the state of the world.â he says. âAnd for the things post-game, it’s not that there are super-detailed canon things, but one important canon information is that Arasaka is weakened and that’s it. And it gives us a lot of opportunities to show the city in a different way.

But again, it’s not detailed. So it doesn’t make any of the endings canon. But the things that happened in the game could lead to that, whatever your choice was.â

I appreciate when creators for choice-driven franchises have this mindset, even if it means that future Cyberpunk projects canât incorporate characters who have multiple fates depending on the choices you make in 2077. Notably, Rogue, the owner of the Afterlife nightclub, makes a brief appearance in the first Edgerunners season, but is never seen in the second season, likely because she can die in one of the gameâs endings. It takes characters who exist in quantum states off the board, but it better allows all fans to enjoy a work without feeling like their choices are being portrayed as incorrect or invalid.

Cyberpunk 2 is currently in development at CD Projekt Red. Weâll see if it sticks to this principle and allows for all potential endings of the first game whenever it comes out.

#3688. A PUBG TV Show Is Coming To Netflix, Starring Donald Glover

Krafton and Netflix today announced a live-action TV show based on PUBG, and it will star Emmy-winner Donald Glover. In fact, Glover will not only star, but also direct, write, and executive produce the show, along with his brother, Stephen Glover, as writer and executive producer.

That's all Krafton had to say in its announcement, so it sounds like early days for the PUBG series. A PUBG animated series is on the way, too, from Castlevania's Adi Shankar.

Donald Glover is no stranger to video games, as he voiced Yoshi in The Super Mario Galaxy Movie this year. He also partnered with Ubisoft for a Far Cry 4 trailer.

Krafton has maintained that it sees PUBG not just as a game, but a connected universe, so it's only fitting that the company would get into TV.

PUBG is a battle royale game where players duke it out to be the last person or team standing. The game remains immensely popular, boasting more than 785,000 peak concurrent users on Steam alone today.

#3686. Artist With Music In GTA 6 Had No Idea About Any Of That

Cliff Richard is among the numerous famous artists who are lending their music to Rockstar's GTA 6, with Richard's classic tune "Devil Woman" appearing in the Netflix Extended Look. Richard, 86, didn't know about any of that, however, or that GTA 6 is a game and not a TV show.

Speaking to The Times (via Dexerto), Richard said of the partnership with Rockstar for GTA 6: "I was told this happened!" He said his nephew's sons told him about it. "They didn't realize I could sing like that," he said.

Richard was eventually made aware of GTA 6, but the singer doesn't know what that is. “The show is a game show, isn’t it, really? One of the biggest on TV?” he asked.

"Devil Woman" was originally released in 1976, so it's now 50 years old. Richard said he's pretty jazzed about the fact that young people will hear his music.

“People will no longer just say, ‘Oh, Cliff Richard is from the past,’” he said. “Because I am, but that past is what makes everything what it is today."

It was reported that Spotify streams of "Devil Woman" surged massively following the Netflix Extended Look in August.

For more on the music of GTA 6, be sure to check out GameSpot's rundown of all the songs in the game. The game's official score by Justice is releasing on December 11, and it will be available to stream and buy on physical media. The same cannot be said for the game itself, which is a digital exclusive. The game will be sold at retailers, but there is no disc: just a code in a box.

GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and the game's file size is gargantuan.

#3685. Sir Patrick Stewart, Theater Titan and ‘Star Trek’ Captain, Dies at 86

Sir Patrick Stewart, the beloved actor of stage, screen, and television, died Wednesday following “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia,” according to his representative, Kelly Bush Novak. The performer, best known in this and every other star system as Captain Jean-Luc Picard of the USS Enterprise, first appeared in the legendary role in September 1987. After seven seasons of television, four feature films, several video games, and site-specific interactive experiences, he returned to the character in the age of streaming, finally warping to retirement and surrounded by his crew, in January of 2020. He was 79 years old.

Stewart began his long and prosperous life in Yorkshire, England, as the youngest of three boys. His father was a World War II veteran, and, as Stewart discussed, suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder. Witnessing violence against his mother as a child, he said, led to Stewart’s later charity work for causes surrounding domestic violence.

He took theater classes in his youth and befriended a slightly older local lad, the actor-mountaineer Brian Blessed. He went on to study at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, a small, competitive conservatory that began with support from Sir Laurence Olivier, and boasts Daniel Day-Lewis, Olivia Colman, Jeremy Irons, Miranda Richardson, and many others as alumni.

In 1966, at age 26, Stewart joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, one of the most prestigious theater companies in Britain. During his time there, he appeared as the lead in The Life and Death of King John, as Oberon in A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and as Shylock in The Merchant of Venice, as well as more than 80 other roles, at the RSC’s main home in Stratford-upon-Avon, in London, and on tour. During this part of his career, he also appeared in supporting roles on television. The two most notable were the BBC production of I, Claudius, in which he played Emperor Tiberius’s double-crossing Praetorian guard Sejanus opposite a who’s who of British thespians (Derek Jacobi, John Hurt, Siân Phillips, Bernard Hill, John Rhys-Davies, Stewart’s old chum Brian Blessed, just to name a few), and as the evil mastermind Karla opposite Sir Alec Guinness in the adaptation of John Le Carré’s Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Smiley’s People.

As the 1970s turned to the 1980s, there were some film roles of note, including the part of Leodegrance in John Boorman’s Excalibur and Gurney Halleck in David Lynch’s version of Frank Herbert’s Dune. At one moment in the film, he leads a charge into battle clutching a cute li’l pug. (This same character, without the use of domesticated pets, was played by Josh Brolin in the more recent iteration.)

In 1986, with the original Star Trek still drawing good numbers in reruns and on videocassette, and with the feature films starring William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy doing well at the box office, Paramount thought it wise to update the series for television. Franchise creator Gene Roddenberry, who had worked on a “Phase II” Star Trek project in the late 1970s (which led, eventually, to the 1979 film) soon found himself at the drafting board for Star Trek: The Next Generation.

With a bridge crew of several writers and producers from what we now call The Original Series, the new version, set a little less than 100 years down the timeline, differentiated itself in a number of ways. The most notable change was reversing many of the attributes between the Captain and his first officer. Whereas Captain Kirk was a man of action, Captain Jean-Luc Picard was more cerebral, calculating, and cultured, sharing many characteristics with TOS’s half-Vulcan second-in-command, Mr. Spock. (TNG’s Commander Riker, played by Jonathan Frakes, was a bit more rough-and-tumble, and also likelier to woo interplanetary women.)

Patrick Stewart was not Roddenberry’s first choice (Belgian actor Patrick Bauchau, Yaphet Kotto, Roy Thinnes, and Dark Shadows’s Mitch Ryan were also in the mix). But in time, the not-too-well-known Shakespearean won out. When the casting was announced, a reporter suggested to Roddenberry that by the 24th century, in a time of faster-than-light starships, surely humankind would have found a cure for male pattern baldness, no? “No, by the 24th century, no one will care,” Roddenberry retorted, to the delight of bald guys everywhere.

As Stewart has repeated time and again, he took the gig thinking it was a doomed project, as no one would want to watch a retread of a classic. He figured he’d make a few quick bucks, secure some contacts, then head back to his real job on the British stage. He later called the decision to join Starfleet “the most important thing” in his career and his life.

But the first season of Star Trek: The Next Generation did not sail out of spacedock without some bumps. (Please don’t rewatch episode four, “Code of Honor,” if you know what’s good for you.) Though wanting to differentiate itself from TOS was the right move, some of the scripts could have used a little more derring-do, and the Picard character comes off at times as a little too cold. This unease was mirrored a bit behind the scenes, where Stewart experienced a little bit of culture clash.

Most of his fellow cast members were Americans who had worked in TV, like Night Court alum Brent Spiner. They were prone to goofing around in between takes, to the point that Stewart actually called a company meeting to scold them. It did not go over too well, but in time, Stewart began to loosen up. (This has now become a favorite thing for the gang to reminisce about during panels at Star Trek conventions, as everyone quickly became, and remained, good pals.)

The chemistry on the USS Enterprise (the Enterprise-D, if we’re getting specific) synched, and the show was a massive hit, making television history as a model for a successful first-run syndication. (If you happened to be a budding sci-fi nerd in central New Jersey that got both New York and Philly stations, it meant you could watch the show twice in the same weekend—not that I would know anything about that.)

From the first episode of TNG in late 1987, through a crossover to Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, and then feature films ending with 2002’s Star Trek: Nemesis, Stewart’s Picard saved the galaxy countless times with class, strength, and poise. Now is not the time to ask, “Who was the best captain?” But one can say, unequivocally, that Picard was the most quotable.

As TNG transitioned from television series to movies, Stewart, with more time on his hands, saw to it that his first role out of the gate would prove his range as an actor. As such, he costarred in the LGBTQ classic Jeffrey, based on Paul Rudnick’s play, as the flamboyant interior decorator Sterling. It may seem like nothing now, but, in 1995, to see a science fiction hero embracing a gay role was a bold move for progressivism.

In the 1990s, between Trek movies, Stewart played Captain Ahab in a USA Network adaptation of Moby Dick, led a one-man show version of A Christmas Carol, and played Prospero in The Tempest for the New York Shakespeare Festival. Then, in 2000, Stewart took on another clutch role in science fiction, Professor Charles Xavier in Bryan Singer’s version of X-Men.

As the schoolmaster/spiritual leader of Marvel’s mutant population, Stewart has played Professor X in eight features, most recently in Sam Raimi’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. It was through the X-Men universe that he and Sir Ian McKellen forged their delightful and public friendship, which led to the two performing in Waiting for Godot together, and McKellen officiating at Stewart’s wedding to jazz singer Sunny Ozell in 2013.

In 2006, Stewart made the first of several returns to the Royal Shakespeare Company to play Mark Antony in Antony and Cleopatra. His most recent turn on the boards at his old haunt was 2011’s The Merchant of Venice, once again playing Shylock, for director Rupert Goold.

But after a slew of television guest spots (from Frasier to Extras) and lending his voice to various projects including several led by Seth MacFarlane, an album with classical pianist Emanuel Ax, and a profitable Pontiac campaign, he found himself going back to the future. Star Trek: Picard launched in 2020 with a rocky first two seasons before the ship righted itself for a final, triumphant season in 2023, shepherded by Terry Matalas, that reunited Stewart with the cast (and the more than 35-year-old ship) from The Next Generation.

Patrick Stewart was not Captain Jean-Luc Picard, but he brought him to life. Over 178 episodes of TNG (and countless novels and comic books that you can pretend are episodes in your head, not to mention daydreams) the French space explorer with the English accent was a beacon of righteousness and leadership. He accepted input and analysis from anyone in his crew, but felt no obligation to consensus when his mind was made up. He was bookish but also sexy and liked to keep his tunic straight.

As Stewart aged, he increasingly recognized the degree to which Star Trek meant something to millions (and would defend those hardcore fans when needed!) In 2010 he was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II. He won a Grammy in 1996 for best spoken word album for children (a recording of Peter and the Wolf) and in 2008 was nominated for a Tony for a production of Macbeth. He was nominated for four Emmys, though none of them for Star Trek.

During the coronavirus pandemic, he initiated a series on social media in which he read a new Shakespeare sonnet each day. We’ll conclude here with the final one.

Apparently, the ad for the bra and panty set was viewed by over 40 million people on Instagram alone! On paper, that's quite a marketing feat. Also, Sweeney’s Birthday Boobs collection, which is currently back on the website, reportedly generated over $2 million in sales.

#3683. WoW: Forever Won’t Have Dead Servers

World of Warcraft: Forever will avoid repeating WoW Classic's mistakes and will have tools to prevent "dead" or "unsustainable" server rulesets, Blizzard said.

In the past, various WoW Classic servers became "dead" over time, as players either stopped playing or transferred to other servers. Those massive drops in population had major ramifications for players left on the server being unable to find groups for raids or dungeons, as well as for the server's economy and auction house. In some extreme cases, Blizzard gave away free character transfers so players could leave their "dead" servers behind.

While Forever is going a different route with what are essentially mega servers tailored around specific rulesets, some players might still have anxiety when it comes to picking a ruleset that will be a healthy place to play long-term. 

In the latest episode of the WoW: Forever podcast, Blizzard said it has tools it can use if a ruleset's population becomes "unsustainable." Senior game designer Josh Greenfield gave the example of Forever's separate RP and (newly added) RP-PvP server rulesets. He said there were initially concerns about splitting up the RP community, fearing that one or both of the rulesets wouldn't be able to stand the test of time. He said Blizzard now believes "it will be fine," but does have options should the worst happen. 

"If someday down the line, if something happens and one or both of those populations can't quite sustain themselves, we have options if we do need to say link up their auction houses or allow them to group for instanced content," Greenfield said.

Greenfield said it's not something Blizzard will jump to unless absolutely necessary and that it's committed to its current separate-ruleset path. Blizzard debated the idea of rulesets during Forever's development and discussed letting players from different rulesets group together for instanced content or combining auction houses.

However, it landed on wanting to maintain distinct communities, in part because of the differences in server economies when it comes to PvE and PvP rulesets, with Greenfield using an example of how it's easier to farm for gold and items on a PvE server. That in turn opened up debates on whether these cross-ruleset players would be able to trade items with one another and the need for other restrictions.

"Ultimately, these are different mindsets, these are different rulesets," Greenfield said the team decided. "Let's keep them separate for now. That is a part of original WoW that we don't want to just throw out completely. But I think the tech is set up in such a way that if we ever did really feel like we needed to make a change, we could do so."

He said those options are merely "levers we can pull if we need to" and that it's important for Blizzard to "stay flexible." That's good news, and will likely give players worried about choosing the wrong ruleset some relief. 

Blizzard is keeping busy in the handful of days left before Forever's launch. It previously detailed how it's making improvements to Forever's divisive layering system in time for release, and announced major changes to racial abilities. 

In a first for WoW, Forever will be fully playable on a controller. WoW executive producer and vice president Holly Longdale recently said Forever's controller support is a step towards WoW being playable "wherever you want" and "on whatever you want."

WoW: Forever arrives November 4. If you want to be ready for launch day, you can technically make up to three WoW: Forever characters right now.

#3681. Patrick Stewart Dies At 86

Beloved actor Patrick Stewart has died at the age of 86. The veteran of stage and screen was best known for his many years as Star Trek's Jean-Luc Picard and X-Men's Charles Xavier, though he also had notable roles in video games, including The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion and Castlevania: Lords of Shadow.

"We announce with grew sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dimentia" a statement on his official Instagram reads. "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace."

Stewart's role as Picard made him a household name, and following the conclusion of Star Trek: The Next Generation, he reprised the role in several Star Trek films as well as the series Star Trek: Picard.

Though best known for his live-action roles like Picard and Xavier, Stewart was also known for his iconic voice. Alongside the aforementioned games like Oblivion and Castlevania: Lords of Shadow (and its sequel), Stewart had voice roles in everything from American Dad to The Prince of Egypt. He also narrated the Ted movies, with his friend Ian McKellen taking over the role for the recent Ted series on Peacock.

#3680. Don’t Expect Destiny 3 At The Game Awards, Bungie Says

Destiny's future lies in its past, as Bungie is working to bring content from the infamous Destiny vault back to the game. Big plans are in place to rework fan-favorite campaigns like the Red War and Forsaken back into Destiny 2, and while that content won't be out for quite a while, Bungie has also detailed what you should not expect from the studio as the year winds down. Long story short: Don't expect to see Destiny 3 teased at The Game Awards.

"Knowing we are early in incubating our future and actively working on projects to bridge us to that new home, don't expect us to make a Destiny announcement at the TGAs this year, or to randomly drop a logo that sets the world on fire right away," head of product Josh Deane wrote.

Bungie says it secured an "initial greenlight to begin scoping the work" back in June, and a yet-to-be-revealed studio will help with its Destiny legacy content revival. To keep fans up to date, the studio has unveiled a progress bar, with which will signal when major milestones have been reached:

"Right now, we are in our pre-production, proof-of-work stage where we will ensure the process is working and hitting our quality bar as we port the legacy content. We expect this part of the process to last until roughly January/February. From that point we expect full production will be about 12 months. to fully complete the porting process. It’s a lot of content," Deane added.

What else is on the Destiny horizon? Deane said that players can look forward to "anchor" events, like a new celebration in Destiny 2 similar to Moments of Triumph, and Destiny Legacy, which Deane described as being "the whole experience" that needs to be served to where players are today. While the wording was vague, it sounds as if Destiny 1 content might come to Destiny 2. Deane said more information will be revealed next year, and both announcements will feature a new progress bar in February. Bungie also teased a mystery third project.

Overall, Bungie says it's on track with plans to unvault Destiny 2 content, has plans to celebrate the franchise, and is "building a new future" for Destiny. At the same time, Bungie is also continuing to make big changes to its extraction shooter Marathon, which launched earlier this year. March 2027 could be make or break for the game, as it continues to build out connected PvE, PvP, and PvEvP experiences, as well as options for solo players and crews.

#3679. Inside Airbnb.org’s Gala With Jimmy Kimmel, Charli xcx, and Brian Chesky

Nothing says billionaire-hosted gala quite like an olive sphere. What’s an olive sphere, you ask? Imagine a bite-sized gelatinous membrane filled with olive juice that is served on a tiny silver platter, and requires two servers—two!—to pass out: one to offer guests the savory blobs, and another to collect the discarded platters.

Before taking the stage at Milk Studios in Los Angeles on Wednesday night, Jimmy Kimmel walked past two olive sphere servers and a third handing out caviar. He told me he’d been listening to The Howard Stern Show on the drive over, and something so X-rated came on that he had to quickly turn down the volume when he pulled up alongside another car. Evidently, it put him in a silly mood by the time he welcomed guests to the first ever gala for Airbnb’s independent nonprofit—or “gay-la,” as he put it, “depending on your sexual orientation.”

Kimmel had been tapped to serve as master of ceremonies at the fundraiser for the home-sharing behemoth’s nonprofit, which was created in 2020 to provide free temporary housing to people displaced by disasters and other crises. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky announced a $500 million funding commitment over the next five years, allowing the organization to expand its services to families traveling for medical treatment and survivors of domestic violence.

Among the guests were people who had lost their homes in the devastating Eaton Fire in 2025. They shared a room with a group of people who presumably have little need for emergency housing: Charlize Theron, Serena Williams, Matthew McConaughey, Katie Couric, Joaquin Phoenix, Rooney Mara, Cynthia Erivo, and Demi Lovato, among others. It was a collision of two Los Angeleses: People who had lost everything, and people who wore bling worth as much as a house in Altadena.

Most of the men were dressed in tuxedos. Williams shined in a sparkly animal-print gown. Paul Bettany wore a black Chairman Mao-style shirt. Jaden Smith wore jeans, apparently missing the black-tie memo.

Kimmel, decked out in a perfectly tailored black tuxedo, had some ground rules as the emcee. Guests were expected to wash their dishes. No pets, except service animals, “which we know none of them really are.” “And absolutely no sitting naked on the furniture or on chef José Andrés.”

Chesky, who hard-launched his relationship with girlfriend designer Carly Helfrich on the red carpet, delivered his remarks with the cadence of Vanessa Bayer’s Jacob the Bar Mitzvah Boy Saturday Night Live character, staring down at the teleprompter positioned on the floor. “People are fundamentally good,” he declared, explaining that Airbnb’s business would have never worked otherwise.

On the red carpet, I asked Chesky whether the Trump administration had made it harder for his nonprofit to house people fleeing tragedy. “No, absolutely not,” he insisted, describing emergency housing as a cause that transcends partisan politics. This was a rather diplomatic answer from a man whose company once ran advertisements welcoming refugees in pointed opposition to Trump’s 2017 Muslim travel ban. But Chesky wasn’t taking the bait. “This is a very united kind of issue,” he said.

The night took an emotional turn when Kimmel talked about his son Billy’s three open-heart surgeries before introducing a video of a young boy receiving cancer treatments who was the beneficiary of the charity’s efforts. At that moment, the child, who was in attendance with his mom and grandma, stood on his chair and made a heart symbol using his two hands. The crowd went wild.

José Andrés, whose name appeared on the menu but who was rather noncommittal when asked whether he had actually designed it, insisted that the evening’s charitable mission was more than an excuse for Hollywood to get dressed up.

By dessert, Kimmel was shaking down the wealthy guests. “Don’t cheap out,” he warned, noting that anyone who could afford the new folding iPhone (which retails at roughly $2,000) could surely spare $110 to provide a family with a night of emergency housing. He also accidentally revealed the evening’s secret musical guest: Charli xcx.

“Oh shit!” he exclaimed, realizing his mistake. “Okay, it’s not a surprise anymore.”

Charli eventually took the stage, with will.i.am and Greta Lee dancing from the front row. “That was soooooo good,” Lee said to me on the way out.

And although the set wasn’t particularly long, Charli rocked it, sending heads banging everywhere. She got the Hollywood room doing what it does best: partying for a cause.

Star Wars Jedi: Survivor was released back in 2023 and is a very good game with some fun Easter eggs and references hidden in it. But one secret remained hidden, even after the developer who included it in the third-person action game teased fans online about it. Now, someone has finally found the secret after inputting the Konami code in a menu.

Back in 2025, Respawn UI director Jordan DeVries posted cryptically on social media about a secret buried in Jedi: Survivor that players had yet to find. “Imagine shipping a (submitted, approved) UI easter egg in your game that no one has yet noticed or found,” posted the developer last year. That kicked off some players digging around the Soulslike Star Wars sequel for this hidden secret. But nobody seemingly found it until now, according to DeVries.

On November 1, DeVries shared on social media that user TowerBunga on Twitter had found the Easter egg after inputting the famous Konami code in the Force upgrade menu in Jedi: Survivor. And once entered correctly, a giant space frog appears and eats a strange moon in the sky. It’s a bizarre but amusing secret that took three years to find.

Kudos to the Jedi Survivor team on a *very* well hidden easter egg https://t.co/aB2Za99XKc pic.twitter.com/rWGa5ca3do

Over on Reddit, DeVries responded to the news that the well-hidden secret had been discovered. “It’s been a long three years…”

I always love when fans find secrets and Easter eggs in games many years after release. Only a few more weeks remain before Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, and while Rockstar Games recently lifted the lid on its big open-world sequel, that's still not enough. There's definitely value in approaching a game with as little knowledge as possible so that you can enjoy any potential surprises, but we're not those people.

Instead, senior video producer Jake Dekker decided to grab a folder of high-resolution GTA 6 screenshots--a whole 99 of them, not including the promotional images for GTA 6's Ultimate Edition--and analyzed dozens of them for hidden details. Here's what he found in the first part of his JPEG investigations.

Unsurprisingly, GTA 6 is loaded with small details, callbacks to previous games in the series, and some technical wizardry. There are frazzled beards, the subtle effects of gravity, realistic scars, and even NPCs showing what the ravages of time and a tropical climate can do to flesh, proving GTA 6's location of Leonida is packed to the gills with small touches. One of the best hidden details in these screenshots is the hard currency: Every dollar bill is printed right in the United States of Paranoia. Hey, it's legal tender in a video game!

For more GTA 6 investigations, you can check out several more videos from the team. #3675. EA Reportedly Chose An Unannounced Star Wars Game Over BioWare’s Next Mass Effect

EA recently announced it was shutting down BioWare, ending a studio responsible for multiple hit games over 30 years. According to a new report, EA's decision was driven by economics, as it had to choose between funding a new Mass Effect and backing the safer bet, Star Wars: Battlefront 3.

Bloomberg's Jason Schreier reported that EA had to choose between two costly projects, and with the added pressure of paying off $18 billion in leveraged debt after its sale to a business consortium and Saudi Arabia's investment fund, Battlefront 3 made more financial sense. To add insult to injury, Battlefront 3 isn't even in development yet, and it hasn't been officially announced.

"They chose to invest in Star Wars and shut down BioWare as a result, said the people familiar, speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to talk to the press," Schreier wrote. "Star Wars: Battlefront 3 has not even begun development yet, but EA executives saw it as a less risky, more predictable bet than a new Mass Effect--and the publisher behind Battlefield has always been more comfortable with shooters than RPGs."

Schreier added that "corporate politics" may have also influenced the decision, as one of the studio's key advocates, senior EA exec Laura Miele, was reportedly sidelined when EA Sports veterans David Tinson and Cam Weber were promoted. BioWare also experienced several flops over the last decade, with Mass Effect: Andromeda, Anthem, and Dragon Age: The Veilguard failing to meet sales expectations, which further influenced EA's decision to shut down the studio.

After BioWare's closure, more details on its Mass Effect project have emerged. A trailer for Mass Effect: Universe was posted online last week; the game's details made it sound like a sci-fi version of John Wick, and video game composer Austin Wintory shared an experimental score as part of his Mass Effect audition tape.

Zendaya, Timothée Chalamet and Florence Pugh have spent enough time promoting the Dune franchise together that you would think they have the group-photo routine down by now. Apparently, all it takes is one camera, one slightly cramped set, and Zendaya trying to maneuver everybody into position to throw that theory out the window. The entire Dune Part 3 cast reunited to celebrate Denis Villeneuve's first two Dune movies heading back to theaters, and the resulting video is wonderfully awkward.

In the video, posted by the official Dune movie Instagram account, Zendaya directly addresses a social media user's question about the first two installments possibly heading back to theaters. In the process, the actres nearly loses control of the whole operation, backs straight into Pugh and somehow leaves Chalamet looking like the guy who accidentally wandered into someone else's photo. Seriously, check out the post below, because you barely get a glimpse of the lead actor's eye, let alone his whole face:

The clip -- which also features Robert Pattinson, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy -- starts simply enough, with Zendaya trying to pull everyone together for the shot. Then she backs up, bumps into Pugh, and has to readjust while laughing through it all. Meanwhile, Chalamet is practically being edited out of his own franchise reunion. It's incredibly silly, especially given how serious these three usually look in the movies.

Of course, the timing makes sense, though. Dune and Dune: Part Two return to IMAX this month ahead of Dune: Part Three's release. IMAX has formally announced that fans can catch both movies as a double feature on November 13, followed by individual screenings from November 14 through November 18. That's already a pretty good excuse to spend nearly six hours back on Arrakis. So Warner Bros. is sweetening the deal considerably.

Every screening will include exclusive footage from Dune: Part Three, which hits the 2026 movie calendar on December 18. That makes the re-release considerably more interesting for fans who have already seen the first two movies. And, if that footage is just nearly as impressive as what's been screened thus far, fans will have more incentive to grab their tickets and sandworm popcorn buckets for the threequel.

Villeneuve's latest film is a book-to-screen adaptation of the second novel in Frank Herbert's series, Dune Messiah, and brings Chalamet, Zendaya, and Pugh back as Paul Atreides, Chani, and Princess Irulan. The cast also includes the aforementioned Momoa, Pattinson and Taylor-Joy along with Rebecca Ferguson, Javier Bardem and franchise newcomer Robert Pattinson.

So Much For Zendaya Taking A Break After Dune 3

We've already gotten some tantalizing information about the movie, including Chalamet saying he approached playing Paul differently this time around. The actor previously explained that while filming his final Dune movie, he dug deeper into tiny details of Paul's world than in the previous installments.

There are also plenty of reasons to keep an eye on Chani and Irulan. Zendaya became much more central to the story in Dune: Part Two, while Pugh's Princess Irulan should have considerably more to do as the story moves into Messiah. The third entry is set to be the final movie in Denis Villeneuve's critically acclaimed sci-fi trilogy, so we can probably expect one heck of an ending. Let's hope the film concludes a lot less awkwardly than this Instagram video.

But, before we get to the finale, audiences get another chance to see the first two movies in IMAX, plus a preview of what's coming next. While we wait, you can also revisit the first two Dune movies at home with an HBO Max subscription.

#3673. A 21-Year Veteran Of Xbox Who Is Suddenly No Longer At The Company Says She Has ‘Serious Concerns’ About The Whole Process

Helen Chiang had been at Microsoft since 2005. She spent over a decade overseeing Minecraft, the company’s most important gaming franchise, and survived this year’s big Xbox “reset” with a promotion to the role of the gaming division’s chief operating officer. Barely three months later, she’s suddenly out at the company she called home for more than two decades, a development which generated tons of speculation about whether she was fired or not. Chiang now says she’s breaking her silence to set the record straight.

“There has been some speculation about my abrupt departure from Microsoft, including claims that I was ‘fired for a policy violation,'” she wrote on LinkedIn, referencing a report last month from Eurogamer alleging she was fired for a “policy violation.” “Thatâs not accurate and while I wonât turn this into a play-by-play, silence should not be mistaken for agreement. What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize. Itâs important to me to set the record straight.”

Chiang went on to say that she never leaked confidential company information to the press or went outside of company-authorized communication channels. She said she also did not leave the company for a competitor, nor did she “engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity.” Chiang added that her past results and record speak for themselves, and that she did not leave the company because she’d been passed over for a bigger role. The chief operating officer role had not been something she’d lobbied for.

“I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others,” she wrote. “Those standards only mean something when theyâre applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously. I share this because I donât want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. Thatâs the legacy I hope to leave behind.”

“We donât discuss individual personnel matters,” a spokesperson for Microsoft previously told Kotaku regarding Chiang’s departure. “Weâre grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well.”

The sudden move comes amid a massive reorganization of Xbox that has seen massive layoffs and studio divestitures as Microsoft seeks to rebuild the platform while also improving its bottom line. As chief operating officer, Chiang would have had a central role in helping to restructure and better optimize the tech giant’s gaming business ahead of the next console generation, Project Helix, which is reportedly set to arrive in 2028. Though the Xbox veteran set out to clear the air amid much of the recent speculation about her departure from the company, it’s still not clear what exactly happened.

“For the first time, we are establishing a Chief Operating Officer with end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services,” Xbox CEO Asha Sharma wrote back in July. “Helen Chiang has been promoted to this role and will report directly to me. Over nearly two decades at XBOX, Helen has helped build some of our most important businesses, from XBOX Live to leading Mojang and the Minecraft franchise. She will bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results.”

Sharma later told The Wall Street Journal “clarity is kindness” when describing the tough choices she was making to set the stage for an ambitious future. “Clarity is Kindness” is also how Chiang began her LinkedIn post today. âThis is not how I ever imagined my story here would end,” she wrote. “And it is not the whole story.â

#3672. New Assassin’s Creed Game Is Out Now, If You Don’t Mind Being Board

If you thought there wasn't going to be a new Assassin's Creed game this year, think again. It's not a video game, but Assassin's Creed: Animus is out today, turning the series into an adventure-style board game for 1-4 players.

A competitive game that pits players against each other as they explore distinct eras from the video games, Assassin's Creed: Animus features four protagonists to choose from in its standard edition: Eivor, Ezio, Altair, and Connor. The Collector's Edition, meanwhile, expands to 10 eras and features 16 protagonists, adding game characters like Edward Kenway, Jacob and Evie Frye, and Kassandra.

You and up to three of your friends (or you alone) work to complete objectives across these eras, taking down assassination targets in the way you see fit via "memory blocks." Whether you go in with your sword drawn or engage in a sneakier approach is up to you.

The standard version of Assassin's Creed: Animus is available to order now for $65, while the limited Collector's Edition costs $229. Alongside the extra characters and eras, this version comes with a storage box, acrylic tokens, a metal Piece of Eden, a cloth token bag, "special event cards," and an Animus Card Holder.

#3671. Actor Keith McDermott on Robert Wilson’s Legacy and Ghostwriting His Memoir: “I Saw a Robert Wilson Play and It Changed My Life”

Over the more than 50-year period of his career, Wilson was arguably the most produced American theater director in Europe, if not the world. His aesthetic style has permeated European theater and opera culture to the extent that few directors have remained uninfluenced by what is commonly referred to as the “Wilsonian” use of lighting, set design, and performance style. However, he is not well-known in his own country.

The Robert Wilson productions that have reached the United States are some of the most iconic stage works of the 20th and 21st century: Einstein on the Beach and Lohengrin at the Metropolitan Opera House and at least 10 full productions at Brooklyn Academy of Music. Even in New York, Wilson’s artistic home, and even among artists, a not uncommon response at the mention of his name is “Should I know who that is?”

However, there is another response from New Yorkers of my generation, those of us living here when the city was at the artistic peak of the ’60s and ’70s, when Balanchine oversaw the New York City Ballet, Joe Papp headed the Public Theater, Andy Warhol ran The Factory, and apartments were affordable. That response, my response, is “I saw a Robert Wilson play and it changed my life.”

In 1975, a friend offered me a free ticket to a Broadway play. The title was A Letter for Queen Victoria, and I assumed I was in for a fusty historical drama, but as a young actor pursuing a commercial career, I never passed up an opportunity to see a play, especially if it was free.

Robert Wilson's A Letter for Queen Victoria.

The play began before the houselights went down as a young man and woman in ordinary dress stood in front of the curtain on opposite sides of the stage slowly turning in place. Nothing about their slow, hypnotic movement suggested “performance” until the houselights began to dim. Still turning, they raised their hands from their sides. Their palms, pressed in turmeric, became a blur of orange as their revolutions increased in speed and the curtain rose. The cast included the director’s grandmother as Queen Victoria, and a neurodivergent teenager, Christopher Knowles, whose nonacting presence broke the fourth wall, as he shielded his eyes from the stage lights to gaze into the house.

Audience members left in droves. A woman shouted something about child abuse on her way to the exit. But I sat mesmerized as the play evolved through a series of scenes unconnected by narrative or plot, fantastic in design, exquisitely lit, and often extraordinarily slow. Those of us who stayed until the end leapt to our feet, applauding and cheering for the actors, call after call. I stumbled from the theater into the city night feeling as if I had fallen in love.

My enthusiasm for that play led to both a professional and personal involvement with Bob (as anyone who knows him calls him). As a performer, I have appeared in five Wilson productions in various parts of the world and understudied him in a one‐man show. As a writer, I published an article about his chair collection and a roman à clef in which a character based on Bob pretty much takes over the book. In addition to our working relationship, Bob, a fellow Texan, has been my friend for over 50 years, and early in 2023 he asked me to ghostwrite his memoir.

Our sessions began formally at the Watermill Center, “a laboratory for the arts and humanities” on the South Fork of Long Island, founded by Bob in 1992. He had an apartment there where he stayed when he was in town. Assuming we’d work through his life chronologically, I came armed with questions about his childhood in Waco, Texas, his parents, and his schooling. But later, transcribing our recorded sessions, I cringed at my attempts to get Bob back on topic as he segued into a tale about absentmindedly depositing his airline ticket into a mailbox, then trying to board the plane with the postcards he had meant to mail, or a harrowing memory of six weeks spent in a Greek prison for a bit of hash discovered by airport security. My interruptions only spoiled the spontaneous flow of Bob’s thoughts.

Bob was a storyteller. Everyone who knew and worked with him was familiar with his stories, often told in a regional Texas twang and often more than once – and occasionally with a remarkable addendum. For instance, I knew that in his 20s, while working as a recreational therapist at the Goldwater Memorial Hospital for the terminally ill, Bob had choreographed a “dance” for quadriplegic patients in iron lungs, tying Day-Glo strings to mouth sticks they used to turn book pages that connected to mobiles hung from the ceiling. But in the retelling, I learned that Bob, after attending an Otis Redding concert, had persuaded the singer to come to the ward to accompany his quadriplegic dancers.

Once we gave up the chronological approach and Bob, unburdened by the need to deliver “The Story of My Life,” began to think in terms of “Life Stories,” our process relaxed and stories flowed. In addition to scheduled sessions, I could collect them everywhere, because Bob told them everywhere: at dinner parties, in the car, over the coffee and English muffins I began to deliver early each morning, or on our daily golf cart trips around the Watermill grounds. I always met him armed with my tape recorder.

A story he told frequently, both publicly, in interviews, and privately, was about seeing a policeman about to strike a young boy and intervening. From the sounds the boy made, Bob realized he was deaf. The boy, Raymond Andrews, was diagnosed as ineducable, but Bob realized he simply relied on visual cues not words. At 27 Bob became Raymond’s legal guardian and enrolled him in a school for the deaf. Raymond flourished in the creative community Bob created at his Spring Street loft (in SoHo before it was SoHo). Using Raymond’s drawings and his own observations of the boy, Bob created Deafman Glance, a seven-hour silent opera that signaled his European renown.

Bob told many stories about Jessye Norman, but the one that always brought him and his listeners to tears was of the great singer attempting to get through a Winterreise concert just after 9/11. During the third song, Norman began to cry and had to stop singing. When she regained control, she stood for 10 minutes, motionless, in silence, while the audience wept.

Bob’s vast social network also included socialites and celebrities, and those stories are filled with irresistible gossip: Marlene Dietrich divulged the name of the only contemporary American performer she completely admired (spoiler alert: it was Tina Turner); Diana Vreeland swallowed vials of cod liver oil to act as a buffer for vodka before an evening out; Samuel Beckett claimed that his lead actress in Happy Days was so brilliant because she didn’t understand a word she said.

In June of 2025, Bob went to Lithuania to stage rehearsals of a new production and then to Ljubljana, Slovenia, to direct Tristan and Isolde. When he was away, he sent me emails with story topics for our next session: “Ask me about my boat trip in the Middle East with Helen de Rothschild,” “Ask me about Louis Malle offering me the lead in Pretty Baby.”

When Bob returned to Watermill in July, we were to meet for final interviews, although by that time, I had all the material needed for the book. Shortly before my travels, I received a message that Bob’s health had declined, and he would be unable to see me. He died a week later on July 31 in his Watermill apartment.

Months after Bob’s death, I was still listening to and transcribing our taped conversations. In one conversation, recorded when we were having dinner at an Indian restaurant, Bob was telling me a story about being dressed as Santa Claus and handing out presents in Bali, where he spent every Christmas. Suddenly, he stopped mid-sentence and after a short silence, said, “I love you, Keith.”

I love you too, Bob, you changed my life.

THE SPACE BEHIND THE FACE, a memoir by the visionary theater director and visual artist, Robert Wilson, is published by Penguin Press and arrives on November 3.

Witney Carson just blew viewers away by competing on this season of Dancing with the Stars during her second trimester of pregnancy. Since she and her partner, Guillermo Rodriguez, were eliminated during Super Bowl night, Carson has been officially putting her focus on preparing for the arrival of her third baby. But that didn’t stop her from showing up for this year’s family Halloween costume. The category was Avengers, and she was electrifying as “Fat Thor”.

The beauty of Halloween is it’s a day where a person can be anyone or anything. For this year's holiday, Witney Carson’s two boys dressed up as Spider-Man and Captain America, and the DWTS pro opted for the Avengers: Endgame iteration of Chris Hemsworth's God of Thunder, who's best known as “Fat Thor” by fans. Check out the amazing costume reveal:

A post shared by Witney Carson McAllister (@witneycarson)

This is so good! In general, it's also so funny and clever for her to channel the version Thor who has let himself go and lost his abs following defeat at the hands of Thanos. I mean, she essentially found the perfect hack for walking around her neighborhood with her kids while in PJs and a robe while six months pregnant, and matching with them. And, by the looks of it, fans are loving it. Just check out these comments:

It seems that as a pregnancy costume, “Fat Thor” has been quite popular as of late, and I love to see it. Funny enough, Hemsworth actually previously said that putting on the fat suit for Endgame actually helped him understand his own wife’s pregnancies better. When the Australian actor wore the suit during the film shoot, people would apparently come up to him and rub his stomach.

Elsewhere, this Halloween has had the likes of JLo going as Barbarella and Zendaya completely channelling Halle Berry, but it’s hard to top how these Avengers Assemble! Here’s another post of the Carson McAllister family all together on their last Halloween before they become a party of five (due to another baby boy arriving) in a few months:

A post shared by Witney Carson McAllister (@witneycarson)

As someone who loves a DIY costume, I find it especially great how attainable this group costume is and can appreciate that it’s also comfy and cozy for everyone involved. I never would have thought about it when Avengers: Endgame came out, but how cool is it that Thor has inspired pregnant women like Witney Carson to perfectly fit into an Avengers lineup with their family without having to wear a skin-tight suit?

While we don’t expect to see Witney Carson much in the rest of DWTS Season 35, new episodes air every Tuesday night at 8 p.m. ET (with the exception of this week’s airing on Monday). They are available to stream live and catch on demand with a Disney+ subscription.

#3668. Developers, Creators, And Fans Remember BioWare: ‘I’ve Been Trying To Replicate That Feeling For Almost My Whole Life’

When I initially put out a call for fans, developers, creators, and media to reach out to me with stories about their experiences with BioWare, the now-shuttered developer of some of the most beloved western RPGs of the past 30 years, I was frankly overwhelmed by the outpouring of responses from people who had a story to tell. I was so overwhelmed, in fact, that I was only able to use a fraction of what showed up in my inbox for this collection of memories, praise, righteous anger, and mourning. Whether they were old heads who had been playing BioWare games since the days of Shattered Steel and the original Baldurâs Gate or folks who fell in love with the Edmonton studioâs work through Mass Effect and Dragon Age, itâs clear that BioWareâs games left an imprint on fans that has outlived the company itself.

(Submissions have been lightly edited for style and clarity.)

If BioWareâs games have proven anything, itâs that everyoneâs story has its own unique beginning, and thatâs reflected in how its fans came to know its work through so many different points of entry.

My first BioWare experience was with the first two Baldur’s Gate games. I wasn’t much of a PC CRPG gamer in 1998 but BG1 just absolutely blew me away with what, at the time, felt like endless options for character customization, the broad sweep of the story that felt like a true investment in the Dungeons & Dragons tabletop I had been playing for only a few years at that point – and the Forgotten Realms where I cut my teeth as both player and Dungeon Master – and the amazing writing on the characters. This doubled in effect when BG2 arrived in the year 2000, and between those two games I lived in BioWare’s Forgotten Realms like it was a second home. â Phil Morgan, host of Deleted Saves Podcast

I swiped Baldur’s Gate from my dad when I was nine – he wasn’t into role-playing games and I have no idea why he had it, but it clicked immediately for me and I spent hours trying different types of characters, killing NPCs I shouldn’t have, and getting to know that world. It blew me away when I realized I could recruit different party members in Baldur’s Gate, and that it had an impact on the story. It meant I could replay the game over and over and make different choices to see what would happen, and that became something BioWare was known for. â Chuck Zimmerheld, Giant Bomb

Years [after playing KOTOR], my next experience was attending a Video Games Live concert with conductor Jack Wall, who was the composer for the first two Mass Effect games, and that’s where I first heard the Mass Effect theme. That song was so beautiful to me that I knew I had to play the game it had come from. I didn’t have a lot of money at the time, but I scrimped and saved and got my brother to go half in with me on an Xbox 360. I bought a used copy of Mass Effect before we’d even gotten the Xbox, I was so excited. It blew my mind AGAIN in so many ways. A shooter RPG. A unique space adventure not tied to the IPs I’d enjoyed all my life. I fell in love with all of the unique characters and the idea of a space-faring future where humans weren’t the dominant species felt so fresh and exciting. â Jeremy Greco, BioWare fan

My first experience with BioWare, and one of my earliest memories of gaming in general, was watching my older brother play Dragon Age: Origins in 2010 on our PS3. I was frankly terrified watching it as an 8 year old. To this day, seeing the Darkspawn still conjures up a deep-rooted childhood fear of the Blight sweeping across the land. I remember playing through the game a few years later, thinking I was braver, and being absolutely horrified by the Circle Mage origin. I mean the Harrowing was insane to me. I think it took me maybe a week of going back and forth to finally finish that prologue. That game absolutely set the bar for me of dark heroic fantasy and hugely influenced my taste in games and stories ever since. â Jerram Carr, junior narrative designerÂ

BioWareâs games were the origin story for many developersâ own careers. You can trace the influences and inspirations that shaped the work of many designers and writers back to the worlds the company created.

I think the most impactful game for me was Dragon Age: Origins. I was in college excited for a new Bioware game, but at the same time struggling with accepting myself as a gay man. I had the chance to flirt with Alistair as a man, and while he ultimately rejected me, he helped me feel seen; that it was okay to be gay. I remember crying on the floor, moved that a 3D character had given me so much grace to be myself. I remember wanting to make games so people could have moments like I did. Moments to accept ourselves and see ourselves reflected positively.

When I did get the chance to make queer people feel seen in Destiny it felt like I was helping pay back the gift the DA:O team had given me. I even talked about it in the Bungie weekly blog.Â  â Nigel Davis, senior producer at Entangled Publishing, formerly at Bungie

The creators at BioWare pushed the industry forward with player choice in games. Optional party members, loyalty quests, morality systems, and huge choices with multi-game impacts. RPG’s aren’t the same without them. â Chuck Zimmerheld, Giant Bomb

Few studios can say that they changed the way genres are made. BioWare can. Thereâs an entire generation of developers and narrative designers that work in the industry because they were inspired by the games BioWare made across a 30-year run that largely produced classic after classic after classic. The systems the folks at BioWare designed worked their ways into other games in ways that you could see and interact with. My buddies and I used to joke that BioWare invented the wheel because Mass Effectâs dialogue wheel felt like it was everywhere after the original game was released. â Will Borger, journalist and consultant

For me, it all traces back to those first two Baldur’s Gate games. There’s a direct line from those to my work today, including my writing on Pacific Drive, where I’ve tried to remember to highlight the everyday as well as the extraordinary, to add jokes as well as drama, to imagine how even the smallest details shape the most fantastical world. And to remember that, if you hide a little secret somewhere, players will always, always find it. I think BioWare understood that players weren’t taking the roles of adventurers, but players are adventurers, always on the hunt for the next clue, character or collectible, and they really enjoyed indulging them as much as they could. â Paul Dean, writer, Pacific Drive

My time in development is not spent creating digital worlds (currently), I design mechanics for expressing actions and desires in the space of a world full of character interactions and player agency. Game theory is a lived experience because I love games, I play them, and they shaped me. Dungeons & Dragons is in some ways closer to my style of product, but it is not what I think of when I am writing. I’m thinking of Liara T’soni, Captain Anderson, Canderous Ordo, Jolee Bindo, Hawke, Varric, Blackwall, Dorian, Solas. â SalubriousBrew, pen and paper RPG developer

I wasnât a fan of much as a kid. I didnât like Star Wars, or RPGs, or games that looked older than me. I didnât even play KOTOR on a half decent console: my first playthrough was on my dadâs iPad! So when I, dorky Nigerian kid, got this weird-looking rpg on a whim, I couldnât have imagined that, well over a decade later, itâd be one of the main reasons I aspire to one day do narrative design for a video game.

Itâs not like I grew up reading stories about millionaire game writers or anything, lol. Iâm not in it for the money. I just think that making something that means to someone else what KOTOR meant for meâthatâd be pretty damn cool. â Mo, BioWare fan

BioWare was the first studio to show me that a game can tell a worthwhile story, that a game can make you cry and make you laugh. These days, I’m making games about fart jokes, but there’s a throughline from Garrus talking about “popping the heatsink” and Kasumi inspecting Shepard’s underwear drawer to what I do now. Other studios left more of a mechanical impact on my game development sensibilities, but BioWare showed me that games could be more than the sum of their parts. â Mira Swor, engineer at Jackbox Games

BioWareâs approach to roleplaying, and the prowess with which the studio pulled it off, became things many RPGs would aspire to replicate in the years that followed, and the opportunity its games provided to explore the perspectives of different types of people was more far-reaching in its impact than even the studio might haveÂ  expected, particularly when it chose to highlight queer characters and stories.

As a trans lesbian growing up closeted in a very rural, very conservative, very religious household in Florida, my opportunities to engage with queerness were deeply limited. When I went off to college, I was free to do what I wanted for the first time. My first week on campus, I walked down to the campus GameStop and bought Mass Effect 1, Mass Effect 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Dragon Age II all at once by trading in some old games. I didnât really do it because I knew they were queer games. I just liked scifi and fantasy.

I popped in ME1 first. I had heard a lot of people praise Jennifer Haleâs performance as FemShep. That was enough of an excuse to bypass my repression, letting me create a female avatar for the first time ever. That alone was a really big deal for me, but the real paradigm shift happened the first time I realized I could flirt with Liara. I remember pausing at the choice for quite some time, feeling sick to my stomach with anxiety. Iâd been raised to believe that the feeling inside me that wanted to explore a lesbian romance was of the devil, a threat to my immortal soul. But ultimately, I forged ahead.

In a very real way, that was the first time I ever chose my burgeoning queerness. Iâd experienced queer feeling before, but always passively. This time I passed a threshold. â Saoirse Stone, BioWare fan, critic, author, Editor-In-Chief at Stone Freedom

Even just having queer characters and the ability to be queer in a mainstream AAA game without it being a joke resonated and reverberated so far through my life that it helped open my closet door just a little more. It was because of Mass Effect and Dragon Age that I got to explore sexuality and gender in a way that felt safe – in the comfort of my dorm room, sure, but also in the comfort of the worlds themselves. To see a gay relationship being celebrated or a trans person existing in the world as just a normal thing – it helped build my courage and eventually landed me where I am today: happy and comfortable in my body and in who I love. There aren’t many games that can say they helped people do that. â- Patrick Quinn, BioWare fan

My first experience with Bioware was Knights of the Old Republic. I grew up a big fan of the franchise and was really curious about a game that let me make all the decisions in it AND it let me play as a woman? I was sold from the jump. But upon exploring the game, seeing new worlds, getting to know my companions, I realized that even my queerness could be explored when I met Juhani at the Jedi Academy. It wasn’t a full romance, it didn’t even trigger real cutscenes. But the moment I learned I could get that conversation loop with her, I would visit her on the ship every time I could, hoping new dialog would loop in our Will They Won’t They. It was the first time I really felt seen as a baby butch in a game and it’s been a standard I’ve held games to ever since. â Erminia, Community Manager

I learned who I am through their games. Itâs not hyperbole. They helped me figure out the kind of person I would grow to be. As a pansexual nonbinary person their games were a safe space to experiment and experience things to see how it made me feel. The joy of falling for characters like Thane and Kaidan and knowing what that kind of love could feel like made me feel seen. Being able to play as a nonbinary Qunari in Dragon Age: The Veilguard and share my own gender journey with Taash to comfort them is one of the most gender-affirming experiences of my life. I never felt more confident about who I was than when I was playing one of their games. â Matt Storm aka Stormageddon, Podcast co-host for the âFunâ & Games Podcast and Reignite â A BioWare Replay Podcast

The passion people have for BioWare games is a shared one, and even though the company is gone, the communities its work fostered will persist long after publisher EA closes its doors. But itâs not just about having forums in which to talk about these games or places to post fan art or cosplay; several people had stories about how BioWareâs games established lifelong connections, made them feel closer to the ones already in their lives, or helped them see a path forward after a loss.

My dad was a submariner. He loves BioWare games, Mass Effect specifically. He saw me playing one day, and asked if I minded if he tried it out. He loves that series. I think he felt a connection to Shepard (specifically Jennifer Haleâs version) as a fellow ship captain. After he retired, the series became one of his projects. Heâs dedicated to the perfect playthrough. Heâs got what we call the Book of Knowledge. In it is the result of every dialogue choice, the location of every collectible (including the ones that arenât in the strategy guides), and how best to complete every quest. Itâs the most complete guide to those games I have ever seen. He has several characters running at once, records all of his playthroughs, and heâs turned that into a story heâs chronicling of his Shepard. Itâs not for anyone else; just him.

When I visit, we talk about Mass Effect and Dragon Age and he asks me when I think the next game is coming out. One year, for his birthday, the only thing he wanted was to hang out with me over the holidays and finish Mass Effect 3 because it was the one I hadnât finished, and he wanted to see how Iâd play it. Weâd sit there and compare choices, builds, talk about the characters. For several years, I just bought him models of the ships for birthdays and Christmas. Weâd go to cons and heâs trying to get the autographs of all the voice actors. It was something we could connect over even though we live on opposite ends of the country. I havenât spoken with him since the closure, partially because the thought of being the one to tell him breaks my heart. I know how much that series means to him, and how much respect he had for the folks who worked on every aspect of it.

I have a better relationship with my dad because of BioWareâs games. For me, thatâs their legacy. I hope the folks who worked there know how much the art they made meant to so many, and that their games connected us to the people we love. â Will Borger, journalist and consultant

While I was already a fan at the time, the most impactful moment for me – and one that solidified how deeply my love for BioWare would go – came in the midst of my grief over losing my mother to suicide in January 2012. Two months after her death, Mass Effect 3 was released. By that point, nothing was bringing me distraction or relief, not even my beloved video games, but I had already preordered it so I picked it up anyway. Played through the campaign, then decided to give BioWareâs first foray into multiplayer a try. It proved to be the only outlet at that time to take my mind off my pain and be elsewhere. Interacting with other fans in the community, fighting the Reapers together, and being head-butted between waves by a friendly Krogan was the catalyst for helping me feel a little bit like my old self again.

It gave me hope that I could find fun once more and could eventually reclaim my life from the depression Iâd fallen into. It was honestly the first time I had smiled and laughed since her death.

All that alone would have been impactful enough, but then things went deeper. BioWare was being lit up online about the Mass Effect 3 endings, and I felt bad for them after the game had personally helped me so much. I decided to write and mail off an old-fashioned letter to the Edmonton studio address, telling them my story and thanking them for creating a game that at least one fan really enjoyed and found succor in. I did it that way simply hoping it would actually be seen by the team rather than an email lost to the void somewhere in all the negative noise. The team not only received my letter, but passed it around and were incredibly touched by it.

So much so that I was surprised one day to find not only a letter back from them, but an autographed lithograph and other goodiesâ¦ including an âHonor The Fallenâ Normandy patch. Iâm tearing up again now 14 years later just remembering it. Chris Priestly, former BioWare community coordinator, wrote to me in that reply letter all those years ago: âWe often lose sight that our games can do more than be mere entertainment and, occasionally, can make a real difference.âÂ  â Tiffany Lowe, BioWare fan

Mass Effect 3 was particularly meaningful to me as it was released during a tumultuous time in my personal life. I was going through a divorce in which the mother of my child (only two at the time) had essentially vanished and left us alone. I was struggling not only with the loss, but with being a single parent all of a sudden. The few moments I got to play ME3 during that time were cathartic. Allowing me to focus on tasks I could handle. It kept me from wallowing. Truly, the “friends” I had in my companions helped pull me through the dregs of my depression and kept me from drowning.Â

All of their games have done something similar for me (I could go on and on), and if there’s anything I want the developers to know about their legacy, itâs this: their work mattered. Their stories touched my life in a way that not only set me on a path to telling my own stories as a professional writer (and writing about games), but got me through hard times. â Jordan Maison, BioWare fan and media

Veilguard came out at a weird time for me. My mother-in-law had died a couple years prior, two days after I had her first grandchild and a few hours after she got to hold that grandchild for the first and last time. We spent a year helping my husbandâs family adjust to this whole new life without the cornerstone of their family, and after that year we decided to sell the house to pay off my six-figure student loans. That plan worked out, but we spent the following year living together with my husbandâs family, mourning together and bringing new kids into a world without their grandmother. By the end of our year living there I had another newborn, lingering health issues from pregnancy, and a new house that I was being pushed to move into a week after giving birth. And then the 2024 election happened. I would not leave my room for weeks. I just wanted to hold my babies in bed where I felt safe.Â

I promised my husband that we could get a PS5 when we moved in, and one of the first games he bought was Veilguard specifically for me. I think it just helped to feel like the world wasnât falling apart, because in a game I have the power to fix it, and to give power to the people who feel powerless in the face of everything moving against them in the world. I donât think Iâd be as well off mentally right now if I didnât have Veilguard at the right time. â Elam Bonebright, illustrator

At some point [while playing Dragon Age: Inquisition], I tweeted about how I needed to find someone else who had played it, anyone, because I was obsessed, and I had absolutely no idea how vast and passionate a fandom I had just alerted to my presence. What followed was 6 years of community and friendship that looking back, probably saved my life. I chatted in Discord servers, I made my first ever fan art and even a few viral memes, and I laughed and I cried at the beautiful things other fans made. I met countless people who loved Dragon Age as much as I did, and some of them have even become real-world friends. Among them are a handful of DA devs whose names made me so proud to see in the Veilguard credits that I cried. Watching the death of the franchise and now the closure of the studio alongside them has been heartbreaking.

What I think is remarkable is that my experience is far from extraordinary: BioWare had a way of writing stories that made people feel seen and could bring them together, and most crucially, could do so for people who didn’t necessarily fit into the “typical” gamer community. While this chapter is over, its impact is not, and I know the many creative people impacted by layoffs and now the studio closure will go on to make more beautiful, uniting things. Before they even added the extended endings, I remember sitting there, thinking of what kind of universe Shepard would never get to see. And, seemingly unlike the rest of the internet, I was content. â Justin Clark, games media

Since then BioWare has been a studio that I associate with telling stories over trying to fit in with what the rest of the AAA competition was doing at the time. â Gabe Titchiner, BioWare fan

I think [what impressed me the most] was how Dragon Age II subverted the expectation of player agency. This wasnât Mass Effect, or Origins, or KOTOR where the right selection of choices could save the world. Your world was going to hell no matter what. The game thereby became an altogether more intimate tale of a found family caught in the tide of history. The cast of violent, sexually fluid weirdos remains one of the all-time great RPG parties, and the deeply cursed city of Kirkwall is an all-time great fantasy setting. With a narrative that spans years, you get to feel like you havenât just gone on adventure: youâve built a life for yourself and your friends. When you must choose who to side with at the end of the game, whether to side with the inevitability of authority or with the chaos of rebellion, that moment carries a weight that most RPGs canât match, precisely because the game has spent its efforts investing you in the characters and the setting, not just the plot.

It challenged my beliefs about what made a good narrative, and that made me a better author and critic. â Saoirse Stone BioWare fan, critic, author, Editor-In-Chief at Stone Freedom

The twist in KotOR was my âI am your father.â It completely got me and Iâve been trying to replicate that feeling for almost my whole life. â Eric Perez, BioWare fan

The Revealâ¢ in KOTOR is legendary, but even outside that, you could already see that this studio was special in the way it could build a universe for you. Learning the ancient history of the sand people hit me in the way the best epic fantasy and science fiction does. […] Whoever wrote and animated the bit in Mass Effect 2 where youâre sneaking onto a Geth station and Joker notes that their stealth systems just hide emissions and anyone could see the Normandy by looking out a window, and Legion explains that windows are illogical while Joker silently makes a robot face and robot arms gestures? I love you. Top five video game jokes of all time. â Chase Wheatley, BioWare fan
