#3617. 10 Shows Like 'Below' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

If horror films have taught me anything, it's that nothing good ever comes out of the fog, but the haze-filled thriller Below has definitely earned record ratings and enthusiastic audiences for Netflix—it's the top debut for a Canadian show in the streamer's history, as it happens. In its wake, consider these 10 other series that take you to isolated and evocative landscapes filled with horrors both human and monstrous.

Claustrophobic, mysterious, and perpetually misty (seriously, you can't see shit in any of these towns), Midnight Mass is very much about the monsters within being no less frightening than those without. It may or may not be the best of Mike Flanagan's Netflix work, but it's certainly the most emotionally devastating. Riley Flynn (Zach Gilford) returns to the tiny, isolated community of Crockett Island, his arrival coinciding with that of Catholic priest Father Paul Hill (Hamish Linklater). Riley is wrestling with his justifiable guilt over a drunk-driving death for which he was responsible, while the charismatic priest is reviving the town's once-flagging religious fervor while exacerbating local tensions. The brewing conflict, involving the limits of both faith and guilt, is fascinating, while the inseparably horrific elements are terrifying. Stream Midnight Mass on Netflix.

Running to the darker end of the spectrum, the often devastating Katla moves slowly until it doesn't, deliberately picking up speed as it builds to an emotional climax. Set in Iceland, the show takes place one year following the eruption of the real-life Katla volcano, which buries the nearby town of Vik in choking ash. The few people who've elected to remain are surprised, to say the least, when soot-covered figures from the past start arriving, including the dead son of the volcanologist studying the meteorite in the nearby glacier. Stream Katla on Netflix.

Each season of The Terror is distinct, but all converge on the idea that real life is far, far more horrifying than the supernatural stuff going on in the background. Season one, adapted from the Dan Simmons novel, is our focus here, involving as it does the true story of two ships, the Erebus and the Terror, searching for the Northwest Passage before becoming trapped in a field of ice. Starvation, madness, and monsters ensue. While set in the 1840s (and in an ice field), the vibe isn't wildly dissimilar to Below. Stream The Terror on AMC+ and Shudder.

This weird, ambitious slice of folk horror finds Jude Law's Sam arriving on Osea Island while grieving his murdered son and trying to save his failing business. After he intervenes when he sees a young woman attempting to hang herself, Sam is caught up in some wildly atmospheric creepiness around the town. Later, Naomie Harris' Helen arrives on the island with her daughters only to discover that everything's gone to hell, and that the causeway that connects the island to the mainland is gone. In between the two halves of the miniseries, the creators produced an immersive 12-hour, single-camera livestream capturing a day in the life of the island, a wild bit of innovation. Admittedly, it's all a bit more vibes than plot, but the vibes are genuinely disturbing. Stream The Third Day on HBO Max.

One of the better creepy-stuff-in-an-isolated location narratives of recent years, moving away from the schvitzy bro energy of earlier seasons in favor of a darker (literally) and frostier mystery involving missing scientists at a research station near a tiny and necessarily remote Alaskan town, where the dark and the cold are practically characters themselves. The resulting case ties together veteran Chief Liz Danvers (Jodie Foster) and Trooper Evangeline Navarro (Kali Reis), two women with complicated pasts and screwed-up present family lives. Stream True Detective: Night Country on HBO Max.

Set in 1945 Gyeongseong (modern-day Seoul), and during the Japanese occupation of Korea, this series finds the title's monster arising out of human experimentation conducted in secret by the Japanese army. The scars of occupation have been justifiably fertile ground for storytelling in the last few years (see also Apple’s Pachinko), and Gyeongseong adds science fiction to that mix. The second season moves the action to the present day, with a third season renewal looking likely. If Below's monster is a primary draw, South Korean import Gyeongseong is about as good a follow-up as you're likely to find. Stream Gyeongseong Creature on Netflix.

Set near the real-life Lago di Resia in northern Italy, this show was inspired by the lake's singular view: the bell tower of a 14th century chapel rising above the water, the only visible remains of a village submerged by a dam in the 1950s. That eerie setting is home to Anna Raina (Valeria Bilello); it was, anyway, until she fled while pregnant with her twin daughters following her mother's tragic and mysterious death. The twins are now teenagers, and the three of them have returned—except nobody seems to want them around. They come to learn that Anna's been having dreams about her mother's death in which she's the killer, and then she herself disappears. It all ties back to that lake and the creepy bell tower—more about family mystery and vaguely supernatural menace than monsters, but the evocative setting ties this and Below together. Stream Curon on Netflix.

Another recent addition to the atlas of regrettable vacation destinations is Widow's Bay, an isolated New England island trying to shrug off its literally cursed reputation in favor of becoming a tourist destination à la Martha's Vineyard—but, alas, the timing isn't great. Cozy and idyllic on the surface, Widow's Bay appears to be "waking up," according to a few of the more tuned-in locals. Mayor Tom Loftus (Matthew Rhys), a relative newcomer, is having none of it—at least until a killer clown and waterlogged lady come for him, convincing him to join forces with local eccentric Wyck (Stephen Root) who seems to be on to something with his crackpot theories. The show is frequently funny, but also legitimately scary, with an everything-and-the-kitchen sink approach to the horror genre. Stream Widow's Bay on Apple TV.

As we in the real world well know, monsters can be tiny at least as easily as they can be large. This import finds us on a Scottish oil rig (obvi) in the North Sea, abruptly cut off by a mysterious fog (never a good thing) just as the facility is beginning to experience catastrophic system and structural failures. The mysterious haze is more than just a weather phenomenon, though, as there seems to be a microorganism carried within it that causes dramatic behavioral changes, and that may have a relationship to every mass extinction event in Earth's history. But hey—anything to push down the price of oil, amirite? Stream The Rig on Prime Video.

The tone is wildly different, but so many of the shows here are included on the basis of their claustrophobic, mist-shrouded settings and similarly hazy human motivations, so it's only fair to give you some actual monsters, and no show has more creatures than this Godzilla spin-off. Monarch does a surprisingly effective job of telling its own story within the universe of all those American Godzilla movies of the past decade or so, bringing the narrative back down to Earth while building out an entire monster-verse mythology in the process. Anna Sawai stars as a young teacher searching for her father, missing since Godzilla's attack on San Francisco (depicted in the 2014 film), and finds herself drawn into the past and present of a secret government agency. Wyatt and Kurt Russell play the past and present incarnations of the Army colonel who helped set the whole thing in motion. Kong and Godzilla make appearances alongside the whole Toho monster stable. Stream Monarch on Apple TV.

#3616. Fans Aren’t Sure If A Survivor 51 Castaway Is Getting A Winner’s Edit Or Being Set Up For Heartbreak

I don’t know what’s going on with the Survivor edit. I’m not saying fans can always tell who is going to win halfway through every season, but typically at this point, there are two or three strong contenders who more educated fans have coalesced around. That’s definitely not the case at this point in 51. Everyone is still all over the island with their predictions, and there’s perhaps no better example of that than Kristin Flickinger.

Arguably the most universally liked contestant on 51 with the possible exception of Ori, Kristin has probably gotten the most consistently positive edit of any player. Every single time she’s on the screen, the editors seem invested in making her look good. We got a segment where she showed off her negotiation skills. We got a segment where we saw her winning over her tribemates after the swap. We’ve gotten multiple segments where she showed off her literal survival skills. We’ve gotten confessionals where she’s detailed all the strong relationships she has on the island. We even got a montage of all of her audition tapes over the years.

It’s the kind of edit Survivor players dream about getting, but is it a winner’s edit? Well, fans and so-called Edgic experts are not on the same page at all. Some see her as overwhelmingly the most likely winner, and some see her as very likely to be eliminated deep into the merge but very explicitly prior to the endgame. Let’s talk out both sides.

The case for Kristin as a winner is pretty clear and many in the community are making it, perhaps most prominently RHAP’s Shannon Guss. No one on the show has gotten more consistently positive content, and you could argue that a few times, the show even distorted the truth to make her content even more positive. For example, she was shown dunking on Kilby during the negotiation, even though anecdotal evidence later told us she didn’t necessarily get better supplies. That’s been a recurring theme. Even the negativity she’s gotten, which has mostly been from Maggie confessionals, has framed her more as dangerous than incompetent or annoying.

If you dig a little deeper, however, there is actually some cause for concern with Kristin’s edit. Many in the community think she’s being framed as a fan favorite we’re supposed to be sad about exiting the game deep into the merge, and there’s definitely some evidence for that. First, while she’s been a consistent part of the show, there are actually seven players who have more confessionals than her at this point in the game: Devin, Jelly, Lewis, Kilby, Brady, Ori and Erik. She’s only middle of the pack among the players who are left, and that’s actually really bad considering she was picked for negotiation, went to exile island, got swap screwed and got prominently injured during an episode.

Given all the plot-relevant moments she’s been involved in, it’s actually kind of weird she hasn’t gotten more content, which is probably because it keeps getting cut. An emotional scene between her and the Survivor doctor where she was informed she would be allowed to stay in the game got cut and released as an online exclusive. Another scene from this past episode where she explained what happened on Exile Island to her tribe got cut and also released as an online exclusive. Given she’s only in the middle of the pack on content, if she were the winner, it kind of feels like the show would find reasons to use her, not cut compelling scenes she’s involved in.

To me, the most likely scenario is probably that she gets taken out in the 5 to 7 range. That’s typically the point in the game where all the remaining players work together to eliminate the people they think are most likely to win a jury vote, and as a strong public speaker with great relationships, a compelling backstory and a passion for the game, Kristin screams jury threat. There’s also the pesky issue of fire hanging over her head too. We’ve been repeatedly shown and the other players have repeatedly seen her making fire very quickly. She’s the type of player you have to eliminate before the final four, which is why that range just outside makes so much sense.

I have no idea who is going to win this season (though I can guess who is going to lose) and by extension, I have no idea where Kristin is going to finish. All I know for sure is that she’s delightful, and the editors clearly want us to have positive feelings about her, whether she's the possible host Jeff Probst was referring to or not. Maybe that’s because she’s going to go on and win the whole thing, or maybe that’s because she’s the emotional gut punch we’re going to get when she’s betrayed by other players who are worried she’ll win the jury vote if she gets there.

#3615. South Park Season 29 Just Found The Funniest Replacement For Kenny

The following contains spoilers for episode 4 of "South Park" Season 29, "Guinea Pig on a Stick."

Season 29 of "South Park" has been a hilarious experiment. After three decades, the adult animated comedy has officially changed its name to "South America," mirroring the titular town changing its name in reference to the sitting President of the United States renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario. After Season 28 took on some shockingly big targets, mostly involving AI and the Trump administration, the current season has taken on billionaires, data centers, the e-bike craze, "looksmaxxing" and "aura farming," and even the beef crisis in the U.S.

Back in the season premiere, "South Park" even brought back Mike Judge as the unmuffled voice of Kenny McCormick — only to kill him yet again in that same episode. We haven't seen Kenny since then, and it appears the show will not bring him back this season. Still, the show must go on, and it seems "South Park" has found the funniest replacement possible.

It's none other than Randy Marsh, father of Stan Marsh. Yes, the adult man with a mustache and a drinking problem is now a main member of the South Park gang, and it works surprisingly well. That's because Randy is now the size and look of a 10-year-old (though still with a mustache) thanks to an overuse of anti-aging creams from Sephora in Episode 3 of the new season. It's ridiculous, it's very funny, and it's pure "South Park America."

One of the biggest issues with "South Park" the last 10 years or so has been the increased focus on Randy Marsh. This alone isn't inherently an issue, as Randy is the focus of some of the all-time best "South Park" episodes, like "The Losing Edge" (an episode that gets referenced in last week's episode of the current season). But a problem arose when writers decided to stick Randy up in his weed farm and separate him from the rest of the town. It was funny for the first couple of episodes, but season after season it quickly lost steam.

So, when Randy finally sold the farm and moved the family back to South Park/South America, things finally were on the right track. Last week, Randy got into looksmaxxing and transformed into a 4th grader, which was funny, but not a big part of the plot. That changed this week, when it became obvious that Randy was going to remain a 4th grader for a while longer. He's even referred to throughout the episode as Little Randy, and is an integral part of the story of the episode alongside Stan, Kyle, and Cartman. This results in some hilarious scenes of Stan being angry at his dad for trying too hard to act cool (like when he shows off his Italian brainrot on Roblox) or for being drunk at school.

Little Randy feels like a uniquely "South Park" way of doing something like "Pickle Rick" from "Rick and Morty," both a dumb one-off gimmick and one of that show's deepest episodes. Little Randy could have been a one-off silly gag about how childish Randy is, but instead the show turns him into an essential part of the story and of the kids' dynamic.

This is important, because one common criticism of "South Park" is how disconnected the adult and kids' storylines feel. Having Little Randy, however, bridges the two. It allows Randy to still be involved in the adult stories because he knows that world, such as in this week's episode when he is the one that suggests the boys try going to a farm to investigate the lack of beef in South America. Plus, seeing Randy be his beer-chugging self at middle school is inherently funny, and adds a new dynamic to the nearly 30-year-old show by placing him with the other 4th graders, especially now that Stan has to be constantly embarrassed by his father hanging around.

The fact that Little Randy is older also allows "South Park" to humorously explore current slang and references in an organic way. There's a lot of potential to mine with Randy being both a kid and an adult for the remainder of the season. If Kenny is gone, at least we have Little Randy.

#3614. 'Vorssaint' Replaced at Least 10 Utility Apps on My Mac

Plenty of Mac apps do one job, and do it quite well. For example, KeyboardCleanTool lets you disable your Mac's keyboard temporarily while you get dust, food particles, and gunk off the keyboard. I love these apps, but if you keep installing utilities, things start to feel crowded; it can be a real problem even trying to remember that you have an app installed for a specific task. This is where Vorssaint comes in: It's the Swiss Army knife of Mac apps, packing over 75 utilities into a single, free resource.

The best thing is that you can choose which of these utilities you wish to enable—if you need only five of Vorssaint's features, you can disable the rest. This prevents the app from becoming a resource hog, which is particularly valuable for those of us with older, base-model MacBooks. Even though Vorssaint has replaced multiple Mac apps on my MacBook, however, it's not always better than the apps it replaces. If you use Vorssaint to set a custom volume level for each Mac app, for example, it doesn't mean Vorssaint can do everything SoundSource does.

Vorssaint is very much a jack of all trades, master of none, and that's perfectly fine for most people. If that sounds like the kind of tool you need, then Vorssaint could be great for you. Here are 10 Vorssaint features that I've used to replace apps on my MacBook:

Unless you're addicted to appearing like you're yelling all the time, you probably don't need the Caps Lock key at all. You can always hold Shift whenever you want to capitalize something, and in my opinion, Caps Lock should be repurposed for something better. Apps such as Raycast allow you to convert Caps Lock into a "hyper key," which means that when you press that button, your computer registers it as a combination of other modifier keys. On my MacBook, pressing Caps Lock equals holding Command-Control-Shift-Alt together, and I've used it to create keyboard shortcuts that don't conflict with those in macOS or third-party apps.

To enable this feature in Vorssaint, open the app, and go to Settings > Features. Go to the "Mouse and keyboard" section, and enable Super key. Vorssaint allows you to map modifier keys to Caps Lock. It also lets you continue using the button for capitalization, switching input sources, or as an alternative way to press the Esc key (useful for keyboards that don't have this button). It works by triggering the "Super key" only when you hold Caps Lock, and toggling the other feature you chose when you press the button once.

Your Mac's Spotlight has a basic clipboard manager, but Vorssaint adds a few more features. The app lets you clean tracking data from URLs, and even adds a "Cut and Paste" feature to your Mac's Finder. The latter is great for people switching from Windows—Finder's cut/paste feature isn't as seamless as the one on Microsoft's platform.

Once you enable these features in Vorssaint, you can cut any file in Finder by pressing Command-X, and paste it elsewhere with Command-V. The URL cleaner is customizable, and it allows you to define parameters to remove. It also allows you to create filters for specific websites, which reduces the chances of breaking URLs when you try this feature. By default, Vorssaint will automatically clean a link the moment you copy one, but you can also manually clean links in the app if you wish to.

The app's clipboard manager has all the basic features you'll need, and it lets you exclude some apps too. This lets you keep Vorssaint from storing clipboard items from sensitive apps. The shortcut to view clipboard history from Vorssaint is Command-Option-Alt-V.

I use Rapidmg, a popular app installer format on the Mac, to auto-mount and install DMG files. After the app is installed, Rapidmg also gets rid of the installer file. Vorssaint has this feature built-in, and you can enable it by going to Vorssaint settings > Features > Disk image installer. It's located under the "Clipboard and files" section.

If you're looking for an app to set a custom volume level for each Mac app, then Vorssaint has a tool for the job. It's good enough to replace basic volume control apps like FineTune, but not nearly as powerful as SoundSource. Vorssaint lets you set a per-app volume level, quickly switch between output devices, and even set priority for audio devices. It doesn't support sending audio to multiple devices at once, tweaking latency levels, boosting volume above the maximum, or sending audio from certain apps only to specific output devices (e.g., Spotify always goes to headphones, VLC always sends audio to speakers, etc.). If you value power-user features, then SoundSource has to be your go-to. For most people, Vorssaint is good enough to get the job done. You can enable volume mixer in the app by going to Vorssaint settings > Features > Volume mixer. It's under the "Sound" section in the app.

There are many good reasons to stop your Mac from going to sleep, such as connecting your MacBook to an external display and using the laptop with its lid closed. Apps such as Amphetamine allow you to keep your Mac from going into sleep mode, and Vorssaint has this feature built-in as well. You can use it by enabling the "Keep awake" feature in the app, which lets you disable sleep mode on your Mac for a custom time interval that ranges from 15 minutes to indefinitely.

If you're missing your iPhone's Dynamic Island on your MacBook, you could install one of several useful notch apps on your Mac. These apps show a now playing widget, brightness or volume levels, calendars, or even have a temporary shelf to help you drag and drop files on your Mac. Vorssaint ships with a notch app, too: Dynamic Island. Once you enable it, Vorssaint's Dynamic Island can show notifications, calendar events, timers, song lyrics, playback queue, etc. Note that this feature is labeled "Experimental" in the app, which means that it's not as stable as most other features. I've also been using it to activate other Vorssaint features such as Keep awake and volume mixer, since Dynamic Island shows toggles to control them.

iStat Menus is one of my favorite Mac apps—it allows me to monitor my MacBook's current load and operating temperatures. Vorssaint also ships with the ability to monitor CPU load, GPU load, RAM usage, network usage, battery temperature, etc. It's not as elegant as iStat Menus, but it'll do the job for those who need a basic system stat monitor. In my tests, though, I observed that Vorssaint incorrectly reports CPU temperature. Two other apps (iStat Menus and TG Pro) reported my Mac's CPU temperature at around 104°F (40°C), but Vorssaint kept showing a number closer to 145°F (63°C). All other temperature readings were nearly identical in the three apps, which indicates that Vorssaint probably has a bug to fix.

Vorssaint can also be a substitute for apps that enhance your Mac's Dock. It allows you to enable features like previewing open windows by hovering over an app's icon in the Dock, quitting apps from the Dock preview, clicking the dock icon to minimize, hide, or cycle between apps' windows, etc. One useful feature allows you to click the green button to maximize any app's window, as opposed to switching to full-screen mode. I don't use it, but I can recommend it to people who switch from Windows and ask me about the maximize button.

macOS doesn't always allow your mouse to work the way you want it to. Third-party "mouse fix" apps add nice features such as smooth scrolling, customizable actions for side buttons, and so on. Vorssaint includes support for smooth scrolling, and a few other features. It lets you map extra mouse buttons to custom keyboard shortcuts, and even has a feature to prevent accidental double-clicks. The latter is good for people who have a mouse with double-click problems. You can enable these features under the "Mouse and keyboard" section in Vorssaint.

Apps like KeyboardCleanTool allow you to temporarily disable your Mac's keyboard for you to give it a good clean, or to allow your cat to sit on the keyboard without disturbing your workflow. Vorssaint supports this, too—you can enable this feature by toggling "Cleaning Mode" under the Tools section in the app. Once you lock the keyboard, you can either click the "Unlock" button or press Esc five times to start typing again.

Every Halloween, I think I've seen the year's best celebrity costume, and then somebody comes along and changes my mind. And while there's plenty keeping me entertained on the 2026 TV schedule, former Riverdale stars Madelaine Petsch and Camila Mendes just gave me a fictional show I'd absolutely watch. Petsch and Mendes spent Halloween dressed as Wilma Flintstone and Betty Rubble, respectively, and their ridiculously glamorous photo shoot has me wishing The Real Housewives of Bedrock were an actual series I could binge.

Petsch and Mendes shared the pictures in a joint Instagram post on Halloween, captioning them "The Real Housewives of Bedrock," complete with a bone emoji. Amber Asaly shot the photos, and they look like promotional stills for the most unhinged Bravo spinoff imaginable. Prehistoric sets, dramatic side-eyes, and enough attitude suggest somebody's about to get kicked out of the Bedrock country club. Seriously, take a look:

A post shared by Madelaine Petsch (@madelame)

Since Andy Cohen recently teased the possibility of more Real Housewives cities, I think somebody should put Bedrock on the list. Seriously, who’s Flintmobile’s stone log rollers do I gotta buff to get this thing greenlit?

Petsch nails Wilma's signature look: red curls piled high, a white one-shoulder dress with a jagged hem, and those enormous pearls. Mendes, meanwhile, makes a fantastic Betty in a blue dress, matching hair bow and sleek dark bob. They've kept the recognizable Flintstones details while giving everything a glossy, fashion-editorial makeover. I'd genuinely love to see the rest of their imaginary cast.

The photos are where the joke really takes off. In one, Betty leans over to whisper something into Wilma's ear, while Wilma looks appropriately scandalized. Another pic shows them posing with champagne glasses, and there are shots of the pair lounging among rocky scenery lifted from the cartoon. They even brought two little white dogs into the mix. I'm not sure what the dogs have to do with prehistoric suburbia, I suppose its hard to secure a tiny dino on short notice, so I’m glad the pups got an invite.

As much as I love the outfits, someone in the Instagram comments deserves a gold star for the funniest response to the entire shoot. User @herecomesjoey wrote:

RIP CW, you would’ve greenlit this show by Monday morning 😭👌🏽🔥😍

I've always had a soft spot for how the 1994 live-action Flintstones movie brought Bedrock to life, and these costumes have that same wonderfully ridiculous attention to detail. Only this time, Wilma and Betty look ready for a Bravo reunion special.

They don’t really produce their own original series anymore, but the CW is still on the air, and I laughed harder than I probably should have. Considering these two spent seven seasons on Riverdale, a show that got increasingly bizarre right up through its series finale, a CW-style Flintstones drama feels almost plausible. I can already hear the trailer voice-over: "In Bedrock, everybody has something to hide."

Of course, Petsch and Mendes have a history of taking Halloween costumes very seriously. Just last year, they dressed as Kim Possible and Shego, proving that transforming into beloved cartoon characters is becoming something of an annual tradition for these two. Before that, they joined fellow Riverdale alum Lili Reinhart to dress as the Gotham City Sirens for Halloween, after previously transforming into the Sanderson sisters from Hocus Pocus. This year's costume is a duo rather than a trio, but Reinhart still showed up in the comments with a perfect one-word endorsement: "Icons." I can't argue with her.

What really sells these pictures for me is how completely the actresses commit to the bit. They look ready to feud over a dinner-party seating chart carved into a stone tablet. Unfortunately, The Real Housewives of Bedrock isn't a real series. For now, it's an excellent Halloween photo shoot and another reminder that Petsch and Mendes know how to have fun together long after Riverdale ended. But if anybody wants to commission a pilot, I expect a reunion special hosted by a particularly exhausted Fred Flintstone.

Riverdale is streaming in its entirety with a Netflix subscription.

#3612. FF7 Remake and Rebirth Are Less than $8 Each on Nintendo Switch 2

Just enough time to catch up before Revelation

If you've been waiting for Final Fantasy 7 Remake and Rebirth to go on sale before checking them out, your patience has paid off. At least, as long as you're okay with a bit of DLSS hair-frizz. Square Enix is hosting a huge sale on the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 eShop, and included in that sale are FF7 Remake and FF7 Rebirth for $7.99 and $7.49, respectively.

The Switch 2 version of FF7 Remake includes the Intergrade DLC. That means you're getting Cloud and co.'s journey through Midgar, in addition to Episode Yuffie, which introduces the Wutai ninja and digs into some of the more obscure lore that plays a part in the broader Remake trilogy. Normally, FF7 Remake on Switch 2 retails for $39.99.

Remake on Switch 2 surprised us with just how well it runs. Barring some occasional choppiness, the frame rate remained steady — including in combat, where it matters most — though the resolution sometimes takes a hit. That hit is comparatively minor thanks to the enclosed spaces of Midgar meaning there's less need to render things at a distance. The hair can be distracting, though. If you've seen Resident Evil 4 remake on Switch 2 in handheld mode, you'll have a good idea what to expect.

Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth is discounted to $7.49, down from $49.99. This is just the game itself. There's a set of deluxe edition DLC that gives you some in-game items, too, which is on sale for $3 (down from $20). Bear in mind there's no story expansion in this DLC, though. It includes:

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Rebirth puts more of a strain on Switch 2 than its predecessor, though that's hardly surprising. It's an open-world game with a lot more going on in it. Asset pop-in is a frequent issue in the open world itself, and character models look less detailed than their PS5 counterparts, for example. But the game still runs well, and if frame drops happen, it's rarely during pivotal moments or battles.

With Final Fantasy Revelation coming up in April, now's as good a time as ever to check out the rest of the remake trilogy — or refresh yourself on its events before the big finale.

#3611. The Man With The Bag Trailer: Arnold Schwarzenegger's Santa Claus Meets Jack Reacher In Holiday Heist Comedy

Arnold Schwarzenegger's Christmas movie "Jingle All the Way" became a box office hit in 1996, and 30 years later he's back with another festive action comedy in "The Man with the Bag." This time, he's brought "Reacher" star Alan Ritchson along for the ride, and we just got our first full look at the holiday heist comedy via its first full-length trailer.

"The Man with the Bag" sees Arnie play Santa Claus himself, who, after his sack of presents is stolen by an elf, enlists the help of a criminal called Vince (Ritchson) to retrieve it. The pairing of Ritchson and Schwarzenegger makes a lot of sense. Both are major action stars who've demonstrated their comedic chops in several projects, Ritchson's most recent example being the Prime Video action comedy "Playdate." In that sense, the "Reacher" star is vying to become the modern-day Arnie and is surely hoping "The Man with the Bag" comes to represent an unofficial passing of the action-comedy torch.

Thus far, it's been tough to know what to make of "The Man with the Bag." In 2024 we learned Schwarzenegger and Ritchson were making a Christmas comedy with an unbelievable premise. Amazon then delivered a teaser trailer in September 2026, which provided a tease of Arnie and his co-star's rapport. Now, we have our first good look at the movie, and it certainly looks to be an enjoyable watch even if it's not necessarily destined to become a holiday classic.

Prime Video has plenty of great Christmas movies already, and now the streamer is hoping to add another to its catalog with "The Man with the Bag." The latest trailer for the Adam Shankman-directed film reveals a lot more about the plot, opening with a scene in which Alan Ritchson's career criminal Vince is seen sitting alongside his daughter, Emma (Berkeley James). It seems he's been away for four years, likely serving a prison sentence, and now that he's out he's back to his old tricks.

His latest client, Kris, is revealed to be Santa himself, who's hired Vince to help retrieve his sack of gifts ahead of Christmas. A "disgruntled elf" who became "obsessed with shiny things" and who calls herself Nadia Nice (Awkwafina) has taken the bag and checked into a fancy hotel. It's here that Santa and his new criminal cohort attempt a heist to retrieve the bag and save Christmas.

It looks as though we'll be getting plenty of amusing back-and-forths between the two leads along the way, with Santa reinstilling some magic into Vince's life and helping him bond with his daughter. We knew the movie was shot on-location in New York (via Ritchson's Instagram) but it's nice to see from the trailer that many of the scenes actually look like it rather than most of the footage looking like it was shot in a streaming-age green screen hellscape.

"The Man with the Bag" is set to hit Prime Video on December 2, 2026, when it will hopefully manage to remind us of the infinite joys of the Christmas action movie.

#3610. Six Things to Do Between Sets at the Gym

Rest is a crucial part of strength training. Depending on the exercise and your goals, you may find yourself resting 30 seconds, or one minute, or three to five minutes. So what do you actually do during that time? Let’s talk about your options, both in terms of training effectiveness and gym etiquette.

As awkward as it may feel at first, this is the best option for most people, most of the time. Actually rest. Don’t stretch, don’t work a different muscle; just allow your body to recover.

Some gyms will have stools, benches, or folding chairs near the platforms where people are lifting heavy (and thus need the longest rests). I’m mostly thinking of powerlifting and weightlifting gyms, but I’ve been to big-box gyms like Crunch that provide seating as well. And impromptu seats are common in many other places—who hasn’t sat on a plyo box or some other convenient surface?

There are plenty of little actions that you take at the gym (or should take) that are not explicitly exercise. The rest between sets is the perfect time to do these little maintenance tasks. Things like:

Change the weights to what you’ll need for your next set.

Write down what you just lifted in your notebook or lifting app.

If you took a video, watch it to give yourself feedback for the next set.

Trim that video so that you (or your coach, or your friends) don’t have to watch all 20 seconds of you fumbling with the camera and adjusting your belt before you actually lift.

Have a drink of water and, if needed, a snack.

Clean up after yourself! Rack any plates and dumbbells you aren’t using.

During the last few sets of an exercise, it’s time to start thinking about what you’ll do next. This could mean grabbing the equipment you’ll need or changing your shoes, but it's also an excellent opportunity to start warming up—especially if it’s an exercise that can benefit from a little gentle mobility work.

Let’s say you have a few sets of squats left, but after that you’ll do some overhead press. You probably want to warm up your shoulders with some mobility work so that you won’t be so tight when you hit that nice stable overhead position. Or maybe it’s the other way around, and you’re pressing, but next you’ll do squats. It’s a great time to start doing some ankle mobility work so that you’ll be able to comfortably hit a deeper squat.

When the weights are routine, I sit and chill. When they get heavy, I need to pace. (At weightlifting competitions, I not only stake out a warmup platform, I also pick out a walking path that I can pace between attempts.)

Or if you’re more of a cheerful, high-energy person, maybe you just want to dance. You’ll see this most often from people who lift at home, or at a chummy small gym where an impromptu dance party might occur between friends. Alone in my garage gym, I’ve been known to put on some good karaoke songs and sing along, with or without dancing.

The idea is not to get some extra cardio or get your steps in, but just to stay busy and loose and have fun—or, if you’re nervous about a big lift, to keep your head. At a busy commercial gym, make sure not to walk too far away, and consider leaving your water bottle or gym bag on your equipment to let people know it’s still taken.

I promise that it is actually OK to look at your phone between sets. You’re probably doing it anyway. There’s your lifting app, your videos that you took to check your squat form—and, yes, your usual texting and social media stuff.

The risk you’re taking here is that you’ll get distracted and rest too long. Too much rest, say more than 10 minutes, can make you feel both mentally and physically unprepared. Long rests can also lengthen your workout. Sticking to the minimum necessary rest times will get you in and out of the gym a lot faster.

From others’ perspective, a person who sits on a machine for 10 minutes scrolling is committing an unforgivable sin in gym etiquette. Don’t take longer rests than you need, if you’re holding up equipment. (That said, if you’re polite to others who approach, and you accept requests to “work in” (take turns) while you scroll, you’re morally in the clear.)

For your own sake, set a timer when you do anything that might distract you between sets. I like how I can program rest times into a Garmin watch workout, but Hevy also has a timer, and you can always use the regular timer function on your watch or phone.

Another tip: Be mindful about what you’re doing on your phone. Now is not the time to get into an argument on the internet, or check your work email and see what will be waiting for you back at the office. It is a good time to play little games on your phone, or read an ebook, or put together your next great workout playlist.

I’m leaving this option for last because I don’t want it to be your go-to. Just because you can do one exercise while resting for another, doesn’t mean you should.

Why not? If you really want to give squats your full energy, for example, don’t do pull-ups on the squat rack in between. You’ll fatigue yourself more than you realize, and you won’t do your best on those squats.

But supersets can be great if you’re willing to sacrifice a little weight for a lot of time. They’re best for exercises where the exact weight doesn’t matter—you can pair bicep curls with tricep extensions, or pull-ups with dips (so long as you’re a person who can bang out multiple reps of each with ease).

To do a superset, you just do a set of the first exercise, then a set of the second, then rest a short time (if needed at all), and repeat. I have a list of the best superset pairs here—usually you’ll want to do opposing muscles, like a push exercise with a pull exercise.

The new reboot of Baywatch is just a couple of months away. We won’t see it on the 2026 TV schedule, but in the depths of the cold winter in January, we’ll be headed back to the beach on Fox. Two stars of the new version, Stephen Amell and Brooks Nader, recently spoke about some of the stars of the original Baywatch possibly returning in the reboot (other than the couple of former lifeguards who have been announced), and that led Nader to talk about some advice she got from Carmen Electra.

While talking to a gaggle of reporters hyping up the show, Nadar told them (via Deadline):

I spoke to Carmen Electra, and she said…. She just was like, ‘Oh my gosh, this is gonna be great.’ All she said about the series is how much hard work you have to actually put into it and how physically taxing it is on your body. And I heard at the beginning of filming, and I was like, ‘Eh, [I] got this.’ She was totally right in every way possible.

This isn’t the first time that Electra has given this advice to the new cast, telling E! back in June the same thing. It also seems as though the cast has gotten the message, as Amell has talked about all the prep he’s putting in to deal with the long, shirtless days and hours in the Pacific Ocean. Nadar has also joked about how her whole life is now “running in slow motion” since landing the gig.

Though Amell and Nadar were a little coy in their answer about returning stars, only hinting that some big names may show up, they definitely left the door open. Electra, of course, was one of the biggest stars during Baywatch’s original run in the 1990s. Whether she is going to return or not isn’t unknown. She’s said in the past that she is interested in returning (and even donned the old red suit earlier this year), provided she doesn’t have to shoot anything in the water.

Elektra has talked a lot about the new show and how hard it’ll be to recapture the magic of the original show. She knows it’ll be hard to replace icons like Yasmin Bleeth and Pamela Anderson, for example. Nadar isn’t taking the responsibility lightly, though, even perfecting her mouth-to-mouth for the show.

Whether the new show can recapture whatever lightning in a bottle the OG show had remains to be seen, but from all the interviews, it seems the cast knows exactly what the goal is, and they are really going for it.

#3608. Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller’s Tragic Love Story

“I think you’re the saddest girl I ever met.”

“You’re the first man that ever said that. I’m usually told how happy I am.”

This exchange, from The Misfits, written by Arthur Miller, shows Marilyn Monroe drawing closer to something other than the “dumb blonde” persona for which Hollywood praised her.

After all, the actor—who was born in Los Angeles in 1926 and died in the City of Angels in 1962 at the age of 36—wanted to be taken seriously as a performer. She never fully identified with the image Hollywood created for her. She spent her limited free time enjoying uncharacteristic pastimes, as evidenced by one of her most famous photographs, which depicts her reading James Joyce’s Ulysses while donning a striped tank top, black shorts, and a deep, melancholic gaze.

Marilyn Monroe reads a book in her room at the Hotel Ambassador in midtown Manhattan, March 1955.

“A sex symbol becomes a thing. I just hate to be a thing,” said Monroe to Life magazine in 1962, reflecting on her strained relationship with Hollywood.

Miller, who was born in New York in 1915 and passed away in 2005, initially believed he would be a good partner for Monroe, whose life was marked by great successes, but also abandonment and her unfortunate inability to have children—one of the most painful issues for Monroe.

Monroe and Miller first met in 1950, when he was in Los Angeles with director Elia Kazan. It was Kazan who introduced them.

Monroe and Miller began talking, and he emphasized her potential to become a dramatic actor on New York stages. He struck a chord.

In the mid-1950s, the star left Hollywood and moved to New York to study, attending The Actors Studio and working with Lee Strasberg. She met with Miller again in the Big Apple, and in 1955, they began dating seriously, joining two seemingly distant worlds.

Marilyn Monroe and playwright Arthur Miller play with his dog Hugo,at Miller’s summer home on June 25, 1956.

Monroe felt respected by him, unlike the way she felt in Hollywood, which she once called “an overcrowded brothel, a merry-go-round with beds for horses,” in her unfinished memoir, My Story.

Miller, who had won the Pulitzer Prize in 1949 for Death of a Salesman, was captivated by her and ended his failing marriage.

The subsequent marriage between Monroe and Miller—her third marriage, his second—took place on June 29, 1956, in White Plains, New York. A few days later, a private Jewish ceremony was also held, following the actor’s conversion to Judaism.

The first major rift in their marriage stemmed from ongoing tension between public and private life. Miller wanted a more secluded, domestic life; Monroe wanted a family, but she was not willing to give up the career she had so painstakingly built.

For the 1957 film The Prince and the Showgirl—directed by and starring Laurence Olivier, with Monroe as the female lead and coproducer—the actor and her husband moved to England, where tensions rose.

Arthur Miller and Marilyn Monroe after their wedding.

Monroe found some of Miller’s notes, in which he expressed disappointment with their marriage and admitted to sometimes feeling embarrassed around his friends in the cultural world.

It was one of the hardest moments in their relationship: Monroe discovered that the man who seemed to recognize her talent and intelligence also viewed her through the very same lens from which she was trying to free herself.

In her own notebooks, she reflected on her fear of becoming “someone’s wife” and losing her independence.

Miller would later say that he wrote very little during the years of his marriage.

Monroe, meanwhile, was struggling to become a mother. During her marriage, she experienced a miscarriage, an ectopic pregnancy, and another spontaneous termination of pregnancy.

On the set of The Prince and the Showgirl, her difficulties increased: She often arrived late, struggled to work consistently, and her relationship with Laurence Olivier became strained.

In the background, Miller faced a trial, as he had refused to name Communist Party members and sympathizers. He was convicted of contempt of Congress in 1957, but the conviction was overturned the following year.

Marilyn Monroe and her former husband Arthur Miller as they leave Doctors Hospital on August 10, 1957, after she recovered from a 10-day hospital stay following an ectopic pregnancy.

Despite Monroe publicly expressing her support for her husband, the cracks in their marriage turned into chasms. Arguments, a lack of trust, disillusionment, drugs, alcohol, all of it became too difficult to contain.

The point of no return was another feature film, The Misfits, written by Miller for Monroe.

The desert setting where it was filmed didn’t help. Amid hellish temperatures, Monroe and Miller were no longer on speaking terms, even though they were staying at the same hotel. Intermediaries were needed just to get them to communicate.

It was during this shoot that Miller met the photographer Inge Morath, whom he would later marry in February 1962.

They divorced shortly after The Misfits was released in theaters.

After The Misfits, Monroe went through one of the most difficult periods of her life. In 1961 she was admitted to the Payne Whitney Psychiatric Clinic in New York. Joe DiMaggio intervened to have her transferred to another facility.

Marilyn Monroe’s photo shoot at Hollywood agent Johnny Hyde’s backyard in Beverly Hills, California, 1957.

Before her death, Monroe nevertheless continued to work, seek roles, and imagine a life different from the one others intended for her.

In a 1988 interview that aired on the Italian network Rai, journalist and writer Enzo Biagi asked Miller: “How do you want to remember Marilyn Monroe?”

He replied: “She made everyone believe she was very happy, but I didn’t believe it. She was very depressed, but she had the extraordinary talent of being able to mask her state of mind. She wore a mask because she was suffering too much. She was completely unable to cope with her depression, but she had been an abused child. She was looking for someone to save her.”

Originally published by Vanity Fair Italia.

#3607. You Can Now Lock Your Private ChatGPT Conversations With a PIN

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you have personal conversations with ChatGPT that you don't want others to see, you can now add an extra layer of security for those specific chats. The new Locked Chats feature allows you to hide sensitive conversations behind a four-digit account PIN (or biometric authentication on mobile), meaning others with access to your device or screen can't read them.

Locked chats are retained in your chat history—unlike temporary chats, which are private conversations that aren't saved by default—so you can return to or continue them at any point. However, once locked, they are hidden from your regular chat history, pinned chats, and regular conversation search. To access them, you have to go to Projects > Locked chats and enter your PIN or device unlock method (such as Face ID or Touch ID).

To start a locked chat for the first time, open an existing conversation that you want to keep private and open the options menu. Select Lock chat > Lock chat and create or enter your account PIN. This moves the conversation to your locked chats project. You can repeat this with any existing conversation or start a locked chat from scratch under Projects > Locked Chats by entering your PIN or authentication method and typing a message to launch the chat. When you're done, select Lock now to end access to locked chats and hide them from the sidebar.

Note that if you don't already have an account PIN set up, you should be prompted to do so the first time you attempt to lock a chat. Select Create a PIN, enter your four-digit code, and enter it again to confirm. You can also enable biometric authentication in Account PIN settings. If you reset your account PIN at any point, all locked chats are permanently deleted and cannot be recovered.

Locked chats are available on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans on both mobile and desktop apps. The feature is not available for ChatGPT for Healthcare. There are other limitations, too: For example, temporary, archived, and group chats can't be locked, nor can those with shared links, scheduled and background tasks, or meeting recordings. OpenAI says locked chats are rolling out gradually, so they may not be available to all users yet.

#3606. Hugh Jackman's 2000s Action Horror Movie Should Have Launched A Franchise

The premise of Stephen Sommers' 2004 action horror film "Van Helsing" is like something out of a 12-year-old's wildest sugar-rush fantasies. Hugh Jackman plays Gabriel Van Helsing, an updated version of Abraham Van Helsing from Bram Stoker's 1897 novel "Dracula," this time serving as a professional monster hunter for a secret human-protection society called Knights of the Holy Order. Jackman's Van Helsing is young, sexy, and equipped with a large panoply of steampunk monster-hunting weapons. He's a franchise hero in a movie that never launched a franchise.

At the beginning of the movie, Van Helsing slays Dr. Jekyll (Stephen Fisher) before spending the rest of the film dealing with the machinations of Dracula (Richard Roxburgh), who wants to steal the secrets of creating life from Frankenstein's monster (Shuler Hensley). Kate Beckinsale also co-stars as a young woman of Romanian descent whom Van Halsing must protect, and Jackman and Beckinsale have never looked better in any movie.

"Van Helsing" is a monster mash along the lines of "House of Dracula," but it's silly enough to be comparable to the underrated Rankin/Bass Halloween film "Mad Monster Party?" (despite being infused with ridiculous action scenes, overwrought writing, and expensive VFX). It was a modest graveyard smash, making over $300 million on a $170 million budget. Of course, with a budget like that, it remains one of the most expensive horror movies ever made.

In a better world, "Van Helsing" would have launched a long series of films. I can easily picture a parallel universe where "Ven Helsing" was a bigger hit than it was, and Jackman returned to theaters every two or three years to fight another famous monster. Or maybe Dracula, as he so often does, rises from the grave repeatedly to battle Van Helsing again and again.

Why wasn't it a franchise? Perhaps "Van Helsing" was a little too eager right out of the gate, as it involved Dracula, Frankenstein's monster, a Wolf Man, Dracula's succubus brides, and Jekyll & Hyde. After that, you only have the Invisible Man, the Creature from the Black Lagoon, and the Bride remaining when it comes to the classic Universal Pictures movie monsters.

Indeed, one can see why Universal Pictures would want to make something like "Van Helsing." The studio has long been associated with its monster movies, which originally saw their heyday in the 1930s and 1940s (although "Creature from the Black Lagoon" arrived in the 1950s). There have been innumerable films featuring Dracula, Frankenstein, the Wolf Man, et al, but Universal had an enormous hit with its 1999 film "The Mummy," which was more like an Indiana Jones-inflected adventure movie than a horror film. Stephen Sommers had directed that movie, in addition to helming 2001's "The Mummy Returns" and co-writing the 2002 spin-off "The Scorpion King," so "Van Helsing" was clearly Universal's attempt to get the rest of its Monster canon into the action adventure mix.

And it's mostly successful. The film is high-energy and boasts a lot of fun steampunk visuals. Personally, I like the design of Frankenstein's monster, as he sports a large, flickering lightning screen in his chest. Plus, as mentioned, Hugh Jackman and Kate Beckinsale are utterly dazzling, reminding us why they're movie stars in the first place. And there is certainly nothing wrong with Dracula leading a monster mini-army in his quest for eternal life, as culled from the study of Dr. Frankenstein (Samuel West).

To offer a bit of comic relief, Stephen Sommers regular Kevin J. O'Connor plays Igor. O'Connor was also in "The Mummy" and Sommers' sea beast film "Deep Rising," and he even had a cameo in the director's "G.I. Joe: The Rise of Cobra." Clearly, Sommers knows how to helm expensive, high-energy B-movies.

"Van Helsing" didn't become a full-blown feature film franchise, but there was a 33-minute animated prequel called "Van Helsing: The London Assignment," which once again starred Jackman and detailed Van Helsing's dealings with Jekyll & Hyde. Back when the movie hit theaters, it was further reported that Universal had indeed begun developing a sequel, only to scrap the idea when the film failed to become a big enough hit. Later, in 2020, it emerged that producer James Wan and "Overlord" director Julius Avery were working on a new "Van Helsing" movie, but that project appears to have since fallen through.

It might not have helped matters that "Van Helsing" got pretty awful reviews from critics. For example, Mick LaSalle haaaated the movie, writing for the San Francisco Chronicle:

"The movie is numbingly hyperactive. Here, vampires can attack day or night, and they do, relentlessly, particularly Dracula's three wives, merry female bats who delight in taunting their victims. In between bat attacks, the slender yet convoluted story doesn't exactly unfold. It just gets announced now and then, as the characters state the premise of scenes to each other as though at a pitch meeting."

He finished his review by writing that "Van Helsing" "has no more art than what a chimpanzee might do with an Etch-a-Sketch." It could have been reviews like that that kept interest in a sequel quite low.

#3604. Hideo Kojima's Next Game Officially Gets New Teaser Image, Fans Already Hunting for Clues

The Metal Gear Solid creator isn't tipping his hand

More than four years after its initial announcement, OD remains one of the biggest mysteries in the video game industry. We know Kojima Productions’ next game is some sort of horror experience, and that genre auteur Jordan Peele contributed to the project, butspecifics are hard to come by. Despite the caginess, we got a new look at OD as part of Kojima Productions’ 10th anniversary exhibition, which is running through Dec. 20 at Azabudai Hills Gallery in Tokyo.

A new promotional image for the exhibition shows Sophia Lillis’ character looking at a levitating red object that could be a broom or something else. The tagline reads, “For all players and screamers.” While the image doesn’t offer much to go on, the floating red broom may hint at the style of occult mystery that OD is going for: witchcraft, ghosts, and other paranormal phenomena seem to be on the table.

Many fans are assuming that the floating red object in the teaser image is a reference to witches. "Is that a broomstick?" one Reddit user wrote. "It’s the same red as Hunter Schafer’s costume in the last image release. Could she be some sort of witch? Wouldn’t predict witches but with Kojima I wouldn’t rule out anything.” The red is also the same red as the door shown in OD’s Knock teaser video from last year. “So Hunter’s character is a witch and she hijacked a plane full of people and the plane went missing. Calling it now!!!” another user said.

Others commented on the teaser's aesthetic. “The vibe this image gives off is brilliant. Instead of the generic dark and gloomy here we have something bright and surreal,” reads one comment. “I might be getting ahead of myself here but I think this game is going to be something special.”

One big point of debate for fans is whether the shot is an in-game render or a live-action photo. Fans were divided, with some thinking it was an in-game screenshot that showed the fidelity of MetaHuman’s 3D facial capture technology, while others believed details like the hair are simply too realistic to have been rendered in-engine.

While it hasn't been officially confirmed, there's a rumor that OD will be made up of multiple episodes handled by different writers, with OD: Knock being Kojima's part. Kojima previously said that the game will bring together an "Avengers" team-up of horror writers.

The most substantial look we’ve gotten at OD so far was the teaser trailer released last year. The trailer begins with redacted text that hints at curses. "This building was [redacted] from a 3D scan of an [redacted] found in an [redacted]," the subtitles read. Lillis’ character opens the door to a dreary apartment that feels reminiscent of the horror game P.T. She begins to light candles.

The new teaser image shows Lillis against a beige wall that calls to mind the blank walls of the apartment from the trailer. Combined with other promotional images, the game seems to contrast mundane backdrops with surreal imagery.

Kojima Productions’ ongoing 10th anniversary exhibition seems to offer more hints about the game, and while photography isn’t allowed at the event, images have leaked. One album posted on Reddit shows the red door from the trailer, along with cards that have dares written on them.

More information about OD may be hard to come by until we get closer to release. Kojima recently said in a podcast that he wants to just “keep quiet" and release the game to maintain a sense of "mystery."

Kojima also made first casting announcements for Physint and announced an AR collaboration with Niantic

#3598. How To Watch Zach Cregger's Resident Evil At Home

This has been a wonderful year for video game movie fans. We've seen both big productions and even indie movies translate the world of video games to cinema with much success (check out our list of the best video game adaptations of 2026 here).

The best movie based on a video game this year is Zach Cregger's "Resident Evil," which actually ignores the exact plot of the long-running Capcom franchise. Instead of being a faithful game recreation, it actually tells an original story that understands the true appeal of the best games in the "Resident Evil" franchise. Cregger crafted a horror comedy that's all about the frustration of finding yourself in an impossible situation where absolutely nothing works in your favor, and the comedy that comes from everything going wrong at the worst possible moment.

After dominating the box office, "Resident Evil" is finally coming home, with platforms like Fandango at Home listing the film with a release date for November 3, 2026 (you can of course choose another platform like Prime Video, or Apple TV). That means you can purchase or rent "Resident Evil" to watch from the comfort or horrors of home as soon as tomorrow, for the typical VOD price of $24.99 to purchase.

We don't know if "Resident Evil" will arrive on digital platforms with any bonus features just yet. That being said, we have seen and heard plenty about the making of the movie. When /Film had the chance to speak with Weta's Kevin Smith, one of the visual effects supervisors in the movie, he talked about how ridiculously complicated the sewer zombie was — especially with all the blood and goop coming out of his guts.

"Resident Evil" does what the best video game adaptations do — makes you feel like you're in the world of the game, even if it's telling an entirely different story than the familiar source mateiral. The film often feels like one of the journal entries you find in a "Resident Evil" game, a tragic story of a poor schmuck who messes around and finds themselves turned into a zombie.

Based on some of his comments about making the film, it seems unlikely Zach Cregger will return to make a sequel, but given how successful it's been at the box office, it's only a matter of time before we return to Raccoon City again.

Woot has dropped the price of the Amazon Basics 20,000mAh portable charger in black to $12.99 from $38.99, making it considerably cheaper than the $34.85 the same model currently costs elsewhere. You also get free standard shipping if you’re a Prime member (while everyone else pays $6), but keep in mind Woot doesn't deliver to Alaska, Hawaii, P.O. boxes, or APO addresses.

For that price, you're getting a fairly substantial backup battery that measures 4.48 by 2.83 by 1.16 inches, making it compact enough to slip into a backpack or tote, although its 0.77-pound weight might make it a little bulky for a jacket pocket. The trade-off is a fairly generous 20,000mAh capacity that should be enough to recharge a typical smartphone several times, making it particularly useful for camping trips or long weekends when access to power outlets is limited. And since you're likely to have more than just your phone with you on those trips, the charger comes with two USB-C ports and one USB-A port, allowing you to charge up to three devices at once.

When used individually, either USB-C port can deliver up to 20W, enough to fast-charge many modern smartphones, while the USB-A port tops out at 12W, making it better suited to older devices and smaller accessories. The catch is that connecting two or three devices reduces the total output to 15W shared across the ports, so charging everything together will take longer than plugging in one device at a time. Both USB-C ports can also be used to recharge the power bank itself, which takes around 4.4 hours, and the box includes a 1-foot USB-C to USB-C cable for charging (it won’t transfer data).

All said, anyone hoping to charge a laptop will need a higher-wattage model, but for occasional travel, commuting, or keeping your phone running during a long day, the capacity and price make a reasonable combination.
