#3587. 5 Best Sci-Fi Movies Where The Hero Dies

Needless to say, this article will be full of spoilers.

There are many things the "Star Trek" and "Star Wars" franchises have in common, not the least of which is hope. The former is set in a utopian future wherein human prejudice, capitalism, and war have all been dispensed with in favor of a society built on diplomacy, peace, and sharing. Similarly, all "Star Wars" stories posit that fascism is an impermanent state that's constantly being batted back down by the forces of good, no matter how often it tries to reassert itself. Heck, the first "Star Wars" movie was subtitled "A New Hope," showing the cycle at work.

But for every "Star Trek" and "Star Wars" film, there are lots of other science fiction movies that end on notes of sacrifice, death, or despair. In our darker moods, we humans often don't feel very good about the future, and that hopelessness can be reflected in our sci-fi tales. For every utopia, there is a dystopia. For every instance of humankind uniting to save their planet, there is a tale of humanity failing to stop its own self-destruction.

Indeed, the following five sci-fi movies feature protagonists who die. Some of the deaths are tragically noble. Others, however, are wasteful and harrowing, providing lessons for audiences about the dangers of various sins. All of them leave viewers in a poignant state, though, so let's look into the shadows of what is to come.

Ted Post's "Beneath the Planet of the Apes" was the first follow-up to Franklin J. Schaffner's 1968 classic "Planet of the Apes." If the original film is an on-the-nose satire of human interaction (transposing apes and humans in the planetary pecking order), then "Beneath" just pushes things into more obvious territory. The movie stars James Franciscus as Brent, a human astronaut who, as part of a rescue mission, somehow ends up on the same distant-future Earth that Taylor (Charlton Heston) did in "Planet of the Apes." Once there, Brent discovers that the apes are gearing up to take over the Forbidden Zone under the command of the gorilla Ursus (James Gregory), which Dr. Zaius (Maurice Evans) objects to.

In "Planet of the Apes," all the humans of the future appear to be mute and feral. Its sequel, on the other hand, reveals there is a subterranean enclave of surviving, ghoul-like humans who've developed psychic powers. The human psychics also worship an unexploded nuclear bomb, admiring its power. Taylor and Brent eventually meet up, but Taylor is naturally terrified when he sees the bomb's Alpha Omega markings, knowing that this particular bomb is capable of, just by itself, ending all life on the planet.

As it so happens, this is Chekhov's doomsday bomb. Once the bomb is introduced, we know that "Beneath the Planet of the Apes" can't possibly end well. Sure enough, when Taylor is mortally wounded at the end of the film, he curses and collapses on the bomb's detonation switch. In this case, the hero dies, along with everyone else on Earth. It's one of the bleakest endings in sci-fi history.

Douglas Trumbull's 1972 film "Silent Running" is so good that it made /Film's Jeremy Smith a lifelong sci-fi fan. More specifically, it's something of a dystopian movie and shows what happens when an idealist with principles butts heads with an uncaring, commercialized future that doesn't care about the calm, complexity, and beauty of the natural world. Everyone ought to watch this one, especially if you liked "Project Hail Mary" (and I know you did).

In the dystopian future of "Silent Running," humans have ruined Earth to the point of killing all its forests. Specimens of many planet species have been kept alive on spacebound repositories, which exist in giant greenhouse-like geodesic domes. Bruce Dern plays Freeman Lowell, a botanist who has been tasked with looking after the samples on a ship called the Valley Forge. The Valley Forge is owned by American Airlines.

When the ship is ordered to jettison its plants and head back to Earth (as it's needed for commercial purposes), Freeman turns on his corporate bosses and proves that he's willing to kill his human crew mates to protect the forest domes. Shockingly, he actually manages to escape with one of the domes, although he loses others in the process. By the end of the movie, Freeman even makes the ultimate sacrifice to keep the forest protected.

Of course, "Silent Running" is a commentary on modern-day environmentalism and how horrible commercialism always seems to outweigh the needs of our planet. Is "Silent Running" preachy? Yes. Is it tragic and great? Also yes.

John Carpenter's 1988 film "They Live" stands as a vital criticism of the United States under Ronald Reagan. In the film, the nameless protagonist, "Nada" (Roddy Piper), finds a pair of alien-constructed sunglasses that allow him to see through all the secret alien disguises on Earth. Certain citizens are revealed to be creepy aliens in disguise, but more so, billboards, magazines, and advertisements are shown to be masking subliminal messages that make human consumers more complacent by ordering them to "OBEY," "STAY ASLEEP," or "CONSUME."

Nada is hardly the best person to make this alien discovery. He's a blue-collar drifter without the means to handle this weird revelation, and when he tries to tell someone else about it, they end up fighting for a really, really, really long time. That's not a joke, either, as Piper and his co-star Keith David beat the hell out of each other for what feels like 20 minutes.

Luckily, Nada has connections within the local shanty town. There, he learns the aliens have been mingling with Earth's wealthy and using brain-scrambling signals to keep the impoverished docile. "They Live" then ends with a raid on the alien compound with Nada, David's Frank Armitage, and a few others trying to shut down the alien signal once and for all.

Although a sci-fi movie, it's easy to believe that "They Live" might very well be a documentary. The ultra-wealthy, we seem to inherently understand, are deliberately controlling us through media and money. It felt true in 1988, and it definitely feels true now. Nada ends up taking care of business, but not before being mortally wounded. In the film's most inspiring scene, his final act on this planet is to flip the middle finger to the aliens, spitting his last breath at them.

In 2011, Lars von Trier released the second entry in what might be considered his "Depression Trilogy," a series of movies that began with 2009's "Antichrist" and ended with 2013's "Nymphomaniac." The second film, "Melancholia," is just as much a metaphor for depression as it is a sci-fi apocalypse flick. "Melancholia" takes place in a world where a rogue planet, known as Melancholia, is going to slingshot around Earth before looping back in space and colliding with it, ending all life. The gravitational loops are a little dance of death, a preview of the apocalypse.

With this impending doom looming in the background, the movie centers on Justine (Kirsren Dunst), a newly-married woman who finds herself sliding back into the depression she has long fought off. When she learns that all life on Earth will end, Justine finds herself grimly pleased. She asserts that all life on Earth is evil, there is no other life in the universe, and that human extinction would be a blessing. Death cannot be stopped, and its coming is a release. Meanwhile, eerie things start to happen as Melancholia approaches. Electricity begins behaving weirdly. Certain characters flee, but where should they go? Justine doesn't panic. She's apathetic.

In the end, no one in the film lives. "Melancholia" is a beautiful, harrowing, and shockingly accurate portrait of a depressed mind. Justine has simply stopped caring about anything because it feels like there is no escape. Because, in the mind of Lars von Trier, there isn't.

You already know if "Melancholia" is your kind of movie. Just be sure to follow it with something more optimistic, like "Apocalypse Now."

Coralie Fargeat's 2024 horror hit "The Substance" is hardly subtle. Demi Moore stars as Elisabeth Sparkle, a celebrated actor who's recently made her living by hosting a TV workout program. Her disgusting boss (Dennis Quaid) fires her early in the film, all but saying out loud that she's too old to be a heartthrob anymore. From there, Elisabeth is put in contact with a shadowy pharmaceutical company that mails her doses of "The Substance," which promises to make her young again ... in a sense.

Sure enough, when Elisabeth injects herself with The Substance, she passes out, her back splits open like a cocoon, and a younger woman (Margaret Qualley) crawls out. These two women are the same person, but the younger one decides to take the name Sue. According to the rules of The Substance, Elisabeth and Sue have to take turns being conscious, one week each, with Sue feeding off Elisabeth's spinal fluids. Naturally, though, "Sue" doesn't want to go back to being the "old" Elisabeth she resents, and the consequences of what happens when the rules of The Substance are broken are quickly made horrifically clear.

By the end of the movie, Elisabeth has become a literal puddle of dead puffy flesh on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. "The Substance" is openly about the callowness of Hollywood and its dogged tendency to cast aside women "of a certain age" in favor of youthful ingénues. It should be recalled that Moore was nominated for an Oscar for Best Actress for "The Substance" but lost to a youthful ingénue, Mikey Madison. The message of "The Substance" played out in real life. How darkly poetic.

Johnny Depp is an accomplished character actor with a long and wildly successful career. Arguably one of Depp's best roles is as Captain Jack Sparrow in the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, which are streaming in their entirety with a Disney+ subscription. I didn't expect the 63 year-old to have jokes when talking about possibly returning to the franchise alongside Orlando Bloom's Will Turner.

While Depp will return to theaters in Ebenezer this month, some moviegoers are hoping to see him return in a future Pirates of the Caribbean movie. During a recent interview with People, the Edward Scissorhands actor was asked about possibly returning to the beloved franchise, and responded with:

Well, I think we should have a contest of who can grow the fastest non-beard. Because neither of us can grow a beard, I don’t think. I can’t, for sure, but maybe he can. I don’t know.

Shots fired. Despite having facial hair in the Pirates of the Caribbean films, it turns out that neither Johnny Depp nor Orlando Bloom can actually grow a beard. While sidestepping whether or not he'd be down to return as Jack Sparrow, the Sweeney Todd actor was sure to poke fun at both himself, and his famous co-star.

Ebenezer marks Depp's first real return to a big Hollywood movie since the verdict of his defamation trial with Amber Heard was revealed. He spent a few years living abroad and getting out of the spotlight, but he's back playing the title role of Ti West's forthcoming holiday movie. Only time will tell if the upcoming book to screen adaptation ends up being considered one of the best Christmas movies of all time, but it seems like a game changer for the actor.

There's been chatter about more Pirates movies for a few years. At one point multiple movies were in development, including one that would star Margot Robbie. Unfortunately, there hasn't been any concrete updates about one of these projects moving forward in the development process. Although with Johnny Depp returning to the big screen, I have to assume that the chatter surrounding the franchise, and his possible return as Captain Jack Sparrow, will get louder.

Depp starred as the protagonist in all five of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, which ran in theaters from 2003 to 2017. The same can't be said for Orlando Bloom, who was absent for On Stranger Tides. He ended up returning in Dead Men Tell No Tales, which is the most recent installment in the action/adventure property.

All five of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies are streaming now on Disney+. Only time will tell if a sixth movie ends up being green lit by the powers that be at Disney, but there does seem to be a ton of chatter about that possibility online.

#3585. Heidi Klum Shocks In Severed Hand Halloween Costume

Heidi Klum has done it again. The Project Runway host exceeded all our Halloween expectations by transforming herself into a giant, severed human hand nearly two meters tall for the latest edition of her annual party, held Saturday night in New York City. The costume, which required hours of work by her makeup and prop team, left no detail to chance: hyper-realistic veins modeled after her own anatomy, wrinkles, red-painted nails, and an exxagerated version of the rings she typically wears.

“Mike [Marino, from the special effects team ProRenFX] has all of these scans of my body, so he was able to use those to create an exact replica of my hand,” Klum explained to Vogue. “We wanted everything to be as realistic as possible—the anatomy, the veins, the muscles, all the little details that make a hand look like a real hand.”

The costume’s structure used the model's legs to form two of the fingers, while her right arm provided mobility for the thumb. Only her eyes and mouth were visible amid the bloody wounds on her palm, from which—to top off the gruesomeness of it all—Heidi Klum would occasionally spit out the fake blood that a team of assistants injected into her mouth. The most macabre part was at the wrist, where a horrific gash exposed a jumble of blood, bones, and torn flesh.

Heidi Klum (L) recieves an injection of fake blood to augment her 2026 Halloween costume.

Other guests at Klum's party included Kyle MacLachlan, who arrived dressed as his character from The Flintstones; Neil Patrick Harris and his husband David Burtka, dressed as the girls from The Shining; and Heidi Klum and Flavio Briatore's daughter, Leni Klum.

Before making her grand entrance, the host had built up anticipation on social media by posting clues about this year’s costume, such as a photo of her real hand that showed her wedding ring alongside the small tattoo of husband Tom Kaulitz's name. It, too, was part of her Halloween costume. “Nothing was overlooked! I love that Mike pays attention to things that most people might not even notice at first. The details make these costumes so special. It’s not just any giant hand: It’s my giant hand!” Klum said.

Heidi Klum 2026 Halloween costume, as seen from the back.

This is the 25th annual Halloween party thrown by the former Victoria’s Secret Angel: The event began in 2000, and has only continued to expand in scope. “ “Can you believe it? Twenty-five years of Halloween, costumes, incredible transformations, and so many amazing memories,” she said.

Last night’s “amputated hand” joins Klum's collection of Halloween costumes that ranges from last year’s mythological Medusa (with a petrified Kaulitz by her side) to E.T., to Shrek’s Fiona, to a disgusting giant worm inside which she feared she might suffocate. We're already looking forward to what she comes up with for next year.

#3584. How To Watch Sense And Sensibility (2026) At Home

There's a reason Jane Austen's 1811 novel "Sense and Sensibility" has been adapted so many times to the screen and the stage. The story of the Dashwood sisters, as they experience love and heartbreak after being forced to move away from their family estate and into the cottage of a relative, is as timeless in its coming of age story as it is timely and relatable in its themes and sharp social commentary.

There are many movies based on Jane Austen books, some retaining the period setting and others taking a more modern approach. The best Jane Austen movies are the ones that simply focus on the relatable and complex heroine and the hardships they endure. Case in point, Georgia Oakley's 2026 adaptation of "Sense and Sensibility" starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as Elinor and Marianne. /Film's own Ben Pearson praised the film as one you absolutely should watch even in a crowded movie landscape, highlighting how "funny, charming, sweet, and full of suppressed yearning" this adaptation is, and even comparing it to Greta Gerwig's 2019 film adaptation of "Little Women."

After the film failed to make much of an impact in movie theaters, Focus Features is bringing "Sense and Sensibility" to digital platforms on November 3, 2026. Those wanting to actually own the movie rather than just lease it from a platform that can take it away from you at their whim, will have to wait until December 15, 2026 for Universal Pictures Home to release the film on Blu-ray.

It's been over 30 years since Ang Lee's phenomenal 1995 version of "Sense and Sensibility," but now we have a new take that offers a similarly gorgeous-looking movie adaptation. Georgia Oakley's movie  gives the relationship between the Dashwood sisters a bigger focus, especially in how they grow and learn from one another amid their respective romances.

The film also stars Caitríona Balfe, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, and Fiona Shaw — who has a standout scene. Even if "Sense and Sensibility" didn't really make a splash at the box office and doesn't make much of an impact during awards season, it is a tale worth experiencing, whether for the first time, or just for a new time.

The home video release of "Sense and Sensibility" also arrives with this bonus content at participating retailers.

#3583. 10 Hacks Ever Siri AI User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

If you're like me, you've spent years ignoring most of Siri's functionality. Sure, it's great for setting timers, making calls, and sending a text. But that's kind of it—Apple's promise of an "always-on" digital assistant never truly delivered.

But that's finally changed with the recent launch of Siri AI. Fifteen years after debuting the app on the iPhone 4S and four years after the release of ChatGPT, Apple has taken the time to build out its own private Apple Foundation Models (with little help from Google) that work both on-device and on Apple's servers to give quick responses to your queries. Siri AI's answers are short, to the point, and actually useful. However, the conversational side isn't the only new thing about Siri AI. In fact, once you scratch the surface, you'll find Siri AI features embedded across the entire iOS and macOS ecosystem. Here's how to get the most out of Apple's new, enhanced digital assistant.

Siri AI is already tuned for brevity. Compared to Gemini or Claude, its responses are short and to the point. But still, if you ask something with your voice, it responds using voice as well. I personally prefer to quickly read through Siri responses. If you’re like me, you can enable a hidden setting that makes sure that Siri always answers silently, no matter if you’re writing to it or using your voice. Go to Settings > Siri > Responses and switch to the Silent Response option.

On the other hand, if you prefer to listen to Siri's responses, it's worth it to spend some time fine-tuning them. If you have an iPhone that’s under two years old, you have access to a more expressive Siri voice. Siri AI has an Expressive Voice feature that works on iPhone 17 Pro and higher, iPhone Air, and Macs with an M3 processor or higher (at least 12GB RAM).

To find this feature, go to Settings > Siri > Voice. Here, you can change the Pace to make Siri faster or slower. The big feature is the Expressivity slider; you can use it to make Siri sound brighter and more enthusiastic, rather than flat. You also have several voice options at the top (color-coded).

Visual Intelligence is deeply integrated into iOS 27 and macOS 27, and it turns anything on your screen into a source that Siri AI can act upon. It can search anything on your screen, and even take action on things it finds out. You can highlight any text on an iPhone, tap and hold, and choose the Ask Siri option. On the Mac, Ask Siri is the first option in the right-click menu. Choose a file, select text, and get started talking to Siri.

But it goes further. Just pull up Siri AI on your iPhone or Mac and start asking questions about what you’re seeing on screen. If you’re seeing a photo of a cafe on Instagram, ask where it is, or ask Siri to open it in Maps. If you’re watching a scene from a movie or a TV show, ask Siri where it’s from.

Clean Up was part of Apple Intelligence features in iOS 18, but it wasn’t great. It used on-device models to remove objects, and the results were lacking. Now that Apple runs its own Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute, it can securely process images on its servers, and the Clean Up process is much better. It now removes objects from photos very reliably, and even accounts for shadows. But to use this, you have to make sure to use the High Quality feature (instead of the default Auto mode).

Tap the Edit button in a photo, go to Tools > Clean Up, and from the top, switch to the High Quality option. Now brush over or tap an object you want to remove. Then, tap Clean Up and wait for a while until Apple’s servers complete the process. Tap Done to save the changes.

One of the most tedious parts of using the Calendar app is manually entering multiple events from a complicated schedule—say, for a season's worth of your kid’s soccer practices, or your college course's weekly lecture schedule. With Visual Intelligence in iOS 27, this is now table stakes: You can point your iPhone camera towards a schedule or take a screenshot of one, then tap the Add to Calendar button. Siri will recognize all the events, and you’ll get an option to add them to the calendar individually or all at once.

Siri AI's Mail integration is a hidden gem. Once your iPhone or Mac is done indexing your local data from Mail, you can use Siri AI to triage and manage your Mail without even opening the Mail app. In my testing, it works really well, especially because Siri AI understands the context of an email. This means you don't need to remember the exact details about the sender or the subject. You can just ask something like, "Find all emails about my flights from last week and send them to my accountant." You can also ask it to do things for you. For example, you can say, "Archive all the emails from Walmart from last month," and it will give you a one-button option to do just that.

When you start using the new Siri AI more often, you'll realize that it asks for confirmation way too often. For things like deleting mail, that's useful. But for sending messages, less so. There is a hidden setting that removes the extra step when it comes to sending messages via Siri. Go to Settings > Siri > Responses and enable Automatically Send Messages.

After the Siri AI upgrade in iOS 27, I find myself using the Camera Control often, and you should try it too. Just press and hold the Camera Control button to launch the camera's Siri mode. Point towards anything you want to find out more about and tap the big Siri icon. In a second or two, you will get the Siri response at the top, along with relevant actions based on what you're looking at. This feature is genuinely useful, and if you don't like using the Camera Control (or don't have access to it on your iPhone), you can also add the Siri AI shortcut to the lock screen, Control Center, or the Action button.

While Shortcuts has been one of Apple's most powerful features, it's also one of the hardest to use. Making an automation requires setting up steps, selecting variables, and thinking about chronology, and more. With Siri AI, Apple is trying to reduce that burden. And when it comes to simpler stuff that an everyday iPhone user needs, it works.

For example, you can open Shortcuts, create a new shortcut, and use the Describe a shortcut feature to talk about a Shortcut you want to build in natural language. You can ask Siri to create a daily morning Shortcut that shows you the day's weather, upcoming calendar events, and the to-do list for the day. You can also ask it to create a Shortcut that converts images in batches and creates new notes with a pre-made template.

While Apple is now using its own Apple Foundation Models for the new Siri AI, ChatGPT isn’t technically gone. If you have a complex question, or if Siri AI’s answer isn’t doing the trick, you can still summon ChatGPT from the Siri AI app (no need to go to the ChatGPT app for this). Tap on the text field in the Siri app, choose the Ask option and then switch to the ChatGPT service. Siri AI is quite intelligent at routing, so if ChatGPT can’t answer, it will route you back to Siri AI’s own models.

Joseph Zada may be the star tribute of Sunrise on the Reaping, but Mckenna Grace is absolutely the victor of the movie's press tour. Lately, she's been wearing a ton of amazing Hunger Games fashion, often inspired by Jennifer Lawrence, but I think she just stepped out in the best one yet on this Monday.

Grace went to the Berlin premiere of The Hunger Games prequel in an incredible reference to the best movie of the franchise. Check it out:

A post shared by visitBerlin (@visitberlin)

My jaw dropped when I saw this on Visit Berlin. Obviously, she's paying tribute to Jennifer Lawrence's fire-catching The Hunger Games: Catching Fire dress. Who can forget the moment when Katniss and Peeta turn up at the Tribute Parade in matching flaming outfits that takes the breath away of Panem? It's a key piece from the movie franchise, and I'm so happy Mckenna Grace decided to put her own spin on it.

I'll never forget the first time this dress came on screen in Catching Fire, and this tribute to it is just expertly executed. Bravo to Grace, and her team led by stylist Molly Dickson. She really is Mckenna's own Cinna.

I mean, it's moments like this what reminds me why I love celebrity fashion!This has to be a custom dress, right? It recaptures the dress from the movie SO WELL, from the halter top to the flames all over it. I especially love how the top of it is shimmery and how the bottom is completely red. It's as if the dress is completely engulfed in flames at its ends. Grace also wore a similar headpiece to the one J-Law's Katniss wears in the movie and had her hair styled in curls.

This is just one of many Hunger Games references Grace has been doing while promoting the 2026 movie release. Last month she also wore a dress very similar to Katniss's white gown and another one that referenced Rue's interview dress. Last week, she also turned up in an ensemble that looked just like the Hunger Games arena in her movie.

It's actually quite perfect for Grace to channel J-Law's Hunger Games fashion because in Sunrise on the Reaping, her character of Maysilee inspires Katniss. She's the first tribute in the games to wear the mockingjay pin. .

Sunrise on the Reaping takes place during the 25th Hunger Games when Haymitch Abernathy is chosen to compete at the age of 16. It doesn't come out until November 20, but the first reactions came in last week, and the prequel is already being called "a near perfect Hunger Games movie".

As excited as I am, I'm also over here on the edge of my seat over what Grace do next as the movie's press tour continues!

#3581. Crystal Lake Does For Friday The 13th What Marvel Once Did To Spider-Man

Creating a brand new take on a classic character who has literal decades of history to their name is no simple task. No one knows this challenge better than folks who've made writing comic books their career, as so many characters have histories and continuity that are so long and complex they practically make new stories almost prohibitive. To help with this issue, major comic labels such as Marvel and DC Comics introduced the concept of retroactive continuity, which began as a way of allowing writers to subtly shift around previously established lore (or, alternatively, introduce new elements that already took place). Given that characters like Spider-Man and Batman have been around for close to 100 years now, this concept of retconning eventually expanded to include the idea of a fully rebooted or an entirely separate, parallel continuity.

That latter example is what writer Brian Michael Bendis attempted with Spider-Man in the fall of 2000, with the series "Ultimate Spider-Man" (which just ended!). Presented as a way of modernizing the character while reintroducing and remixing his history, supporting cast, and rogues gallery, the series served as both summation of the character up to that point as well as a new beginning. This month's "Crystal Lake" series essentially does the same thing to "Friday the 13th" and Jason Voorhees. Almost as if to prove the similarity, the reaction to "Crystal Lake" has been as passionate and polarizing as the fan reaction to "Ultimate Spider-Man" was. While the two projects share a lot in common creatively, the key difference is that "Ultimate Spider-Man" was always presented as separate from the main "Amazing Spider-Man" continuity, while it remains to be seen where "Crystal Lake" intends to position itself in "Friday the 13th" lore.

While neither "Ultimate Spider-Man" nor "Crystal Lake" would have been worthwhile if the writing had been subpar (or the artwork/performances of the cast had been bad, respectively), by far the most exciting aspect of both projects is the way they took the elements and histories of their respective franchises and examined them anew. In "Ultimate Spider-Man," bringing the character to a then-modern era did a lot of the heavy lifting in making the Spidey mythos feel fresh. Yet on top of that, Brian Michael Bendis added some wrinkles to the mythos which ended up influencing future Spidey adaptations. He came up with the idea of a genetically modified spider as opposed to a radioactive spider that delivers the fateful bite to Peter Parker (which appeared in Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man"), and later the development of Peter's Aunt May discovering his secret identity as Spider-Man, as seen in the final moments of Jon Watts' "Spider-Man: Homecoming." Yet even with these new elements, "Ultimate Spider-Man" retained the core tropes and flavor of "Spider-Man."

In a similar fashion, "Crystal Lake" showrunner Brad Caleb Kane has allowed his series to reap the benefits of "Friday the 13th" lore without having to conform to it. Unlike Bendis, Kane did not modernize the Voorhees mythos and instead sets the series in the early 1970s, which is ostensibly the correct time period (more on this in a bit). The legend of Jason (Callum Vinson), his accidental drowning through negligence, his mother Pamela (Linda Cardellini) turning to madness through her grief, and the death curse on Crystal Lake are all present. Yet there are various twists, turns, and expansions on the characters and story which feel fresh, including a new concept for Jason's origin which has already become hotly debated.

A big part of why "Ultimate Spider-Man" and Brian Michael Bendis got to enjoy such creative freedom is due to the comic being part of Marvel's "Ultimate" line, which allowed their various creative teams to essentially make an adaptation of the Marvel Universe. That's because the general idea with the "main" Marvel Universe is that it's on a vague sliding scale of continuity. That's also generally been the idea with the "Friday the 13th" films so far, with even the one remake in the series, 2009's "Friday the 13th," being so close to the core elements of the character that some fans see it as more of a sequel. This is because Jason and his mythos already went to some wacky, improbable places before that film. This dubious veracity was established in the very first few "Friday the 13th" movies, in which Jason is explicitly said to have died in 1957, yet turns out to still be alive somehow.

All this raises the question: Is Brad Caleb Kane's "Crystal Lake" an adaptation of the "Friday" mythos, akin to "Ultimate Spider-Man," or is it intended as a loosely related entry in the main franchise? Though there is much in the "Friday" films which seems to contradict plot points in "Crystal Lake" (like the aforementioned time period change), the show could be establishing a new retconned backstory in a similar fashion to something like what "Freddy's Dead" did for the "A Nightmare on Elm Street" series. Whatever ends up being the case, it's been a treat to see Kane get to play around with Jason, Pamela, and the "Friday" lore, and while it may be upsetting the more literal-minded horror fans, for us longtime comic book nerds, it's all gravy, baby.

#3580. Jurassic Park Meets Outlast in Terrifying Steam Game Coming Next Week

For some reason, there haven't been that many truly great dinosaur video games throughout history. Ark: Survival Evolved had plenty of success despite the fact it was quite janky, and The Isle has spawned myriad viral videos thanks to its proximity chat. Jurassic World Evolution 3 is by far the best licensed dinosaur game, but it focuses on managing the theme park, as opposed to fighting and surviving.

Enter Wilderdark. Launching on Steam on Tuesday, Nov. 10 from indie dev Team Junkfish, this is a survival horror take on the stuck-on-an-island-with-dinosaurs concept. The inhabitants of the island aren't your standard dinos, though: they're infected with a "mysterious ectoparasitic organism," according to the game's Steam page. This manifests as glowing, grotesque growths on each creature's skin, and it's spread to plenty of the flora inhabiting the island too.

Where Jurassic Park has a "theme park gone wrong" setting, Wilderdark instead focuses on the protagonist, someone sent to the "unnatural island in search of immortality." Plenty of people have tried to uncover the island's secrets before, including your own parents, but they've all vanished.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Since this is a survival game, you can also expect some crafting. You'll set up camp, gather resources, and collect samples from the various creatures and plant life that make up the island. You'll also need to use a camera to take photos and scan every living organism you come across, so stealth is of the utmost importance.

If you want to try before you buy, there's a free Wilderdark demo available right now, from the latest Steam Next Fest. Reviews are currently mixed for the demo, but that's mostly down to technical issues that stemmed from an older demo build. At this point, I've accepted that Taylor Swift operates on an entirely different creative clock than the rest of us. Of all the behind-the-scenes stories to come out of the 2026 movie schedule, I wasn't prepared for what Toy Story 5 director Andrew Stanton had to say about how quickly she wrote "I Knew It, I Knew You" after seeing the Pixar sequel. The guy has spent decades making some of animation's most beloved films, but apparently even he couldn't keep his language family-friendly when he heard what she'd done. Here’s his NOT PG reaction after Swift wrote the song in less than a day.

During a recent Q&A with Swift, Stanton recalled how the singer ended up contributing a song to the film. Swift's brother Austin had urged her to watch an early cut while she was exhausted from the Eras Tour, and she finally agreed once she'd recovered. She immediately connected with Jessie, the cowgirl at the center of the sequel, and called Stanton from the screening room that afternoon. Hours later, Disney's music team called him again, this time with news he couldn't quite believe:

You [Swift] saw it that morning with your brother, and that was at 10 o'clock. And then at noon my FaceTime rings, and it's from Tom, but it's you guys, you and Austin, and you're still in your seats and you're gushing about the movie. And you said, ‘You want to do the song?’ Like, there wasn't even a debate about this or a discussion. It was just, ‘You want to do the song?’ We're like, ‘Great, great, great.’ And we almost got off so that you couldn't change your mind.

I love that Stanton's first instinct was to end the call before the “Shake it Off” performer could reconsider. Getting her to agree to write the song was already a pretty big deal, but he had no idea just how quickly things were about to move. He continued:

And then I go home that night, and Tom calls me, the head of music, and says, ‘She wrote the song.’ I'm like, ‘What?’ And I'm like, ‘No, no, no, no. She found it or she had it already. She relabeled it.’ And he's like, ‘No, she's in the studio and she's written the song, and I'm driving right now to hear it.’ I'm like, ‘Wow, get the f out of here.’

I kind of love that his first assumption was that Swift must have quietly pulled an old song off the shelf and given it a Toy Story label. He seemed genuinely baffled that someone could watch a movie in the morning and have a song ready before dinner. Apparently Stanton wasn't the only Toy Story veteran surprised by the music icon's involvement.

Stanton's day somehow got weirder. Around 9 that evening, he got another FaceTime call, this time from Disney CEO Bob Iger, who stood beside Swift and raved about the track. Stanton recalled asking the music A-lister if she'd really written it before calling her "a beast." The director didn't hear the finished song in person until several days later, when he flew to Los Angeles. He added:

I got choked up when I heard it. And the only other time I've heard a song that just dropped from thin air and was perfect was when Randy Newman came in and played 'You've Got a Friend in Me" on a piano with six of us.

That's serious praise, especially coming from someone who helped shape Pixar's original era. Newman's "You've Got a Friend in Me" remains one of the most recognizable movie songs of all time, and Swift has said she didn't want her contribution to feel out of place. She wrote and produced "I Knew It, I Knew You" with longtime collaborator Jack Antonoff, drawing on her country roots and Jessie's complicated history of being left behind.

While the song came together ridiculously fast, Stanton offered a beautiful explanation: Swift's lifelong connection to Toy Story prepared her for it. The filmmaker said the tune really took "a lifetime" to write, starting with her watching the films as a kid. I think that's a much sweeter explanation than the one he gave on that first phone call.

Toy Story 5 is now streaming with a Disney+ subscription, with the Taylor Swift and Antonoff track playing over the end credits. And if you need a reason to revisit the flick, picture Stanton losing his mind and dropping F-bombs on FaceTime over the song.

#3578. Everything You Should See Along With ‘You Can See Everything’

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

You Can See Everything, the new documentary about Theranos founder (and accomplished con artist) Elizabeth Holmes from filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is breaking records (and brains). Not only is it raking it in at the box office in a way that few documentaries can manage, it’s also dominating the pop culture chat right now thanks to genre-defying techniques; a huge, rule-breaking twist (that I won't spoil); and its unrepentant and inexplicably mesmerizing subject.

While some might argue that you should head into this incredible film experience fresh, if you’re unfamiliar with any of the three major figures involved, you will benefit from a little prep work before you head in—and if you've already seen it, you're no doubt eager to dive even deeper into this truly remarkable (in every sense of the word) story. Here’s what you should watch, read, and listen to before or after You Can See Everything.

To put it simply: There’s a lot going on here. To ensure you can appreciate the film, you should make sure you know at least the basics about three things: Elizabeth Holmes (and why she’s infamous), and the work of both Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Here’s the crash course.

The 2019 podcast The Dropout is one of the most efficient ways to get the background on Holmes and Theranos. In the style of a true crime podcast, this show from ABC and journalist Rebecca Jarvis offers a deep dive into Holmes and her crimes that will give you all the background you’ll need.

John Carreyrou is the journalist who broke the Holmes story wide open, and his award-winning book Bad Blood offers a more journalistic and less sensational investigation than other accounts, providing a close-up look at Holmes in her CEO persona—an alternately terrifying and charismatic person who comes across as a “character” Holmes is playing. The book will inform your viewing of the documentary in important ways.

While Nathan Fielder is getting most of the attention for You Can See Everything, co-director Lance Oppenheim brings his signature technique to the film—it wouldn’t be nearly as interesting without his visual sensibility and framing.

Oppenheim has helmed several notable films, as he’s made a name for himself as a brilliant documentarian over the last few years, but to get ready for You Can See Everything, check out Spermworld, his 2024 exploration of unregulated sperm donations (you read that right). The doc deals with people who are as reality-challenged, manipulative, and possibly delusional as Holmes, and it will prep you for his visual style of extreme close-ups and excessive coverage that seems almost impossible in a normal documentary setting. You can stream Spermworld on Hulu.

If you’re unfamiliar with Nathan Fielder’s work, you need to strap in, because he’s unlike any other comedian or documentarian you’ve ever encountered.

To get a sense of his style, start with Nathan for You, a comedy-documentary-reality TV hybrid in which Fielder—as a version of himself—tries to use his business experience to help struggling people and small businesses. Presented as totally sincere, Fielder’s ideas are nevertheless increasingly elaborate and, in a word, unhinged. This show will familiarize you with Fielder’s persona and approach, but if you only have time to cram one episode, check out the series finale, “Finding Frances.” It follows Fielder’s attempts to reunite one of his earlier clients with his long-lost love, and it is a nearly perfect encapsulation of his style and approach. You can stream Nathan for You on HBO Max, Hoopla or Paramount Plus, or rent it episode-by-episode on Prime Video.

You should also watch at least some of Fielder’s other series, The Rehearsal. Here, Fielder (again, portraying a version of himself) attempts to help people prepare for difficult conversations utilizing increasingly outlandish techniques and scenarios that spiral into comedic insanity, including building sets, hiring actors, and immersing himself and his subjects in an alternate reality of sorts—an approach that will prepare you for some of You Can See Everything’s swerves. If you don’t have time to watch the whole thing, just check out the first episode, “Orange Juice, No Pulp.” It’s a self-contained chapter and will give you the basics. You can stream The Rehearsal on Apple TV or HBO Max, or rent episodes on Prime Video.

Have more bandwidth before watching You Can See Everything, or want a deeper dive after the documentary has melted your brain? Here’s what else you can check out.

The companion podcast to Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood: The Final Chapter, is well worth a listen. Hearing the journalist’s perspective about his investigation and work during and after Holmes’ trial offers additional insight into her personality and methods that will really resonate after watching her in Fielder and Oppenheim’s doc.

Once you’ve noodled on You Can See Everything for a moment, there are two more movies you should check out.

For more on Holmes’s specific grift and how she pulled it off, Alex Gibney’s excellent The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley is the way to go, especially if you didn’t follow the Theranos story closely at the time and your main visual guide to Holmes is the new documentary. Gibney’s film is more traditional, but offers a wealth of insight into Holmes and her bubble. You can stream The Inventor on HBO Max or rent it on Prime VIdeo.

If you more from co-director Lance Oppenheim, watch Some Kind of Heaven, his 2020 breakout documentary about The Villages retirement community in Florida. It’s the film that put Oppenheim on the map, and offers hints of the same detached observational style that makes You Can See Everything so arresting. You can stream Some Kind of Heaven on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Speaking of which, if you loved the visual style and “enhanced” reality of You Can See Everything and want to see more of that, catch the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime, still in theaters. It’s Oppenheim's narrative film directorial debut, and combines his hyperstyled visual flair with thriller pacing and a narrative based on a true story.

The Curse, Fielder’s 2023 TV series, is his first work of fiction, and it offers some fascinating insights. It follows a newly married couple (played by Fielder and Emma Stone) who struggle to get an HGTV-style show off the ground as things get excruciatingly awkward (and, eventually, kind of surreal). After watching You Can See Everything, it will be interesting to see how Fielder views the power of editing, the ethics of reality TV, and working with a name actor to get the results that he wants. Plus, similarly to the film, The Curse swerves into a final act that will melt your brain. You can stream The Curse on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

You should also definitely watch The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu series starring Amanda Seyfried. It’s a well-made film, and Seyfried’s performance was rightly praised for capturing the weirdness of Holmes' public persona. You can stream The Dropout on Hulu.

#3577. Godzilla Minus Zero's King Ghidorah Design Leaks Online Thanks To Merchandise

Not even the King of the Monsters is immune to that most terrifying and undefeated of foes: merchandise. "Godzilla Minus Zero" director Takashi Yamazaki has kept his cards close to the vest on the highly-anticipated sequel, even with multiple full-length trailers hyping up the carnage that's to come in post-War Japan (and possibly New York City). But, as we creep closer to the impending release and what looks like a potential box office record in the making, there are always certain aspects bound to escape containment no matter how hard the concerned parties try — like the look of the kaiju-sized villain that Godzilla will be squaring off against this time around. Needless to say, what follows will count as major spoilers for those who wish to go in 100% fresh and unblemished, so don't say we didn't warn you!

For those who're still here and decided to ignore my helpful advice, well, it's hard to blame any of you. In fact, it's kind of hard to consider this a "spoiler" in any real conventional sense, either. "Godzilla" fans who've been following along closely already know that Ghidorah, the famous three-headed dragon from outer space, is set to play a huge role in "Minus Zero." But, despite keeping any actual glimpse of the flying, electricity-spewing monster away from the marketing, the bad guy's final look has leaked out courtesy of a Desktop Monster toy listing that you can see here.

Ghidorah Minus Zero toy design pic.twitter.com/g7slE3UPNr

Yup, sure looks like a three-headed dragon to me! The thing is, the whole look and feel of Ghidorah has been fairly set in stone over the years, and any deviations would have to be considered minor cosmetic tweaks, at best. That's certainly the case here, though diehards will inevitably notice some key details. Let's break them all down below.

Love it, hate it, or something in between, there's no denying the fact that 2019's "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" managed to visualize each and every one of its iconic kaiju — from Big G to Mothra to Rodan — in all their majestic splendor. But everyone's favorite extraterrestrial from outer space, Ghidorah, was a particular highlight. Lifted directly out of the old Toho movies with an updated and modernized spin, the final result raised the bar impossibly high for any other adaptation to come in the future. Needless to say, "Godzilla Minus Zero" has embraced that challenge and come out swinging with its own spin ... and it looks just different enough.

Let's get the obvious disclaimer out of the way: There's only so much you can do with the general look of a giant, golden, three-headed dragon, and "Minus Zero" certainly isn't reinventing the wheel. The snakelike heads, the webbed wings, and club-like tails are all present and accounted for this time around. But a closer look reveals some key differences. There's some gnarly-looking quills/spikes running up and down King Ghidorah's back, reminiscent of the spikey plates Godzilla sports. The wings are more of a wyvern-like design, too, with Ghidorah's "arms" resembling that of a pterosaur (those birdlike beasts that coexisted with dinosaurs, for the uninitiated).

But the most interesting twist is how much this Ghidorah resembles the one featured in Japan's "Godzilla the Ride: Giant Monsters Ultimate Battle" — an indoor theme park with a short film directed by Takashi Yamazaki himself, featuring his design for Ghidorah. If it ain't broke, don't fix it! Yamazaki appears to have taken that to heart.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" stomps into theaters November 6, 2026.

#3575. Heat Director Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself at LA Gun Range

Michael Mann was rushed to the hospital Saturday, after the director of films such as Collateral, The Insider, and Ferrari accidentally shot himself at a Los Angeles gun range. According to People, the bullet from Mann's gun struck his leg while the 83-year-old artist was returning the firearm to its holster.

“On Saturday, at a gun range, a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered, resulting in a superficial injury to film director Michael Mann. He was treated and is being released,” a spokesperson for Mann said in a statement to media.

In a separate statement that did not name Mann, the Los Angeles Police Department confirmed the incident, which TMZ reports occurred at The Range LA, a members-only shooting club on the Westside region of Los Angeles.

Robert DeNiro, Al Pacino, and Michael Mann at the world premiere of Heat.

“Yesterday at around 4 p.m., officers responded to the 11000 block of Missouri Avenue for a radio call for shots fired at that location," the LAPD statement reads. "Responding units’ investigation determined the shooting to be accidental. The subject was transported to a local hospital in stable condition. An injury report was completed.”

According to Deadline, the incident is not expected to delay work on Heat 2, which is scheduled to begin production in January, 2027. The director, who has been nominated for four Academy Awards and is the winner of two Emmys and a BAFTA, is also responsible for films including Hunter (1986) and The Last of the Mohicans (1992); he is also known for creating the acclaimed television series Miami Vice.

Michael Mann's latest film, the sequel to 1995 crime classic Heat, will explore the origins of the characters played by Al Pacino and Robert De Niro in the original film. Its cast reportedly includes Leonardo DiCaprio, Christian Bale, and Adolescence creator Stephen Graham.

#3573. Why Criminal Minds: Evolution Was Canceled At Paramount Plus

"Criminal Minds" has been running since September 2005. But the show is set to come a close with its upcoming 20th Season, marking the end of an incredible run that already included one previous cancellation. The original "Criminal Minds" aired on CBS and ended after its fifteenth season back in 2020, after which the show was reborn as "Criminal Minds: Evolution." This latest incarnation of the procedural crime drama has been available on streaming service Paramount+ since 2022, but it seems the FBI's Behavioral Analysis Unit (BAU) will finally close up shop after Season 20.

Originally created by Jeff Davis, "Criminal Minds" has followed the investigations of the BAU as they've help track down dangerous criminals via their profiling expertise. The show debuted with Mandy Patinkin playing FBI Senior Supervisory Special Agent Jason Gideon, alongside Lola Glaudini as FBI Supervisory Special Agent Elle Greenaway, Thomas Gibson as FBI Supervisory Special Agent and Behavioral Analysis Unit Chief Aaron Hotchner, Matthew Gray Gubler as Spencer Reid, Kirsten Vangsness as Penelope Garcia, and A.J. Cook as Jennifer "JJ" Jareau. But as you might expect given the show's impressive run, "Criminal Minds" has undergone major changes over the years, with Mandy Patinkin's Jason Gideon leaving after just two seasons ahead of several other major departures.

Today, only Cook and Vangsness remain from the original cast, and it seems it's now time for their "Criminal Minds" journey to come to a close. For fans, the show's cancellation will have come as somewhat of a shock, especially since "Evolution" seems to have been faring well on Paramount+. For now, it remains unclear exactly why the series was canceled, but it likely has to do with a combination of cost, the show's broadcast roots, and new leadership at Paramount.

"Criminal Minds: Evolution" Season 19 debuted in May 2026, by which time the show had already been given an early Season 20 renewal in March 2026, with Paramount+ announcing a 2027 debut for Season 20. All of which seemed to bode well for the show. But this was prior to the completion of the Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger becoming official in October 2026. Paramount's takeover of the historic studio completed early that month, and by October 30 Deadline reported that "Criminal Minds: Evolution" had been cancelled, making the 20th season its last.

As such, the show became the first victim of the new Paramount+ leadership, but it seems the writing was on the wall even before the merger. Deadline cited sources as having claimed that the previous Paramount+ regime recommended cancelling the series prior to new Co-Chair & Chief Content Officer for Skydance Direct to Consumer, Casey Bloys, taking over. The outlet also noted that "Evolution" was still performing well and could, at the time of writing, be found in the Paramount+ Top 10. As such, it's likely the show's cancellation came down to cost or, as Deadline notes, the fact that "Evolution" retains much of the broadcast sensibility of the original show despite being a streaming series.

Meanwhile, HBO Max, which is now under the same leadership as Paramount+, is following a new "The Pitt"-style approach that, like broadcast, keeps the episode count high each season and follows a yearly release schedule while maintaining the production values of premium streaming series. It seems as though "Criminal Minds: Evolution" might not have fit that approach.

"Criminal Minds" executive producer/showrunner Erica Messer seemed surprised by the news of its cancellation. "It's hard to put into words what 'Criminal Minds' has meant to all of us who have been fortunate enough to be part of this extraordinary journey," she said (via Deadline). "[...] While suddenly navigating the end of this chapter, I'm filled with gratitude for our remarkable cast, writers, directors and crew who have poured their hearts into this show, and for the incredible fans around the world whose unwavering loyalty has kept 'Criminal Minds' going for two decades." The showrunner added that she was looking forward to Season 20, which wrapped filming by the time the cancellation was confirmed, meaning it likely won't provide a definite ending to the story.

Elsewhere, the "Criminal Minds: Evolution" cast reacted to the cancellation via social media. Emily Prentiss actor Paget Brewster kept things simple, posting a photo to Instagram of herself smiling with the words, "Free Agent..." Similarly, A.J. Cook took to Instagram to post a photo of herself in front of a tombstone for her character, alongside the caption "Rest in peace JJ (for now)."

Meanwhile, RJ Hatanaka, who plays Special Agent Tyler Green, posted a photo of the cast alongside the caption, "Just the finest group of people." Finally, Penelope Garcia actor Kirsten Vangsness — who has been part of every season of "Criminal Minds" — posted an Instagram video expressing her gratitude. "My heart fireworks in appreciation for the time at this job," she wrote, while using the video to speculate that the show could still continue elsewhere. For now, nothing has been confirmed, but as Vangsness points out in her video, showrunner Erica Messer has said that there are still stories to tell.

I Have A Theory About Dexter: Resurrection And His Downfall. Why I Think Season 2 Could Address It

I guess I fear that Dexter is becoming an Avengers-level type of anti-hero, and it feels like we haven't seen him face any real adversity. #3571. Tomi Adeyemi Does Not Want to Talk About the Children of Blood and Bone Movie

“You are a once in a generation talent,” says Tomi Adeyemi, tears in her eyes. The author is not paying me a compliment; she is reading a line from one of her numerous fan letters.

Adeyemi is a New York Times bestselling writer, a feat she accomplished at twenty-four with her 2018 fantasy debut novel Children of Blood and Bone—the first in her Legacy of Orïsha trilogy, which marries old-fashioned American YA with West African mythology. Her new novel, The Siren—released in September—follows Emery, a freshman at Dartmouth desperate to find her place as she undertakes a series of trials to join the titular group of powerful girls on campus.

This is Adeyemi’s first time since childhood not writing fantasy; maybe her first time period, since she says the first book she ever wrote was a Parent Trap fan fiction. But it’s also an attempt to move past the widely successful young-adult fantasy with which she made her name—as well as the drama surrounding the film adaptation of Adeyemi’s debut novel, an experience she has called the worst thing she ever lived through.

In now-deleted TikToks, Adeyemi said that she’s distancing herself from the film, she won’t watch it, and that she blocked one of its leads, Amandla Stenberg, on social media. Sources indicated to VF this summer that Adeyemi got more creative control over the film than most first-time authors do, including a co-screenwriting credit; they also noted that she's switched talent agencies multiple times since striking an initial deal with ICM. “There must be something [going on] because she’s burned every bridge,” one insider who works in the book-to-film space said.

When we meet, Adeyemi says that she doesn’t want to talk about that.

Instead, she talks about how she used to exclusively write fantasy because the world wasn’t safe enough for her to write anything else. Now, though, she no longer feels like she has to hide behind magic. “I’ve become someone who can inhabit it fully,” she says. “When you allow a woman to grow her claws, I am more akin to a jungle cat than I am a house plant.” She breaks into a chorus of Frank Sinatra’s “My Way,” adding a Jackson 5-esque run: “Da-da-da, oh, baby, yeah-yeah.” She tells me that sometimes, when she connects with certain people—like me—she just can’t help herself from singing. “The stars, the moon!” she belts—lines from Florence + the Machine’s “Cosmic Love.”

Adeyemi’s a musical person. She saw Florence play at Lollapalooza: “Somehow, Florence wielded her magic so I was able to get to the very front row, and she’s singing to me. I’m like, Look at this wild woman, howling to the moon.” This reminds her of a scene from her new book: when Roux, the girl Emery idolizes, is introduced. Adeyemi writes Roux dancing on a table, kicking glasses, alive and wild. Emery wants to be like that; so does Adeyemi. She explains this before singing some more: “You woke up like that, you woke up like that.”

Adeyemi’s admiration for Roux is almost tangible. She smiles dreamily when she speaks about her creation, leaving you to wonder if there was a specific person this character was based on.

Though Adeyemi started working on The Siren in 2020, she says the novel’s published version was written entirely last year. She’s gotten used to trying, and trying again; while applying for fiction writing classes in college, Adeyemi says, she was rejected five semesters in a row. One professor actually told her he couldn’t teach her to write, an anecdote she’s happy to relate now: “Hello! So many bestsellers later.” She spent four and a half years writing her first, unpublished novel, which she says was rejected 63 times. Only then did she write Children of Blood and Bone.

Adeyemi says she writes to free herself—and while one can’t be sure exactly what she had to free herself from last year, the film adaptation of Blood and Bone was shot in 2025. That’s also when Adeyemi allegedly fell out with Stenberg. And while they’re spelled differently, it’s notable that Roux—The Siren’s charismatic villain—has the same name as one of Stenberg’s most popular characters, Rue in the first Hunger Games movie.

Female authors are often asked, unfairly, whether they are writing their own lives into a story. Yet it’s also impossible to ignore the parallels between Emery and Adeyemi herself. Both are Ivy-educated writers and self-proclaimed outsiders. Adeyemi also doesn’t shy from comparisons between herself and her most recent main character: she says that all authors write themselves, because doing so is a vehicle for understanding. Reading The Siren is like stepping into her consciousness.

So is interviewing her. Adeyemi has a tendency to go off on tangents about astrology, tarots, mystical energy. “Do you remember how it felt when the entire universe came alive? All these spindles, nerve endings rise,” she asks me at one point, holding out her arms. “If you could feel the stars and taste the wind?”

The novel is wrapped up in themes of belonging, identity, and loneliness—a narrative Adeyemi tells me she relates to. “I think if you don’t belong to yourself, you don’t belong anywhere,” she says—though Adeyemi also thinks that her Aquarius placements mean people like her will never fit in, because they are not designed to. Take “our most iconic Aquarius rising, Audrey Hepburn,” or SZA, who famously wears fairy wings onstage and on red carpets. “How painful must it have been when you were on land?” Adeyemi asks her fellow Aquarius rhetorically. “How painful must it have been to learn how to fly? How painful is it for the butterflies inside before they become their butterflies?”

Adeyemi herself appears on the cover of The Siren—something that “has never been done before,” she says. “But a lot of what I do has never been done before. I remember choosing the image because I saw the darkness, that power in Emery. I’ve never seen that look in anyone else’s eye.”

There was a time where having her books adapted for the screen felt like the epitome of Adeyemi’s work. The author no longer feels that way: “I am the epitome of my work,” she says. And as she said on those now-deleted TikToks, she really would rather not talk about the film adaptation of her first novel at all.

We avoid the topic during our initial conversation. When our time runs out, though, Adeyemi tells me she’d like to talk more at a later date. When I do eventually speak to Adeyemi again—and ask about the Blood and Bone film—she shuts down physically. Her smile drops; the question throws off the energy of the conversation, almost like a betrayal has occurred. I ask another question, and Adeyemi tells me that she is getting a call. She turns off her camera, and I sit in silence for seven minutes.

Eventually, Adeyemi returns and asks if I am still there. She tells me, “The Siren is number three, New York Times.” She’s feeling the hot flash version of goosebumps, she says, like she just finished a marathon.

Adeyemi says that all of this—her career, her work, her writing process—was inspired by extreme fear. She speaks about it in the second person: “An agonizing understanding that you’ve been taught to work so hard to build a better life, [but] you might not get to build that life. It could be snapped away from you like that. I live in that terror.” She’s gone through her own trials: not just the long journey to publishing Blood and Bone, but the internet’s scrutiny over the comments she made about the Blood and Bone adaptation. “I’m exceptionally proud of who I am today,” she says, though “life is terrifying.”

In our first conversation, Adeyemi had said The Siren might be her last book—that she might be finished with writing altogether. “You can depart from all these previous eras of your life with a gentle sort of ruthlessness,” she said, “and then tomorrow can actually be a new day.” Now, she seems reenergized by the idea of work, telling me that she’s met children’s literacy organizations that try to inspire kids with the work of James Baldwin, Octavia Butler, and herself. “I’m proud of writing this from a really hard time and place,” she says, “and I wanna continue Emery’s journey.”

I ask her what changed between that interview and this one. Her smile freezes; she laughs awkwardly before hesitantly replying, “I think it’s interesting talking to you in the summer and then talking to you post this tour. I don’t know how the piece will end up, since you’re getting two very distinct cross sections.”

She takes another beat. “So that quote felt more… there was more of a resonance the first time we spoke. As I’m sitting here with you now, I just have a vision of myself writing deeply.”

The time between our talks seems to have given her space for deep reflection. I remind Adeyemi what she’d told me about feeling more like a jungle cat than a houseplant, and ask if she felt she had to be a jungle cat during her journey with the Blood and Bone film. “I think all women have to be in tune with their power. I think Black women have to be in tune with their power, dark-skinned Black women especially,” she answers. “There’s a sense of gravity that wouldn’t have been there without knowing what it is to step into my power and voice. You owe it to yourself to feel safe, and if you’re the only one there to defend yourself, you have to have the claws.”

As the film’s January release inches closer, one has to wonder if Adeyemi has a desire to retract her claws—and her statements about the movie. Or at least whether everything that’s transpired has changed her relationship with her debut novel. “I think my relationship with myself has changed more than anything,” Adeyemi answers. When narrating the audiobook for The Siren, she noticed that Emery doesn’t recognize her own genius. That broke Adeyemi’s heart, because the character’s insecurities came from a personal place. The difference between her character and her own feelings also shows Adeyemi’s own growth: “You don’t feel that way anymore,” she told herself.

When asked whether she might try to make another movie someday—or adapt The Siren—she answers firmly: “I’ve already done that journey. It’s a lot of work, but it’s not work that is for myself. When you commit to doing something on screen, it’s more about everyone else on the other side of that screen. I think because I have such a directorial and cinematic approach to my writing, I do value having experienced everything.” Selling the rights to your novel means essentially giving it away to other people, she says. That was extremely difficult for her. “I don’t need anyone in this world.”

Maybe Adeyemi’s film future lies instead in front of the camera. She did film a cameo in Blood and Bone, and one in the second Devil Wears Prada film: “At the beginning of the year, I thought, Oh, I would like to try acting,” she laughs now. “By the end of the year, I had a cameo across from Viola Davis and another across from Meryl Streep.” In the future, she’d be interested in voice acting and animation. Or live-action—but maybe only if, say, Jon Chu asked her to star in a Bollywood rom-com with Dev Patel.

“SASUKE!” She yells the name of a Naruto character in a high-pitched voice, then adds in her normal voice, “I’m clearly a very animated person.”

#3570. Daniel Craig's Taut 92-minute Thriller Is Blowing Up on Streaming

The 007 star's lesser-known thriller is climbing the HBO Max charts

Daniel Craig has established himself as one of Hollywood's most reliable leading men, particularly when it comes to action movies and suspenseful thrillers. From his gritty breakout role in Layer Cake to the high-stakes mysteries of Knives Out and The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo, Craig has built an impressive filmography outside his best-known role as James Bond.

Craig played the iconic British spy across five films, beginning with Casino Royale in 2006 and concluding with No Time to Die in 2021. Now, with the search for his successor officially underway, movie fans have another reason to revisit the franchise and Craig's career as a whole.

But while audiences wait to find out who will inherit Bond's license to kill, one of Craig's more overlooked thrillers is attracting attention on streaming. The film wasn't exactly a hit with critics when it first arrived, but that hasn't stopped viewers from giving it another look.

Dream House, a 2011 psychological thriller directed by Jim Sheridan, is currently climbing HBO Max's international movie charts, according to FlixPatrol. It's ranked #3 in several countries.

Dream House follows Will Atenton (Daniel Craig), a successful publisher who leaves his job in New York City to move his wife, Libby (Rachel Weisz), and their two daughters to a quiet New England town.

Their fresh start takes a disturbing turn when Will discovers that their new home was previously the scene of a gruesome murder. A mother and her two children were killed inside the house, and the surviving husband was suspected of committing the crime. With the help of Ann Patterson (Naomi Watts), a neighbor who was close to the murdered family, Will begins investigating the tragedy. However, the deeper he digs, the more unsettling the mystery surrounding the house becomes.

Unfortunately, Dream House wasn't particularly well received when it premiered in 2011. The film currently holds a dismal 7% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes, alongside a somewhat more forgiving 36% audience score. Critics largely took issue with its slow pacing and predictable psychological thriller twists.

That's hardly the kind of reception that inspires confidence in a thriller, but more than a decade after its theatrical debut, Dream House is getting another chance to find an audience.

#3568. Who Is The Longbow Killer In Absolute Green Arrow? DC's Murder Mystery, Explained

This article contains spoilers for "Absolute Green Arrow."

DC Comics' "Absolute" Universe has made major changes to classic heroes like Batman. "Absolute Green Arrow," which recently completed its first arc, "The Longbow Killer," leans more toward mystery. Despite the title, the main character here is Dinah Lance, the Black Canary, and she's investigating who the Green Arrow is.

An "Absolute Green Arrow" series from writer Pornsak Pichetshote and artist Rafael Albuquerque was announced in July 2025. Classic Green Arrow Oliver Queen (aka Ollie) then debuted in the "Absolute" Universe in October one-shot "Absolute Evil," by Al Ewing and Giuseppe Camuncoli. An archery-loving billionaire who wants to be a hero, Oliver is murdered by the evil oligarchs who call themselves "The Justice League."

In "Absolute Green Arrow," the murder mystery isn't who killed Oliver Queen; the audience already knows that. The question is why the "Longbow Killer," dressed like a cross of Robin Hood and the Grim Reaper, is murdering people connected to Oliver's death.

The comic presents lots of suspects, like "Absolute" versions of Oliver's traditional sidekicks Roy Harper and Mia Dearden, as well as his illegitimate son Connor Hawke. All three of them are archer heroes in the main DC Universe, and therefore are prime Longbow Killer candidates. Dinah is reluctantly working security for evil businessman (and Justice League member) Hector Hammond. Her partner is Malcolm Merlyn, aka Green Arrow's classic "Dark Archer" nemesis. Considering the comic features zombie villain Solomon Grundy, some readers (and Dinah) even suspected the killer was a vengeful, undead Oliver.

But "Absolute Green Arrow" #6 pulled back the Longbow Killer's hood, revealing Merlyn and Connor Hawke. Oliver was not in Connor's life when Connor was growing up, so Malcolm raised Connor instead. The Longbow Killer has been targeting people like Hammond because Connor is avenging his father's death and redeeming Ollie's mistakes.

DC promoted "Absolute Green Arrow" like it was a slasher movie, with Green Arrow himself being described as "a Robin Hood who is less Errol Flynn and more Michael Myers." Except this slasher is targeting corrupt billionaires, not dumb teenagers. During "Absolute Green Arrow," the Longbow Killer becomes a social media hero because many people think his targets deserve it. But Connor and Malcolm aren't killing to spark a revolution.

"Absolute Green Arrow" gradually reveals Hector Hammond is performing illegal human experiments into anti-aging via advanced cellular regeneration. Jubal Slade, Ollie's former business partner and a Jeffrey Epstein-esque child trafficker, was supplying Hammond with test subjects.

It turns out "Malcolm" is actually Arthur King, a mercenary hired to investigate the disappearance of one of Jubal's victims. Once Arthur and Connor got close to the truth, Connor brought it to Oliver; his dad had always resisted actually standing up to Slade, and Connor wanted to shock him into action. It worked, but Oliver moving against Slade and Hammond is why he was was silenced. Cue Arthur going undercover as "Malcolm Merlyn" to investigate Hammond and provide inside protection for Connor's crusade.

There's a classic red herring where, after Connor is introduced in "Absolute Green Arrow" #2, the Longbow Killer seemingly murders him. In reality, that was Connor and Arthur redirecting Dinah's suspicion. But Arthur dies genuinely in "Absolute Green Arrow" #5, leaving Connor as the only living Green Arrow.

Pornsak Pichetshote initially compared "Absolute Green Arrow" to the 1997 slasher "I Know What You Did Last Summer," which is about a group of people with a dark secret being murdered one by one. But the reveal of the Longbow Killer's identity borrows from a different slasher franchise: "Scream," where there is almost always more than one Ghostface killer.

Oliver Queen's legacy influences Connor's choice of weapons. Ollie made his money with a company called Greenarrows Trading (a reference to the real financial app Robinhood Markets). When we first see the Longbow Killer in "Absolute Green Arrow" #1, he pointedly leaves two green arrows in the eyes of Jubal Slade's corpse. His bow is also made from two swords latched together. It's a similar touch to "Absolute Batman" making Batman's chest symbol into an axe; the hero's symbol is a collapsible weapon.

Jubal Slade is a reinvention of a slumlord villain from Denny O'Neil and Neal Adams' "Green Lantern" #76, the beginning of the famous and bitingly political "Hard-Traveling Heroes" arc starring Green Lantern and Green Arrow. The "Longbow Killer" moniker comes from another "Green Arrow" comic, Mike Grell's 1987 "The Longbow Hunters." After Oliver Queen died in 1995's "Green Arrow" #101, Connor Hawke took his father's place as Green Arrow.

Pornsak Pichetshote was also once an executive in DC's TV department, where he helped spearhead TV shows like "Arrow." His previous experience reimagining Green Arrow clearly shaped his latest attempt. In "Arrow" Season 1, Oliver Queen (Stephen Amell) is out to kill or ruin the names of people on a list given to him by his father, Robert Queen (Jamey Sheridan); Robert was once part of this conspiracy and wants his son to enact vengeance. Connor being the Longbow Killer makes "Absolute Green Arrow" into the same story: A son goes out to avenge his father's murder by killing a list of his dad's shady associates. "Absolute Green Arrow" also employs a flashback storyline much like "Arrow" did, and the name "Malcolm Merlyn" comes from "Arrow."

Oliver was presented as a kind of serial killer in "Arrow" Season 1. (Season 2 was even all about him swearing that "I can't be the killer I once was.") "Absolute Green Arrow" embraces that approach, and then some.
