One of Natalie Portman’s most iconic roles, even twenty years later, is V For Vendetta. How can one forget how great she looked with a shaved head? She just shared her personal takes on what it was like to be without hair for awhile, I didn’t see this recommendation coming from her.

Portman first rocked a buzzcut in 2005 at the premiere of Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith at Cannes Film Festival. It had been freshly shaven on set when she hopped on a plane to go to the glitzy event in between filming. As she recalled about attending the event with the fresh cut in her words:

Everyone was like, ‘Oh wow, she has no hair.’ And then I went back, got on a plane and went back to Berlin and started shooting again on Monday. It was pretty wild to be out in public exposed like a baby bird. I feel like it's something every woman should do at least once in her life. It feels so amazing to have rain on your head for the first time.

Wow, what a glowing review from Natalie Portman about shaving one’s head! While speaking to Harper’s Bazaar, the actress suggested that “every woman” give it a try at some point in their life. She loved it because it felt amazing to feel the rain on her head – which funny enough is the same thing Millie Bobby Brown pointed out about going bald for Stranger Things. Portman had a really positive review for shaving her head, but there is something she didn’t like so much:

I did not love growing it back. I have curly hair, and so when it grows back you just look like a little boy for a very long time.

Another solid point. I guess there’s always a baseball cap for those awkward growing pains? In V for Vendetta, Portman’s character of Evey has her head shaved against her will when she’s captured, imprisoned and tortured in the dystopian thriller. The moment when her head was shaved off had to be captured in one take with three cameras at once. During rehearsals for the scene, Portman said a bunch of men on the crew offered to have their heads shaved in order for it to be tested and ready for Portman.

Portman is one of quite a few actors who’ve left their hair behind for a while for a role. Emma Stone is the most recent example for her film Bugonia, but in her case, she made her director Yorgos Lanthimos do so too “in solidarity”. Though, the pact wasn’t as satisfying as Stone thought it would be. Florence Pugh also shaved her head for We Live In Time, and has talked about how she was worried she might look like “an egg” before officially committing to it, and embracing the haircut wholeheartedly.

You can check out Natalie Portman in V For Vendetta with a Paramount+ subscription. It’s still arguably one of her best movies, so her bold haircut was absolutely worth it.

#3549. Ta-Nehisi Coates on Haley Stevens, Abdul El-Sayed, and the Right’s “Campaign of Hate”

When Michigan congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers yesterday, she offered a curious framing. “I’m choosing country over hate,” Stevens claimed. “This is not anti-Muslim at all.”

Rogers, for his part, invoked Martin Luther King Jr.: “You cannot solve darkness with darkness; you have to solve it with light. You can’t solve hate with hate; you have to solve it with love.” For the site of their hard launch, the odd couple chose Perfecting Church, a Black church in Detroit, evidently seeking to exploit the aura of social justice implicit in the Black faith tradition.

Aura farming aside, it is very hard to square the claims of patriotism and love with the actual campaign that Stevens now supports. Indeed, since the moment Abdul El-Sayed triumphed in the Democratic Senate primary, Rogers has made his views of his opponent clear. “I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice,” he claimed the morning after El-Sayed won. “Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.” (Never mind that Hasan Piker, not El-Sayed, said the 9/11 quote, which El-Sayed has disavowed.)

Indeed, a consistent theme of Rogers’s campaign has been the implication that El-Sayed is a tool for shadowy forces originating in the East. “The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year,” Rogers claimed. “Abdul El-Sayed’s.” As a factual matter, the attack is highly dubious. But facts are not the point, so much as the deployment of “Muslim” as a slur.

To understand this, one need only look to the overlord of the Rogers campaign, President Donald Trump. As is his wont, Trump delights in mangling El-Sayed’s name, referring to him as “Abduladadalalalala” or simply “Mohamed.” “Somebody said his name isn’t Mohamed,” Trump told attendees at a rally. “I’m the president, I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he’s Mohamed.”

The Trump theory of El-Sayed holds that his ascendance is being facilitated by the machinations of Wayne County, a “strictly Third World” jurisdiction that seeks to elevate to Congress a “jihadist” who shouldn’t even be eligible for “a seat on an airplane.” If seated in the world’s greatest deliberative body, El-Sayed, the theory holds, would execute his dastardly plan to ban Christmas and—you guessed it—impose Sharia law.

Trump’s attacks have been echoed and amplified by right-wing news outlets like Newsmax, which has lambasted El-Sayed as an “anti-Israel Muslim,” an “immigrant from another Muslim country,” and a Midwest variant of that other alien, Zohran Mamdani, the “socialist Muslim who’s always smiling.” For those too dense to catch the message, the Newsmax chyrons have helpfully driven home the point—“THE LEFT IS FORGETTING THE HEINOUS ATTACKS OF 9/11,” “DEMOCRATS DROOL OVER NON-WHITE SOCIALISTS,” “MUSLIMS TELL US THEY’RE TAKING OVER, AND THEY ARE.”

Lest one think that this bigotry is merely limited to the crude ramblings of unlettered ogres, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has stepped in to offer some intellectual heft to the attack. The Muslim Brotherhood, according to Kennedy, is responsible for not just the menace that is El-Sayed, but also the dark age that has fallen over the entirety of the Arabdom. “There’s 500 million Arabs in the world,” Kennedy claimed, “and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Field[s] prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce the literature they used to produce.”

Again, facts aren’t really the point here, and there is no wisdom in debating a quack whose brain has literally been infected by a worm. Nonetheless, it is worth noting the particular history at work. During both his run for president and his time in the White House, Barack Obama endured his share of racist attacks. To Rush Limbaugh, Obama was “Barack the Magic Negro.” To Newt Gingrich, he was America’s “food stamp president.” At the Value Voters Summit, a vendor hawked “Obama Waffles,” a product featuring a racist caricature of the president on the packaging. The tagline was: “Point box toward Mecca for tastier waffles.” That last line deserves particular attention. Indeed, by 2016, the political scientist Philip Klinkner would find that the best way to discern whom a voter would support in the upcoming election was to pose a simple question—“Is Barack Obama a Muslim?”

Stevens, in joining Rogers, has allied herself with this odious culture war, one that is itself tied to a very real war. The campaign of hate, of which El-Sayed is the latest victim, has a simple goal: to render Muslims and Arabs more killable. The latter does not require the former. In 1953 the CIA backed a coup that overthrew a democracy in Iran. In 1965 it supported a coup in Indonesia, the country with the largest Muslim population in the world, that killed between 500,000 and a million people. During the Cold War, the justification for this death toll was the threat of communism; post-9/11, it is racism. In 2008, John McCain confronted a supporter and disputed the claim that Obama was Arab. “No, ma’am,” McCain told his supporter. “He’s a decent family man.” This moment is often referenced as an act of patriotism, and perhaps it was one. But the notion that “decent” people exist in one place, while Arabs exist in another, is the major premise for a syllogism of violent, chauvinist power—wedding parties droned, governments overthrown, schoolgirls bombed, and inconvenient people eliminated.

This long war on the Muslim and Arab world has reached its apogee in the concentration camp of Gaza, where every single bomb was dropped from a plane of American extraction. And the genocide is but the latest chapter in a book authored by Israel, a state whose own basic laws reserve full rights for its “decent” people and something less for everyone else. This is the state that Haley Stevens has claimed to literally see in her dreams. And it is ultimately the defense of this state that drove Stevens into the arms of Mike Rogers. From this perspective, Stevens’s defection isn’t a story about party intrigue. It is a story about Stevens waking up and choosing violence.

#3548. 10 Shows Like 'A Different World' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The original A Different World was a groundbreaking sitcom in its era, spending six seasons highlighting Black academic drive among a cast of characters so indelible that we're now checking in on them decades later. Spearheaded by Queen Sugar's Felicia Pride, the update has been a critical and ratings hit for Netflix, earning the rarest prize of all in streaming television: a quick second season renewal. While you're waiting for season two, here are some other smart coming-of-age shows that blend heart and humor with realistic drama.

An easy pairing with A Different World, this show follows Black-ish's Zoey Johnson (Yara Shahidi) as she leaves home to attend a (fictional) California liberal arts college (the last couple of post-graduation seasons shift the focus to her brother Andre, played by Marcus Scribner). The emphasis is on driven young people who are capable of making big mistakes on the path to adulthood. A true comedy-drama, Grown-ish feels real(-ish) in a way that few other college shows have managed. Stream Grown-ish on Hulu.

Adapted from and expanding upon the 2014 movie, this show takes us to a (fictional) Ivy League school for a comedy-drama that tackles campus life and politics from a rather different perspective than that of Rooster. Logan Browning leads the ensemble cast as Sam White, who kind of inadvertently starts the titular radio show following a racially charged incident on campus. Far from the racial screed that some bad-faith YouTubers seem to find it, it's never shy about confronting the complicated and occasionally silly contradictions of campus activism, with each episode approaching life at Winchester University from a different character's perspective. Stream Dear White People on Netflix.

Kimberly (Pauline Chalamet) is an endlessly naïve scholarship student; Bela (Amrit Kaur) is an aspiring comedy writer on the make for the hottest guys; Whitney (Alyah Chanelle Scott) is an overachieving athlete and senator’s daughter; and Leighton (Reneé Rapp) is a closeted sorority girl. They're all randomly assigned to room together as freshmen at the fictional Essex College in Vermont. Created by Mindy Kaling and Justin Noble, this comedy-drama isn't nearly as salacious as its title suggests. There's sex for sure, but mostly it's a funny, queer-friendly show that's a little less about one overarching romance than it is about growing up, and the value of female friendship. Stream The Sex Lives of College Girls on HBO Max.

Even though we're backing up a couple of years to follow teens in their high school years, this British import's setting is a decent match, finding its students living away from home and family for the first time in their lives. At the fictional prestigious boarding school St. Gilbert’s, five Black teens are newly attending on scholarships, but their integration into the existing cliques is less than smooth—especially given that they're there largely as a PR stunt. Boarders blends teen romance, coming-of-age drama, and a delightful willingness to take the piss when it comes to the whole "rich private school" thing. Stream Boarders on Tubi.

Another modern take on a beloved '80s/'90s sitcom, this one's a bit different, serving as a total reimagining with no narrative connection to the original. And while A Different World is a comedy with dramatic heft, this one's more of a straight drama. It’s jarring for fans of the beloved original to tune in to find a serious show with the same premise as the Will Smith original—one that often leans into heavy realism. Jabari Banks plays, er, Will Smith, a 16-year-old from West Philadelphia who moves in with his auntie and uncle in Bel-Air following a gun charge and a run-in with a Philly drug lord. Banks is charismatic and believable, bringing a ton of personality to a show that occasionally veers down dark alleys. Stream Bel-Air on Peacock.

Comedian Benito Skinner plays himself, kinda, in this buzzy comedy that sees a former high school jock facing his freshman year in college while desperately trying to convince himself and everyone else that he's as straight as they come (relatable, except for the jock part). Much of the appeal is in its deft blending of tones: It's both a frequently raunchy college comedy and a sweet coming-of-age story about accepting yourself without worrying about what everyone else thinks. The cast includes Adam DiMarco (The White Lotus) and Rish Shah (Ms. Marvel), and, though it's more a story of one young man's coming of age, there's a strong ensemble backing him up. Stream Overcompensating on Prime Video.

The heart of All American (for most of its run) is Spencer James (Daniel Ezra), based on real-life NFL linebacker Spencer Paysinger. A star player for his high school team in Crenshaw, he's recruited by the coach (Taye Diggs) of a team in Beverly Hills to come and play for them, forcing Spencer to navigate two very different worlds while trying to build a life and potential career. Stream All American on Netflix.

Following a family tragedy, the already awkward 15-year-old Devi Vishwakumar (Maitreyi Ramakrishnan) has a pretty terrible freshman year of high school, and decides that she’s going to turn things around the following year, hoping that a nearly academic study of sex will get her the boyfriend(s) her raging hormones have begun to demand. It works, to a point—but getting a surprise yes to sex from her crush leads her to question what she’s really ready for. More about burgeoning sexuality than sex specifically, this Mindy Kaling-produced series is both honest and charming. Stream Never Have I Ever on Netflix.

For realism in a show about the college experience, you could do a lot worse than this docuseries following several students at Gallaudet University, a school for deaf and hard-of-hearing young adults. In one sense, it's a specific setting where perspectives on deafness vary wildly, even in Gallaudet's self-contained world (aside from being a show about academically driven and horny college students, this is also a great primer for hearing people about some of the issues). But even for all of that, the challenges in building a life and future away from home are pretty universally relatable. Stream Deaf U on Netflix.

There's a reason A Different World has returned in 2026, and a lot of that has to do with the fact that there was nothing else on TV quite like it back in the late '80s and early '90s. For all of its sitcom sensibilities, the show tried hard (especially after multi-hyphenate creator Debbie Allen arrived to rework things after its first season) to paint a realistic picture of college life and an HBCU. Of the few shows on TV with largely Black casts, almost none would go so far as to highlight achievement and excellence; A Different World managed to do so while building a cast of characters so memorable that we're more than willing to catch up with them nearly forty years later. Stream A Different World on Netflix.

#3547. Dead by Daylight Fans Are Uninstalling the Game in Protest

Behaviour Interactive is under fire following Halloween livestream fail

Some Dead by Daylight players are expressing disappointment with developer Behaviour Interactive — and vowing to uninstall the game — after the studio appeared to show support for divisive streamer TheBurntPeanut.

During TheBurntPeanut's Halloween livestream, a Behaviour Interactive employee gifted the VTuber all available DLC for Dead by Daylight. Given the streamer's controversial nature, fans did not take this lightly. To show how displeased they were with the situation, some players uninstalled the game and requested a refund in protest.

Dead by Daylight is a multiplayer survival game where a player takes on the role of a killer and tries to track down and eliminate survivors. It features an array of well-known characters from all sorts of horror franchises alongside original creations. Thousands of players logged in to play this Halloween weekend, including VTuber TheBurntPeanut. During the stream, he received all of Dead by Daylight's paid expansions in his inbox — a gift from someone at Behaviour Interactive.

TheBurntPeanut is a controversial streamer, so many fans were immediately unhappy to see Behaviour Interactive supporting him. Seeing this, Peanut offered to return the items; the employee responded, "We can take the heat! They are yours to keep." The way that they dismissed fans' reaction only made matters worse.

Players were particularly upset over the fact that many Dead by Daylight content creators have been waiting for a long time to get approved for the Creator Program. All while controversial streamers continue to get accepted and receive support from the developers. This has resulted in Dead by Daylight veterans voicing their disappointment and uninstalling the game.

After quick backlash from the community, the official Dead by Daylight account responded, underlining that the anonymous employee's decision was made without proper approval and that their comments and conduct were not a reflection of Behaviour Interactive's values. The studio apologized for letting down the community and promised to review internal processes to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.

TheBurntPeanut responded to the situation during a Minecraft stream, denying the accusations made against him. The streamer is known for not sticking with games for long, so it is entirely possible that he will not return to Dead by Daylight. Nevertheless, for many, the damage is still done.

#3546. Marvel's X-Men Movie Casts The Long Walk And Hunger Games Actor As Iceman

Marvel Studios is continuing to build out its roster of mutants. Marvel's "X-Men" movie reboot cast was partly revealed at D23 earlier this year, but there were still some key roles left to be filled. Indeed, the latest actor to join the film's ensemble is Ben Wang, the star of "The Long Walk" and the upcoming "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." He's now set to portray Iceman, aka Bobby Drake, in the forthcoming relaunch.

According to Deadline, Wang is currently circling the role. While he hasn't signed on the dotted line, unless something wild happens, it sounds like he is Marvel and Disney' choice for the role. Marvel's "X-Men" reboot has also found its director in "Thunderbolts*" helmsman Jake Schreier. Plot details remain firmly under wraps, but this movie is clearly a top priority for the next phase of the Marvel Cinematic Universe after "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Avengers: Secret Wars" close the book on the Multiverse Saga.

This particular casting certainly lines up with Marvel's specific plan to make the "X-Men" reboot a box office success. It's no secret that the MCU isn't the surefire money-maker it once was, so the idea is to mostly cast fresh faces and emerging stars here, thereby saving money by not having to pay A-listers. And while "Star Wars" sequel trilogy veteran Adam Driver is on board to play the villain Mister Sinister, he's more of an outlier in this case.

Wang, meanwhile, fits in well with most of the rest of the movie's cast, which is composed of either up-and-comers or actors on the verge of breakout status. That includes Inde Navarrette ("Obsession") as Rogue and Christopher Abbott ("Kraven the Hunter") as Professor X, just as a couple of examples.

This is undoubtedly going to be the most high-profile role in Ben Wang's career to date, but as a star in the rise, it's certainly not the first time he's shouldered the responsibility that comes with a major franchise. After all, he was chosen to lead last year's "Karate Kid: Legends" as Li Fong and had a role in the 2024 "Mean Girls" stage musical movie adaptation.

It certainly doesn't hurt that Wang starred in the emotionally obliterating all-time great Stephen King adaptation "The Long Walk" as well. Some of his other notable credits include the recent comedy "Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass" and the Disney+ TV series "American Born Chinese." He will also be seen in Season 6 of Apple's acclaimed sci-fi series "For All Mankind."

#3544. Google Quietly Linked Your Phone Number Across Your Accounts, but You Can Stop It

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In recent weeks, Google has been automatically connecting Android users' phone numbers to every Google account they are signed into on their devices—without requesting consent to do so. This means that if you are logged into personal, work, and disposable accounts on your Android phone, Google may have silently verified and linked your number with all of them even if you've deliberately kept them separate. If you that's not something you want, there's a way to fix it.

As Android Authority reports, some Android users have recently received confirmation emails from an official Google address stating that their phone number has been verified. Google has required occasional phone number re-verification but appears to have updated its support documentation about a year ago to make this feature opt-out by default. As part of this process, Google also adds your phone number to all Google Accounts that are signed in on the device, including current accounts and phone numbers and any that are added or updated in the future.

Updating this setting does not disconnect phone numbers and Google accounts that have already been linked. You can find out which are which via your Google Account Personal Info page. Select your profile picture in the upper-right corner to go through each signed-in account and open the Phone section to select and delete any numbers you don't want associated.

Finally, Malwarebytes advises scrolling down to the Usage section on the Phone page to view which services are listed as well as reviewing your Security & sign-in settings. If you added your phone number for two-step verification or to a separate app like Google Pay, deleting it from the Phone page won't remove it entirely from your account, and you'll need to update those settings separately. Automatic phone verification shouldn't be the culprit here, but it's useful to audit what your number is being used for and on which accounts if you want to keep things separate.

If you've never used bone conduction headphones, they're worth a try, and the Shokz OpenPro are a great introduction to the technology. Previously, bone conduction headsets tended to suffer from poor bass compared to in-ear models. The OpenRun Pros are designed to compensate for some of that—you won't get the same thumpy bass you'd get from regular headphones, but it'll be the best you can get from any other bone conduction headphones.

As the name implies, these are meant to be used on outdoor runs. You can use them as everyday headphones too; they can take calls, but you'll need to be mindful of the fact that they don't block any competing sound. #3540. Avengers: Doomsday Ticket Presales Top Supergirl's Worldwide Box Office Run

Superhero movies have been experiencing troubled times of late. But "Avengers: Doomsday" might just be able to save the flailing genre. Thus far, the upcoming Marvel Cinematic Universe team-up movie has already set box office records with pre-sales, and now, it's just passed another significant milestone. According to a Forbes report from October 31, 2026, "Doomsday" took $125 million in pre-sales by the end of October across all cinema formats. This means that, by now, it has passed the entire box office gross for DC Studios' "Supergirl."

For the most part, DC Studios co-heads James Gunn and Peter Safran have gotten off to a decent start with their DC Universe. The fledgling franchise has delivered such hits as the charming crowd-pleaser "Superman" and the HBO series "Lanterns," proving this latest cinematic enterprise can deliver everything from lighthearted superhero shenanigans to gritty comic book crime dramas. But there has been one glaring misstep thus far: "Supergirl."

Though the movie itself isn't actually all that bad (/Film's review noted that Milly Alcock shines as the self-destructive savior of the DCU in "Supergirl), its box office returns were less than heroic. Indeed, "Supergirl" took in just $126.5 million against a $170-186 million budget, which means "Doomsday" has now matched the film's entire gross before it's even hit theaters.

To be fair, that's more embarrassing for DC Studios than it is encouraging for Marvel Studios, as "Supergirl" isn't a major event movie featuring beloved characters that have been at the forefront of pop culture for the last 20 years. But while a movie that includes everything the MCU has to offer beating "Supergirl" at the box office in pre-sales alone isn't quite as big an accomplishment as it may seem, it's also a reminder that DC can't afford another "Supergirl"-level flop anytime soon.

Back in September 2026, "Avengers: Doomsday" set a major box office record for Marvel when it surpassed $50 million in pre-sales 100 days ahead of its release on December 18, 2026. That was good news for Marvel Studios and fans of the franchise, which has been conspicuously struggling in recent years as mass audiences tire of the interconnected superhero narratives being told by studio head Kevin Feige and his collaborators. As Forbes pointed out, however, "Doomsday" is far from a sure bet for the company.

According to the outlet, pre-sales are almost certainly coming from die-hard fans who want to secure their chance to see the movie as soon as it drops. But 2025's "The Fantastic Four: First Steps" also saw a solid turnout from die-hards before its box office took a hit. That said, it seems unlikely "Doomsday" will suffer a similar fate. Not only is this an Avengers movie, which carries a certain amount of prestige and recognition, Marvel Studios has packed this thing with fan-favorite characters a là 2024's "Deadpool & Wolverine" — which, as it happens, was a major box office success.

With Robert Downey Jr. set to make his MCU return as Victor Von Doom, alongside beloved MCU characters of the past and the 20th Century Fox-era X-Men, it seems likely "Doomsday" will succeed simply by sheer crowd-pleasing power. Meanwhile, there's no getting around the fact that "Supergirl" flopped hard at the box office earlier this year, and DC Studios will want to avoid any similar occurrences with its upcoming slate.

In light of how superhero movies have struggled in recent years, "Supergirl" seemed doomed from the outset. Taking lesser-known characters and turning them into cultural icons worked for Marvel Studios back in the late 2000s and 2010s after 2008's "Iron Man" became the unlikely superhero movie that changed Hollywood forever. But that started yielding diminishing returns by the 2020s, as audiences grew tired of having to keep up with wider developments in the shared universe via middling streaming series and bland, paint-by-numbers movies.

As such, James Gunn's decision to follow up "Superman" with "Supergirl" seemed sort of baffling. We'd seen Milly Alcock's Kryptonian show up briefly in "Superman," but otherwise, this was an unknown iteration of a second-tier DC character who quite clearly had very little box office pull at the time she was given an entire movie. Jason Momoa's Lobo was on-hand to try to increase the appeal, but it was obvious that mass audiences weren't going to turn out. With that in mind, it's not surprising that "Doomsday" has already surpassed the entire box office take of "Supergirl."

Now, the question becomes whether "Doomsday" can, in fact, overcome the issues highlighted by Forbes to establish itself as the true savior of the MCU. The original "Doomsday" teaser trailers were boring, frankly, and RDJ's return as Doctor Doom was met with confusion among fans who remain perplexed as to why the actor is playing a major Marvel villain rather than Tony Stark/Iron Man. But Marvel has clearly managed to increase the hype for this movie since those early days of "Doomsday" promotion. The film matching the box office for "Supergirl" is just the latest sign that things are headed in the right direction.

#3539. You Should Update Your Garmin Watch's Heart Rate Zones

Zone 2 training is still having a moment—even if no one can agree on what it actually means. Legend has it that your easy, conversational-pace cardio—aka your Zone 2 heart rate—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine, to faster race times, and even to a longer life.

Whether Zone 2 deserves quite this much hype is debatable, but still, there are plenty of good reasons to master heart rate training more broadly. To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you your desired workout. Even if you believe every word of the Zone 2 gospel, it's completely pointless if your watch has the wrong idea of what your Zone 2 is. If you train with a Garmin watch, here’s how—and why—you should reset your heart rate zones now (and periodically).

When you first set up your Garmin, it asked for your age, weight, and a few other details. From there it generated heart rate zones, often using a default formula based on a maximum heart rate estimated from your age (typically some version of 220 minus your age). But these formulas are often wrong, since they give a single number for everybody at the same age, while real maximum heart rates vary from person to person.

Plus, there isn’t one universally agreed-upon heart rate zone system. So if your watch assumed a max of 180 and yours is actually 195, every zone it gave you is shifted. Your "Zone 2" might really, for you, be Zone 1 (AKA a pace so easy it barely feels like a workout). Or your "Zone 2" might actually be a moderate-to-hard effort that's digging you into a hole, while you think you're taking it easy. At every step of the way, there’s a different formula and definition that determines what heart rate zone shows up on your watchface.

To complicate things further, Garmin gives multiple options to set up your zones:

Percent of max heart rate. This is the simplest approach. You enter (or let the watch estimate) your max, and each zone is a slice of that number. It's only as good as your max heart rate figure, which, as noted above, is often a guess.

Percent of heart rate reserve (HRR). This method factors in both your max and your resting heart rate, so zones are based on the range your heart works across rather than just the top of it. It tends to produce more personalized zones, but it means your resting heart rate needs to be current, too.

Percent of lactate threshold heart rate (LTHR). Here, your zones are anchored to the effort level where your body starts producing lactate faster than it can clear it, a point that's closely tied to how you actually perform. Many coaches consider this the most meaningful anchor, because it reflects your real physiology rather than a formula.

That third option raises its own question: Where does your lactate threshold number come from?

In the past, getting a lactate threshold estimate from a Garmin meant wearing a compatible chest strap and doing a guided test, which involved a structured, hard run on your part. On newer models, however, that's no longer the case. Garmin has been rolling out an updated lactate threshold detection that works from the wrist's optical heart rate sensor, with no chest strap and no dedicated test. Instead, the watch estimates your threshold automatically from regular outdoor runs. This feature is typically on by default and generally requires a baseline VO2 max estimate and a run or trail run recorded with heart rate. If you'd rather not leave it up to the algorithm, you can turn auto-detection off and enter your own lactate threshold heart rate manually in the heart rate zone settings. Which watches have this varies by model, so check your specific device.

Even if you set your zones carefully once, they don't stay accurate forever. Several things change over time:

Your fitness changes. As you get fitter, your resting heart rate often drops, and your lactate threshold heart rate can shift. Zones based on where you were a year or two ago may not reflect where you are now.

You age. Your maximum heart rate tends to decline gradually over the years.

You change sports. Running, cycling, and swimming each have different heart rate behavior, and Garmin lets you set sport-specific zones for exactly this reason. If you've never touched them, you may be using running-based numbers on the bike, or vice versa.

You switched watches or imported old data. Zones can carry over from a previous device or a profile you set up years ago.

Your resting heart rate has changed. An outdated resting number could be throwing things off.

None of these have dramatic consequences, but if you’re focused on heart rate training, it’s worth trying to be as accurate and up-to-date as possible. If your zones are set too high, you may not be getting the aerobic stimulus you think you are. You'll also underestimate how hard your harder sessions really are, and your training load and recovery metrics can end up skewed.

On the flip side, if your zones are set too low, your "easy" runs could actually become the classic trap of training in the gray zone: too hard to recover from well, too easy to drive big gains. And because Garmin's training status, recovery time, and load features lean on your heart rate data, bad zones can quietly nudge those numbers off as well.

The good news is that fixing all this should take less than 10 minutes. First, decide whether you want zones based on max heart rate, heart rate reserve, or lactate threshold. There’s a good chance you can trust the lactate threshold your watch gives you, or you can find your actual max heart rate.

The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded. If you want a more deliberate test, a coach or a structured max-effort protocol can help, but only attempt hard testing if you're healthy and your doctor is comfortable with it. Also keep in mind that reading from a wrist-based sensor can also spike unreliably, so a chest strap gives more trustworthy numbers when accuracy matters.

Next, check your recent average resting heart rate in Garmin Connect and make sure the number your zones are using is current.

In your watch's user profile or in Garmin Connect, find the heart rate zone settings. From there you can adjust your max, change how zones are calculated, and set different zones for different sports.

Finally, put these new zones to the test. Go for an easy run or ride at what your watch calls Zone 2. Can you hold a conversation, breathing comfortably in full sentences? Does it feel sustainable for a long time? If it feels either laughably easy or surprisingly taxing, your zones probably need another look.

Maybe Zone 2 is the cornerstone of your training, or maybe you think it's completely overrated. Either way, the principle is the same: You should be able to train by feel, and your watch can only help you do that if the numbers behind it are right.

Garmin gives you more ways to set your zones than most brands do. Spend 10 minutes figuring out which method your zones are using, confirming the number behind it is current, and updating it in your settings. It’ll make every easy run, hard interval, and recovery metric on your wrist more useful.

#3538. Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’

Ruth Madeley originally thought she’d become a screenwriter, attending Thornleigh Salesian College where she studied English and creative writing with an emphasis on scriptwriting. “I wanted to be a storyteller,” “Being Heumann” star Madeley told IndieWire. “It’s not that I didn’t want to be an actor, or I didn’t pursue it. I didn’t even think it was an option.” And it’s easy to understand why. Born with spina bifida and growing up as a wheelchair user, Madeley was aware that disabled actors, and roles written for them, weren’t exactly plentiful. “I never saw anyone who looked like me,” she said. “So to even know that that was potentially an option was madness to me.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves

When Madeley thinks back on some of the earliest disabled representation she saw in popular culture, her answer is similar to countless other disabled film and TV lovers: it was an abled actor playing a disabled part. “There’s a soap back at home where there was a wheelchair user, and I was like, ‘Oh, his wheelchair looks like mine.’ And then I found out the actor wasn’t a wheelchair user.” With that type of representation being the norm, it’s unsurprising that Madeley saw acting as something she was barred from. That is until 2009, when “Half Moon Investigations,” a children’s crime/comedy show, needed a wheelchair user for an episode. “I auditioned purely to be nosy and extend my network, and I got the role. I remember being terrified in the audition, thinking: ‘Why do people do this? This is awful,” she said in an interview with The Guardian earlier this year.

That role kickstarted a film and television career that has flourished over the last decade. Now, Madeley is the star of “Being Heumann,” which details the life of disabled activist Judy Heumann and the 504 sit-ins in 1977. It’s a performance that could not only make history if she and the movie are Oscar-nominated, but also finally give young disabled girls someone who looks like them onscreen. Something Madeley didn’t have growing up. “As a disabled person, being aware that you might make history, that’s huge for me,” she said. “It’s huge for the community. That’s a really heavy and exciting thing to have.”

But Madeley doesn’t want that history, or getting caught up in the discussion of representation, to overshadow the film’s content. “I’m not just a random wheelchair user they pulled off the street,” Madeley said. “This is my job, so talking about the actual craft is really exciting for me.”

And that craft was multifaceted. Not only was Madeley portraying an actual person, a legend in the disabled community. She also had to do accent work, ASL work, and appear in nearly every frame of the movie. The accent was particularly important to get right, as Heumann’s Brooklyn upbringing was a huge part of her life, and indicative of her prickly personality. “I don’t find [accents] easy,” she said. “I have to work at them, and learn the science of it, and the tongue placement. All of those interesting fun things that I get to play with. She was such a proud Brooklyn woman, I wanted to be able to sound so specifically like her.”

That specificity was imperative to Madeley in every aspect of playing Heumann. “Siân [Heder, director] and I spoke so much about movement, because we’ve been so starved of seeing disabled people on screen that you don’t always see how a disabled person moves through the world.”

Both Heder and Madeley were intrigued by the juxtaposition of Heumann’s desire for movement with her paralysis forcing her to be still. “Siân and I both were fascinated by Judy’s speed and freedom when she was in her chair; she was never still,” said Madeley. “Versus when she’s out of her chair, and she is in such a different state of vulnerability.”

The sequence in the trailer, where Judy is forced to wait for her in-home health attendant to show up so she can use the restroom, makes this painfully apparent. “Once she was in bed, she had all of these pillows, and she knew that she had to be comfortable when her attendant left because the second that attendant left she couldn’t move herself for the whole night.”

It was seeing the authentic lived experience of a disabled person, activist aside, that was so compelling to Madeley. “The worst thing I can watch on screen is if something looks too easy,” said Madeley. Too often movies made after the passage of the Americans With Disabilities Act present a rose-colored view of accessibility, or at least do so by never discussing it. Here, the movie authentically details what being a wheelchair user, a blind person, or a deaf person was like in 1977. The landscape is riddled with different access barriers, both individually and societally. But Heder and the production team made a point of showing all of those, not just the stairs crafted to enter buildings, but putting the wheelchair-using cast in actual wheelchairs from the 1970s.

“The 1970s chairs helped [with authenticity] because nothing is easy in those things for anyone,” said Madeley. “There were so many people on hand to help, which was so invaluable because even if the place was fully accessible, being in those chairs makes things so much harder. They weighed so much. Why did people keep them? That’s what I don’t get.”

Because the wheelchairs were so unwieldy, the actors needed to get out of them to relax their bodies. It was also a chance for Madeley to realize her own limitations as a disabled person, and remember that no two disabled people have the same experience. “I recognize my privilege. I’m an ambulatory wheelchair user. I can stand up and stretch if I need to. There were other people that couldn’t… So that was a learning curve as well throughout the process of filming. People need to get out of these every few hours.”

On the page, Heumann isn’t sanded down, and Madeley is happy with that. “I’m all for a messy queen!” Her Judy is impatient, stubborn, downright rude at times. But Madeley wanted to make sure that was placed alongside Heumann’s joy, warmth, humor, and vulnerability. Without that delicate balance, the character could have come off as too bitter, on one end of the spectrum, or too tragic.

“That feeling of having to be easy, or grateful, or nice, so that people — all of those things that society expects of a disabled woman–I’m not those things all the time, and no one is,” she said. “I love the fact that I got to play somebody who didn’t have her edges rounded off. I love the fact that she was able to be prickly.”

In the end, Madeley wants to keep showcasing flawed humans, not necessarily flawed disabled humans. “I’m just driven by character,” she said. Too often, disabled actors are only hired for disabled roles, and that’s something Madeley wants to subvert. “I don’t only have to play disabled. I can play the messy mom of two who’s got knocked up again, and who is completely inept.” Madeley continues to show that the different sides of disability will no doubt finally turn the tide on what disabled actors can do. It’s a far cry from the type of representation she, and many other disabled people, had growing up.

“Being Heumann” opens from Apple TV in select theaters starting Friday, November 6. The film streams on Apple TV starting Friday, November 13.

#3537. Nintendo Officially Comments on Zelda Remake's Divisive Graphics

Link, Zelda, and others have a distinct style to them

Nintendo's upcoming remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time looks drastically different from the Nintendo 64 original. That's understandable, given the nearly 28 years that have passed since the first 3D Zelda debuted. Beyond the graphical advancements, however, the Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time makes some bold character design choices, some of which have divided longtime Zelda fans.

In a new interview with the developers of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, we finally get, we finally get some explanation of why Nintendo made certain aesthetic choices, including the decision to make Link, Zelda, and others look more like puppets than strictly photorealistic people.

Nintendo developer Aya Shida, who served as art director on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, said that, "When we first considered how to leverage the capabilities of Nintendo Switch 2 to explore new forms of visual expression, a fairly natural direction seemed to be to create a richly detailed world that felt as though it could truly exist. But our goal wasn't simply to make everything look realistic."

Shida noted the contrast between the dark but beautiful setting of Hyrule and the game's colorful, quirky characters in the original game.

"I felt that this contrast was what gave The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time its mysterious, almost dreamlike charm," Shida explained. "So for this game, we wanted to rebuild Hyrule as a rich, dense world that felt as though it could truly exist, while retaining the feel of the original. At the same time, we wanted its colorful and quirky characters to feel like a natural part of that world. Figuring out how to strike the right balance became one of the main themes of the art development."

Shida revealed that some of the game's art direction was guided by certain keywords: "a puppet-show feel" and "the analog feel of practical effects films." Those phrases refer to creating "a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds."

"We also felt that there was some overlap between these forms of expression and the distinctive nostalgia evoked by the original game," Shida explained. "We began by drawing sketches of Link, Zelda, and the other characters. At the same time, to show the kind of world they would inhabit, we created a 3D model of the Great Deku Tree that looked truly alive, carefully adjusting the lighting and textures. We then presented the concept to Aonuma-san, explaining that we wanted characters like these to blend naturally into a world like this."

Longtime Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma weighed in on that choice, highlighting how nostalgia for the original Ocarina of Time played into the remake's visual style.

"Back when we were developing the game for Nintendo 64, we thought we were making something cutting-edge for the time," Aonuma said. "We weren't trying to create anything nostalgic. But after all these years, the current development team feels a certain sense of nostalgia when they look back at the original. And their efforts to express that nostalgia led them to an analog, puppet-show-like feel. As one of the original developers, that progression made sense to me."

Players will get a chance to immerse themselves in the reimagined Hyrule later this week, when The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time arrives on Nintendo Switch 2.

#3536. One Of 2026's Best Anime Movies Is Based On The Same Book As A Tom Cruise Sci-Fi Classic

In Doug Liman's 2014 sci-fi action movie "Edge of Tomorrow," Tom Cruise plays William Cage, a cowardly public relations officer drafted to fight in the front line of an alien war. Dying due to exposure to an alien's acidic blood traps Cage in a time loop, and with help from decorated soldier Sergeant Rita Vrataski (Emily Blunt), he has to find a way to break the loop and win the war. The movie did not perform especially well at the box office, grossing $381 million against a $178 million budget, but it earned good reviews and, to this day, fans and the creative team remain hopeful about an eventual "Edge of Tomorrow" sequel.

You might assume the nifty premise of "Edge of Tomorrow" is just an action movie riff on "Groundhog Day," but its real origins are more obscure. The movie adapts a 2004 Japanese light novel, "All You Need Is Kill," written by Hiroshi Sakurazaka with illustrations by Yoshitoshi Abe ("Serial Experiments Lain"). The movie and novel share a basic premise, though the movie moves the setting from Japan to Europe. It also turns the novel's hero, a young Japanese man named Keiji Kiriya, into Cruise's William Cage.

Fitting for a story that's all about its characters caught in a loop, "All You Need Is Kill" has been adapted several times. In 2014, Weekly Young Jump serialized a 17 chapter "All You Need Is Kill" manga written by Ryosuke Takeuchi and drawn by Takeshi Obata, artist of "Death Note." Most recently, Japanese studio Studio 4°C turned the story into a mostly 3D-animated film that opened in theaters this past year. The "All You Need Is Kill" anime does justice to the story while making some of the biggest changes to it yet.

The anime "All You Need Is Kill" retains the title of the novel, unlike "Edge of Tomorrow." ("Edge of Tomorrow" was originally titled "All You Need Is Kill," but was then renamed in 2013 ahead of release. Confusingly, it's also since been labeled as "Live Die Repeat" on home media.)

You might expect that the animated "All You Need Is Kill" is a more faithful adaptation, one that strives to tell the real story after Hollywood distorted it. But that's not quite true. While the animated movie retains the Japanese setting, it flips the story in another way: Rita Vrataski is the protagonist. In the novel and "Edge of Tomorrow," she's a soldier who got caught in a previous loop, escaped it, and walked out a hardened battlefield hero distinguished by her large war axe.

In the animated "All You Need Is Kill," we see her stumbling through loop after loop learning to fight. She's more like the novel's Keiji but with Rita's name, and then Keiji being caught in her same loop is the midpoint twist. The movie's ending also echoes "Edge of Tomorrow." The hero (William/Rita) breaks the loop, defeats the aliens, and arrives back at the beginning of the story (but now free of the loop). They then reunite with their partner (Rita/Keiji) with the hope they'll become close again.

The novel and manga's final twist is that, to escape the loop, one of Rita and Keiji has to die. Rita lets Keiji kill her, and he has to carry her sacrifice through to all his tomorrows. Therein lies the meaning of the title, "All You Need Is Kill."

In "Edge of Tomorrow," the soldiers fight with mechanical exoskeletons with guns directly attached to their forearms, while the alien "Mimics" resemble writhing, glowing masses of black tentacles. The manga has a similar aesthetic; Takeshi Obata draws the soldier's uniforms resembling Spartan armor from "Halo" (a vibe also seen in "Edge of Tomorrow" concept art), while the Mimics are also depicted as pure black orbs with large, toothy mouths.

The aesthetics of "All You Need Is Kill" are much stranger and more alien. Rita's armor more resembles an astronaut or a deep sea diver's suit, complete with a transparent bubble helmet. The limbs of the armor are also lanky and exaggerated, with digitigrade legs. The suit looks like it was designed for wider reach than a human can manage, but it doesn't scream "armored" or "intimidating" like the manga or "Edge of Tomorrow" suits do. The aliens are also even weirder, resembling giant, mobile flowers with bright purple-green color schemes.

In an interview with Animation Magazine, "All You Need Is Kill" director Kenichiro Akimoto explained he wanted to depict something a bit different than the "space marines blasting aliens" look of past iterations:

"I wanted to depict a colorful, vibrant hell. The thinking behind that was that this time loop repeats the cycle of life and death. Rita needs to live repeatedly, beautifully, as she faces this inevitable death. I wanted to send the message that life can be beautiful — that's the reason for the film's hypersaturated color palette."

The palette does indeed clash with past iterations' violence and brutality, resembling a landscape of imagination more than a warzone. But at its heart, "All You Need Is Kill" is a romance, and the movie's look grows out of that.

#3534. ‘Earthlings in Love’ Review: A Sentimental Sci-fi Journey Makes the Leap from TikTok to the Tokyo International Film Festival

It’s a queasy proposition for cinephiles: Take a TikTok series, retrofit it into a feature film, and premiere it at a major international film festival. But that’s exactly what happened with “Earthlings in Love,” the latest project from Japanese director Shinichiro Ueda. It’s the first so-called “microdrama” (also known as a “vertical drama”) to premiere at the Tokyo International Film Festival, an unusual choice given that in Japan, as abroad, these short-form videos are designed for casual viewing on smartphones, not the formal atmosphere of a film festival. “Earthlings in Love” was originally released in 30 parts on social media, then recut for its TIFF debut; this version is significantly longer, going from a 76-minute runtime to an 102-minute one. It’s also — and this is crucial — much better than anyone might expect, given its provenance. Related Stories Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’ Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place

It’s not terribly surprising that Ueda in particular would be open-minded about working in a new media format: His “One Cut of the Dead” broke out internationally in large part because of its ingenious approach to low-budget storytelling. “Earthlings in Love” is similar in that it takes its limitations and turns them into strengths, thoughtfully incorporating the vertical-video format both into the film’s mise en scene and its structure. It would be disingenuous to say that you forget about the vertical framing after a while — I certainly didn’t — but Ueda makes the most of the tight 9:16 aspect ratio, shooting dialogue scenes from the waist up and composing shots so that they move the eye upwards rather than across the frame.

Even more clever is the way that Ueda, who also wrote the script, incorporates the feeling of claustrophobic disconnection into the story itself. This is a movie about selective memory, centered on a fortysomething film director named Shinpei (Kato Shinsuke) whose career has been prematurely halted by early-onset dementia. Returning to his hometown for the funeral of a former classmate, Shinpei tries to recall why he and his friends never finished their zero-budget high-school sci-fi opus, “Earthlings in Love.” Shinpei remembers a dramatic classmate quitting the shoot because he felt the movie was beneath him, and his secret crush encouraging him to keep going. But is that what really happened?

That’s what we see in the first 20 minutes or so of the movie, as Ueda blends “Rashomon” with “Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind” by having Shinpei consult a service that offers to recover his fading memories by feeding photos and diary entries into an AI-generated recreation of his own past. As we find out, the AI is reflecting Shinpei’s own faulty recollections back to him; Ueda insists that this isn’t a commentary on AI per se, but it does bring to mind the way that LLMs create feedback loops that have led to the pop-psychological phenomenon of AI psychosis. Luckily for him, Shinpei has Nagisa (Kiyose Yaeko), another former classmate with whom he reconnected on his trip back home, to keep him grounded in the present. Her role in Shinpei’s life is unclear at first, not least because he keeps forgetting where he knows her from. Over time, however, she becomes the story’s most tragic figure.

As with “One Cut,” the plot structure of “Earthlings in Love” is built on a series of dramatic twists. This is where Ueda puts the “microdrama” format to its most ingenious use, revisiting moments we’ve already seen from new perspectives that reveal important pieces of information previously left out of the frame. Simply by panning a few feet left or right, Ueda can completely change the narrative and emotional stakes of the film. And the way he applies this technique feels fresh and genuinely innovative, not to mention organic to a potentially offputting new style of storytelling.

The story itself is not as fresh, leaning on themes of high-school nostalgia and missed connections that are common in Japanese popular cinema. However, they’re given an earnest, if sometimes overly sentimental, airing here thanks to Ueda’s personal connection to the material. The director has not been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s, but he was a prolific amateur filmmaker beginning in junior high, and the flashback scenes of “Earthlings in Love” are set in the year 2000, when Ueda was a sophomore in high school. The fact that this ‘00s nostalgia piece was made via a very 2020s model of filmmaking is just further evidence of Udea’s casual formal brilliance.

These scenes are not the only ones that ring true, however, as Kato and Kyose successfully carry the plot through outrageous coincidence and into three-hanky tearjerking. “Earthlings in Love” aches for a lot of things, chief among them the simple joy of creating something with your friends just for the fun of it. Its core message is ironic, given the disposable nature of its initial release: Human memories fade, but movies are forever. Now that it’s a proper film, its lifespan has a better chance of being extended.

“Earthlings in Love” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3532. As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually

Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing expanding California’s current film and television tax credit program from $750 million to at least $1 billion annually as the state is struggling to attract entertainment industry jobs. The move comes as a report last month by FilmLA found that production levels fell 3.7 percent in the third quarter even as California has continued to enhance its tax credits. Many of the major studios and streamers are headquartered in Los Angeles, which makes the contraction in production jobs more painful.

Last year, Gov. Newsom pushed to increase California’s film and TV incentive from $330 million to $750 million annually, and the state’s film commission saw an initial rise in applications before the number of productions began falling again. California is not only grappling with increased competition from states like New Jersey, New York, and Georgia that offer richer incentives, but they are also facing off against foreign production hubs such as the United Kingdom and Hungary. Related Stories ‘Earthlings in Love’ Review: A Sentimental Sci-fi Journey Makes the Leap from TikTok to the Tokyo International Film Festival Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’

In a press release, Gov. Newsom said the proposed expansion would include credits for above-the-line talent, as well as rewards for companies that commit to fielding more than one production in California. If enacted, the tax credit will be extended through 2040, which would give companies more certainty about the incentives they can access. The previous incentives were scheduled to last through 2030. It would also increase independent film funding to $100 million annually, up $26 million from the current program.

“California created the modern entertainment industry; we’re the capital of entertainment and we’re going to keep it here,” Newsom said in a statement. “At least $1 billion in tax credits means more investment flowing into our economy and more opportunity across the industry. Through this expansion, we will maintain the momentum and success of our historic expansion last year.”

The governor also urged national lawmakers to pass a federal film and television incentive, which could augment states’ efforts to bolster local production.

“States can’t shoulder the cost alone, which is why I am calling on Congress to back up an expanded tax credit by passing national film and TV tax credit legislation already on the table,” Newsom said.

#3531. The 6 Most Fun Godzilla Movies of All Time, Ranked

At the time of writing, there is a new Godzilla movie coming out, and so it’s as good an opportunity as any to talk Godzilla. Admittedly, there’s almost always a new Godzilla movie on the horizon, because the series has been very healthy since about 2014. There have been American-produced MonsterVerse films alongside Japanese Godzilla movies, plus that anime trilogy (okay, not great, but still, uh, content for what it’s worth), and then there have also been shows, like Godzilla Singular Point and Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, in case all the movies weren't enough for you.

That Godzilla movie on the horizon, or rapidly approaching at the time of writing, is Godzilla Minus Zero, and it’s been well-received for sure, albeit leaning a bit more toward serious (and horror-focused) territory by the standards of the series, like its predecessor. So, if you're more into Godzilla at its silliest, or if you want a movie that might well contrast with Godzilla Minus Zero, these are the most fun Godzilla movies ever made. It should be stressed they're not necessarily the best, but they're good if you're after something kind of silly (in good ways, of course).

So, it’s one of the goofiest of all the Godzilla movies, and it also came out very early within the history of the whole series: 1962’s King Kong vs. Godzilla. It was the first time the two titular monsters battled, but they would go on to be in a couple more movies together, one of which is going to be mentioned below… not because it’s amazing, but because it is a lot of fun. And King Kong vs. Godzilla is also fun, and unapologetically simple. It gives you what you'd want and expect based on the title, but that smack-down feels a little more impressive in hindsight, arguably, since this was Godzilla’s third time on the big screen, and it also marked the third time King Kong had ever been in a feature film (the first time in nearly 30 years, too).

It's the series in full-on schlock mode; a taste of things to come, because some later Showa era Godzilla movies would really double-down on that kind of thing, for better or worse.

It doubles down on silliness while giving its human characters a particularly minimal number of things to do, and those human parts are awkward for sure, at least at times, but some of the non-monster stuff is funny from a certain point of view. Also, the monster fights are pretty funny, because it’s the series in full-on schlock mode; a taste of things to come, because some later Showa era Godzilla movies would really double-down on that kind of thing, for better or worse. If you like more serious or weighty Godzilla movies, maybe skip this one, but if you want goofy fun, King Kong vs. Godzilla has that in spades.

So, few people are going to call King Kong vs. Godzilla a masterpiece, and then maybe even fewer would be willing to go that far for the similarly-titled Godzilla vs. Kong (2021). It was a long time coming, as a rematch of sorts (only “of sorts” because it’s technically a different continuity and all), and so the fight here might've felt more monumental. Both monsters had been in more than two previous films and all, compared to how grand they were as cinematic icons back in 1962, and both characters had huge legacies that went back either close to 90 years (in King Kong’s case) or almost 70 years (in Godzilla’s case).

As a more modern film, all the battling once more promised in the title was more explosive than what was found in the earlier film. And the fighting was fun! It’s harder to say nicer things about the parts of Godzilla vs. Kong that aren’t focused on action, though thankfully, there also isn't too much of this movie that doesn’t showcase some kind of spectacle, destruction, or fighting. There are two big monsters, and then maybe a third one near the end, and a lot of destruction, so even if it’s brain-dead, it’s the good kind of brain-dead entertainment. Like the cinematic equivalent of binging on potato chips; that sort of thing.

As mentioned before, some of the Showa era Godzilla movies got pretty silly, and Godzilla vs. Megalon is well and truly in that camp, and maybe it is also kind of campy. It feels like it might well have been trying to outdo King Kong vs. Godzilla on that front, and it did a great job in that regard, if that was the case. It manages to look a good deal cheaper, just with all the costumes and sets in this one feeling a little below the standard of the series, yet this does add a certain charm to things. Tonally, this is also comparable to King Kong vs. Godzilla, but maybe even a little more kid-friendly, seeing as one of the main characters in this film is a kid, and then there’s also a robot in this called Jet Jaguar who ends up (eventually) fighting alongside Godzilla.

The titular Megalon is also a potentially underrated villain, and then there’s also some Gigan as well, and he’s pretty much always welcome. Narratively, it’s fairly standard stuff, since there are aliens that want to take over the world, and their plan does involve monsters, and so Godzilla – plus Jet Jaguar – have to stop them. Honestly, Jet Jaguar comes close to stealing the movie from Godzilla, and he would've earned the right to be in the title if they wanted to throw him in there. “Wouldn’t that be too crowded, having Godzilla, Jet Jaguar, and Megalon with their names in one title?” you might ask. Nope… not in a series where one of the best entries is literally called “Godzilla, Mothra and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack.”

If you like Godzilla movies that throw even more monsters into the mix than Godzilla vs. Megalon and Godzilla, Mothra and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack, then Destroy All Monsters is probably going to be your cup of tea. Or your cups of tea, because uh, if the monsters are tea, you're going to need several cups of a fairly large size to hold all the tea. Or hold all the monsters. Like, this one rounds up most of the usual suspects up until that point in the series in spectacular fashion, being a big celebration of all that had come before, and also done in a way where Destroy All Monsters could well have been like a finale for the entire series.

Like, you know how there are shows like Seinfeld that, for better or worse, bring back a bunch of one-off or recurring characters and shove them in that one final episode? That’s what Destroy All Monsters does, both thanks to its story being about monsters being released by aliens (those pesky alien invaders again) to rampage around and weaken the world, and then also thanks to the battle at the end, which gets all the monsters in the one space for a big fight. There’s absolutely nothing deep, but it’s a blast, and none of it’s trying to be thought-provoking or anything, so you'd probably have to be in a fairly bad mood before watching to not get any kind of enjoyment out of this one.

Gonzo, silly, ridiculous, or over-the-top… pick one of those words, or another kind of similar one, and you’ve probably got a decent one to use to summarize Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah, which is the movie in the series that famously, or maybe infamously, uses time travel. Actually, for a third option, it might not be famous or infamous, since Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah is kind of a deep-cut by most standards, known by fans of the series, of course, but probably not the kind of Godzilla movie you might hope a few non-fans might well have caught at some point (they're probably more likely to have seen a Godzilla movie with a slightly more serious tone, in all honesty).

In Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah, the human race is given a chance to go back in time and stop Godzilla before he gets too powerful, and they do, but the group of people who passed such technology onto them (unsurprisingly) have other motives, and things get complicated the way they always do in time travel movies. This is probably the most fun Godzilla movie that does touch upon some slightly serious themes at points, because World War II is quite relevant to Godzilla’s past. It’s handy if you want to “Well, actually” someone who says Godzilla Minus One is the furthest a Godzilla movie has gone back in time, because yes, that one did play out shortly after the end of World War II, but part of Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah technically goes back to during World War II, so do with that information what you will.

And yet for as maximalist as Destroy All Monsters and Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah were willing to get, it’s Godzilla: Final Wars that ends up getting the wildest and most over-the-top in nature. But it’s worth bringing up Destroy All Monsters again, because the premise is basically the same, but there are more monsters this time around, with the series celebrating 50 years with Godzilla: Final Wars. There are more foes to bring back, and also, it shares with Destroy All Monsters the feeling that it could well have worked as a finale for the entire Godzilla series, had they chosen to end it here.

A difference, though, is that Godzilla: Final Wars has a lot of action even without the expected kaiju stuff, since this might well be the silliest Godzilla movie on a human character front (they get action scenes without monsters and all). It is, undoubtedly, one of the most chaotic giant monster movies of all time, and if you have a particular craving to just watch something noisy, amusing, and absolutely brainless for a couple of hours, Godzilla: Final Wars is the Godzilla movie that you're looking for. It might technically get better than this, if you're looking at the more high-quality and “important” Godzilla movies, but it might not actually get any more entertaining than this.

Merritt Grove was most likely privy to the information that Kate and Foreign Secretary Dennison found out at The Diplomat season 1 ending, hence why he stressed the urgency of meeting with Kate. Grove probably figured he could offer Hal the sensitive information he was aware of, who then could transfer it to Kate.

The car bomb that killed him was blamed on Iraqi terrorists who looked to disrupt the government.

Grove was killed by Trowbirdge to cover his tracks, but Dennison could actually know much more about Lenkov than he's telling Kate.

Merritt Grove going around his own government to reach out suggests everyone on Trowbridge's side was always aware of his motivations, including Roylin and Dennison. It was unclear when season 1 ended but Stuart and Hal both managed to make it out of the explosive alive, ensuring Kate had some allies in season 2.

Merritt Grove's death means that he's not really in The Diplomat season 2 but as expected, the explosion set the stage for some major story aspects. Season 2 picks up immediately after the explosion, which led to many theories and was used by the Conservative government to frame Iran as the attackers. The idea was to gain influence on the British citizens through fear and distract them from tensions within the government.

There was also the hint that Grove was planning to share crucial information that would've put him at odds with Hal and fellow members of his party. It was also implied that Grove's death stemmed from a call Kate put in asking about him, setting the events in motion. Grove's death was actually very convenient for those in power, making it unclear at first who was behind it.

Ultimately, The Diplomat revealed that Margaret Roylin was behind both the explosion and the HMS Courageous attack. First, she enlisted Merritt Grove to hire Roman Lenkov, a Russian mercenary, to attack the HMS Courageous. When it was discovered that Grove was planning to speak with Hal about the false flag operation, Roylin acted again. She got Lenny Stendig to set up the car bomb that ultimately killed Grove out of fear that the Americans would learn everything about the HMS Courageous attack. Roylin says it was all about saving the kingdom. Scotland's secession movement had been picking up, and the conspirators needed a tragedy to bring the UK together. Trowbridge had no knowledge of the plot, and the only ones in on the plan were Grove, Roylin and far-right MP Lenny Stendig.

#3526. Why the Holidays Are Actually the Best Time of Year to Start Working Out

If you have even the tiniest inkling that you might want to get in shape in the new year—or anytime really—don’t wait until January. This isn't a "winter arc" self-improvement pitch; it's just facts. The best time to start a gym habit is before the holiday season. Heck, in December, you’ll even have the place mostly to yourself.

Sure, technically “right now” is always the best time to start exercising, but the holiday season is special. If you wait until January, gyms will be packed. The first two weeks of the year, everybody thinks they’re at the start of an amazing new fitness habit...and by February, most of them have forgotten all about it. Don’t make life harder for yourself by starting during the big rush. Classes will fill up, you’ll have to fight people for the squat rack, and it will be hard to have any real fun. So start now.

In October and November, gyms and classes are at more or less their normal capacities. This is a good time to feel out the vibe of a new place. But it gets better: Once December rolls around, the fair-weather gymgoers will be off shopping for gifts after work and attending holiday parties on the weekends. They won’t feel like getting out of their warm beds in the morning, either. When you arrive, the squat rack will be free. You’ll have your choice of treadmills. The gym will be your oyster.

If you start now, you'll have about two months to get up to speed before the rush starts in January. And that is a perfect little time frame to set a small goal and keep it. Vow to hit the gym three times a week, and you’ll be able to get in 24 workouts before Christmas, even if you take a few days off for festivities. You can get a lot stronger in 24 workouts. Or run, if that's the fitness journey you're most excited about. If you start a couch-to-5k running plan now, you’ll be routinely running 30 minutes at a stretch by the time we get to January.

Yes, the holiday season can be busy and stressful, but remember that working out tends to help our brains manage stress. Mark workouts on your calendar, and keep those appointments with yourself.

Don’t worry about missing out on deals. Any gym or studio that offers a January special probably offers sales year-round anyway. And ultimately, if you get into the habit of actually using the gym, you're getting a lot more value for your money than somebody who joins in January and quickly stops showing up.
